questions.stem: What is the purpose of providing waterproof tiles?
questions.solution:
**Prevents water from entering.**

A waterproof tile finish acts as a **barrier against water penetration**. Left unprotected, moisture seeps through the surface into the screed and the structural slab beneath, and the consequences accumulate: efflorescence and staining, softening of plaster, fungal growth, corrosion of the reinforcement, and eventual spalling of the concrete.

Waterproof tiling is therefore used wherever water is present continuously or repeatedly — **toilets, bathrooms, kitchens, terraces and flat roofs, water tanks and swimming pools**.

Why the other options fail. A smooth surface (b) and some sound damping (c) may be incidental properties of a tiled finish, but neither is the reason for specifying a *waterproof* tile. Fire resistance (a) is a property of the ceramic body, not of the waterproofing.

**How the waterproofing is actually achieved**, since the tile alone is never sufficient:
- A **waterproof membrane** — bituminous, polymer or cementitious — laid below the tile bedding.
- **Waterproofing admixtures** in the screed and bedding mortar.
- Tile joints filled with **epoxy or waterproof grout** rather than plain cement, because the joints are the weak path.
- Adequate **slope to the outlet** (about 1 in 100 on a terrace) so water is shed rather than ponded, and the membrane **turned up at the perimeter** and around every penetration.

The general principle across all such work: **water is excluded by a continuous system, not by a single product.** The same logic governs the damp proof course, which stops water rising from the ground rather than falling from above.

examTip.trick: Waterproof tiles solve a **water exclusion** problem, not a structural or aesthetic one. Their purpose is to keep water out of the layers below.
examTip.mnemonic: **Waterproofing works only if it is CONTINUOUS** — the tile itself is impervious, but the joints and the upturns at the edges are where water actually gets in. Detail the perimeter, or the tiles are decoration.

questions.stem: Commonly used steel section for columns is:
questions.solution:
**ISSC** — Indian Standard Steel Column section.

The designation says what the section is *for*, and that is the whole of the question. **ISSC** sections are proportioned specifically as compression members: they are relatively **wide-flanged and stocky**, so the radii of gyration about the two principal axes are more nearly equal. A column can buckle about either axis, so the efficient section is one with no markedly weak direction.

The rolled section families and their intended duty:

| Designation | Full name | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **ISSC** | Indian Standard Steel **Column** | **Columns** — balanced radii of gyration |
| ISMB | Indian Standard Medium **Beam** | **Beams** — deep, high Z about the strong axis |
| ISLB | Indian Standard Light Beam | Light beams, purlins |
| ISHB | Indian Standard Heavy Beam | Heavy beams and, in practice, many columns |
| **ISWB** | Indian Standard Wide-flange Beam | Beams; also used for columns |
| ISA / ISJC | Angles / Junior Channel | Bracing, trusses, light members |

**Why a beam section is a poor column.** An ISMB is deliberately deep and narrow to maximise the section modulus about the axis of bending. That same shape gives it a very small radius of gyration about the minor axis, so as a column it would buckle early about the weak axis unless laterally braced. The slenderness ratio λ = l_{e}/r_{min} is governed by the **smaller** r, and IS 800 caps it at 180 for a member carrying dead and live load.

In practice a column may also be **built up** — two channels laid back to back or toe to toe, or a plated I-section — precisely to equalise the two radii of gyration and to suit heavier loads than a single rolled section can carry.

examTip.trick: Column sections need a **large radius of gyration about BOTH axes**, because a column can buckle either way. A deep narrow I-beam is very weak about its minor axis.
examTip.mnemonic: **Beams are deep and narrow (bending about ONE axis); columns are square-ish (buckling about BOTH).** That is why beam sections and column sections look so different — and why a section chosen for its beam properties makes a poor column.

questions.stem: When condensation takes place below freezing point it is known as:
questions.solution:
**Frost.**

Water vapour in the air condenses when the surface it touches falls to the dew point. **Which form** the condensate takes depends on whether that temperature is above or below freezing:

| Dew point | Condensate |
|---|---|
| **Above 0°C** | **Dew** — liquid droplets |
| **Below 0°C** | **Frost** — ice crystals, formed by direct deposition |

So frost is the **solid** form of condensation: the vapour passes straight to ice without an intermediate liquid stage (deposition), forming the familiar feathery crystals on grass, glass and metal surfaces on a clear cold night.

The other options are all suspensions of droplets in the **air**, not deposits on a surface, and are distinguished by what they are made of and how far you can see through them:

| Phenomenon | Composed of | Visibility |
|---|---|---|
| **Fog** | Water droplets suspended in air | **< 1 km** |
| **Mist** | Water droplets, thinner | 1 – 2 km |
| **Haze** | **Dry dust, smoke, salt particles** — not water | Reduced, but not by condensation |

Note that haze is the odd one out entirely: it is **not** condensation at all.

**Why frost matters in civil engineering**, which is why this sits in the hydrology and meteorology syllabus:
- **Frost heave** — water freezing in the subgrade expands about 9%, lifting the pavement; on thawing the soil is left saturated and weak, causing failure. It is countered by placing a granular, non-frost-susceptible sub-base and by lowering the water table.
- **Frost action on concrete and masonry** — repeated freeze–thaw cycling spalls the surface, which is what the **soundness test** on aggregate (Q23 of this paper) is designed to screen for.
- Frost damage to crops and to exposed water mains in hill districts.

The companion question in this paper, Q67, asks the same fact from the other side: with a dew point **above** 0°C, **dew** forms.

examTip.trick: Condensation **above** freezing gives **dew**; condensation **below** freezing gives **frost** — water vapour goes directly to ice.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dew above zero, frost below.** In pavement and foundation engineering the concern is **frost heave**, where capillary water is drawn up to a growing ice lens. **Silt is the most frost-susceptible soil** — enough capillary rise AND enough permeability to feed the lens.

questions.stem: In engineering drawing, a centre line is represented by a:
questions.solution:
**A thin chain line** — long dashes alternating with short dashes or dots.

A chain line is instantly distinguishable from every other line on a drawing, which is exactly why it is reserved for axes and centres: the reader must never mistake an axis of symmetry for a real edge of the object.

The line types of IS 10714, and what each means:

| Line | Use |
|---|---|
| **Continuous thick** | **Visible outlines and edges** |
| Continuous thin | Dimension lines, extension lines, hatching, leader lines |
| Continuous thin freehand / zigzag | **Break lines** — limits of a partial view |
| **Dashed (thin or thick)** | **Hidden edges and outlines** |
| **Thin chain** | **Centre lines, axes of symmetry, pitch circles** |
| Thin chain, **thick at ends and at changes of direction** | **Cutting plane** for a section |
| Thick chain | Surfaces requiring special treatment |
| Thin chain double-dashed | Adjacent parts, outlines of alternative positions |

Two conventions on centre lines that are examined alongside: they should **extend a short distance beyond** the feature they locate, and a **long dash** — never a short one or a gap — should fall at each end and at every intersection, so the crossing point of two centre lines is unambiguous.

Line **thickness** follows a √2 ratio, with thick lines typically twice the width of thin ones (commonly 0.7 mm against 0.35 mm), so the hierarchy stays legible after reproduction.

**A note on the printed question.** The original asked "Symbol for Center line is?" with the four options given only as the letters a, b, c and d, referring to a figure of line types that the source scan does not reproduce. The answer key shows that figure as a table of nine standard lines and keys option (b). Because the figure is unavailable, the stem has been rewritten here as an equivalent text question testing the same fact — that a centre line is a thin chain line — so the item remains answerable and useful.

verification.notes: The printed question referred to a figure of line types with options given only as bare letters a-d; that figure is not in the source scan. The answer key's own table identifies the keyed option as the thin chain line. The stem has been rewritten as a text question testing the same fact so the item is answerable without the missing figure.

examTip.trick: Line conventions carry meaning: **continuous thick** for visible outlines, **dashed** for hidden edges, **thin chain (long-short)** for centre lines and axes, **thick chain** for cutting planes.
examTip.mnemonic: **Chain line = centre line.** A centre line should **cross at the centre with the long dashes**, not the gaps — a small convention that a marker will notice.

questions.stem: Channelized depressions that form along the wheel track of a flexible pavement are called:
questions.solution:
**Rutting.**

A rut is a **longitudinal depression in the wheel path** — a permanent deformation accumulated under repeated passes of traffic, always following the tracks the wheels actually take rather than the width of the carriageway.

**Mechanism.** Each axle pass produces a small permanent strain. Where a layer is under-compacted, or the mix has insufficient stability, those strains do not recover, and they add up over thousands of repetitions into a visible channel. The deficiency can lie anywhere in the structure — surfacing, base, sub-base or subgrade.

Causes, in rough order of importance: **inadequate compaction** of one or more layers; excess bitumen or too soft a grade for the climate; low Marshall stability in the mix; overloaded axles; high pavement temperature; and a weak or saturated subgrade.

**Why ruts are dangerous, not merely unsightly:** they hold water, so a vehicle can **aquaplane**, and they make the steering pull. They also concentrate further loading in the same track, so the distress accelerates once started.

Distinguish the neighbouring distresses, which the options name:

| Distress | Appearance | Main cause |
|---|---|---|
| **Rutting** | **Longitudinal depression in the wheel path** | **Inadequate compaction; permanent deformation** |
| Longitudinal cracking | Cracks parallel to the centre line | Poor joint construction, differential settlement |
| Shear failure | Localised depression with upheaval alongside | Very weak pavement against a heavy load |
| **Bleeding** | **Shiny, sticky film of binder on the surface** | **Excess bitumen**, low void content, hot weather |

Maintenance depends on the cause: a shallow rut confined to the surfacing can be milled and overlaid, but a rut originating in the subgrade needs reconstruction, because an overlay over a weak foundation simply ruts again.

**A note on the printed question.** The original read "Which failure is shown in figure" and depended on a photograph absent from the source scan; the key answers (b), rutting. The stem has been rewritten here as an equivalent text question describing the same distress, so the item is answerable without the missing figure.

verification.notes: The printed question showed a figure of a pavement failure, absent from the source scan, with options a-d. The key answers rutting and its explanation describes 'channelized depressions, particularly in the wheel track'. The stem has been rewritten to state that description directly so the item is answerable.

examTip.trick: **Rutting** is a **deformation** failure: permanent longitudinal depressions in the wheel paths, from accumulated plastic strain in the layers or subgrade.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rutting = too soft or under-compacted. Cracking = too brittle (fatigue or ageing).** The two failure families need opposite remedies, so diagnosing which one you have is the first step in any pavement investigation.

questions.stem: If the total lost time is 10 sec and the sum of the ratios of normal flow to saturation flow for two directional traffic is 0.6, then the optimal cycle length is:
questions.solution:
**50 seconds.**

**Webster's formula** for the optimum cycle length — the one that minimises total vehicle delay at a signalised intersection:

> C_{o} = (1.5 L + 5) / (1 − Y)

where L is the total lost time per cycle in seconds and Y the sum, over all phases, of the ratio of normal flow to saturation flow.

**Substituting L = 10 s and Y = 0.60:**
> C_{o} = (1.5 × 10 + 5)/(1 − 0.60)
> C_{o} = (15 + 5)/0.40
> C_{o} = 20/0.40 = **50 seconds**

**The terms in more detail:**
- **Lost time** L = 2n + R, where n is the number of phases and R the all-red time. It is the part of each cycle during which no useful flow occurs — start-up delay and clearance.
- **Y** = Σ(q/s), each term being that phase's design flow divided by its saturation flow.

**The critical feature of the formula** is the (1 − Y) in the denominator. As Y approaches 1, the cycle length **tends to infinity** — the intersection is saturated and no signal setting can clear the demand. In practice **Y must stay below about 0.85 to 0.9**; beyond that, the geometry itself has to change (extra lanes, channelisation, a flyover or a roundabout), not the signal timing.

Practical cycle lengths run from about **40 to 120 seconds**. Too short a cycle wastes a large proportion of time on lost time; too long a cycle imposes excessive delay on stopped vehicles.

Once C_{o} is known, the **green time** for each phase is apportioned in the ratio of the y-values:
> G_{i} = (y_{i}/Y) × (C_{o} − L)

examTip.trick: **Webster's optimum cycle: C₀ = (1.5L + 5)/(1 − Y)**, where L is the total lost time and Y the sum of the critical flow ratios. Substituting L = 10 and Y = 0.6: (15 + 5)/0.4 = **50 s** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **As Y approaches 1 the cycle time goes to infinity** — the intersection is saturated and no signal setting can clear it. That is the mathematical statement of a junction that has run out of capacity, and the answer then is geometry, not timing.

questions.stem: What is the meaning of SC in soil classification?
questions.solution:
**Sand with plastic fines** — that is, clayey sand.

The Unified Soil Classification System uses a **two-letter** group symbol. The first letter names the dominant fraction, the second describes its gradation or plasticity:

| First letter — major fraction | | Second letter — gradation / plasticity | |
|---|---|---|---|
| **G** | Gravel | **W** | Well graded |
| **S** | **Sand** | **P** | Poorly graded |
| **M** | Silt | **M** | With silty (non-plastic) fines |
| **C** | Clay | **C** | **With clayey (plastic) fines** |
| **O** | Organic | **L** | Low plasticity (LL < 50) |
| **Pt** | Peat | **H** | High plasticity (LL > 50) |

So **S** = sand and **C** = clayey fines, giving **sand with plastic fines**.

The distinction that matters, and which option (c) is placed to catch: the second letter separates **SC from SM**.

| Symbol | Fines | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **SC** | **Clayey — plastic**, plots **above** the A-line | Cohesive, low permeability |
| **SM** | **Silty — non-plastic**, plots **below** the A-line | Little cohesion, more permeable |

The test that decides between them is the **plasticity chart**, using the A-line PI = 0.73(LL − 20).

A coarse-grained soil is one with **more than 50% retained on the 75 μm sieve**, and it is then classified on how much passes:
- **Fines < 5%** → gradation governs: SW or SP, judged by C_{u} and C_{c}.
- **Fines > 12%** → plasticity governs: **SC or SM**.
- **Fines 5–12%** → borderline, given a **dual symbol** such as SW-SC.

Examples of the family: **GW** well-graded gravel, **SP** poorly graded sand, **CL** low-plasticity clay, **CH** high-plasticity (fat) clay, **ML** low-plasticity silt.

examTip.trick: Unified/IS symbols are read **letter by letter**: first letter the **major** fraction (**S** sand, **G** gravel, **M** silt, **C** clay, **O** organic), second the **qualifier** (**W** well graded, **P** poorly graded, **M** silty fines, **C** clayey/plastic fines).
examTip.mnemonic: **SC = Sand with Clayey (plastic) fines; SM = Sand with silty fines.** For fine soils the second letter is the plasticity: **L** low (LL < 35), **I** intermediate (35–50), **H** high (> 50). So **CH** is a fat clay and **ML** a low-plasticity silt.

questions.stem: The formula for area ratio of a soil sampler is:
questions.solution:
**A_r = [(D₂² − D₁²)/D₁²] × 100**, where D₁ is the **inner** and D₂ the **outer** diameter of the cutting edge.

The ratio measures how much soil the sampling tube must displace relative to the volume of sample it recovers. The numerator (D₂² − D₁²) is proportional to the **cross-sectional area of the tube wall** — the metal that has to push soil aside — and the denominator D₁² is proportional to the **area of the sample** collected.

**Two checks settle the answer without recalling the formula.**

*Sign.* Since D₂ > D₁ always, any expression with (D₁² − D₂²) in the numerator is **negative**. An area ratio cannot be negative, so options (a) and (d) are impossible on inspection.

*Denominator.* The ratio is defined against the **sample** recovered, so the denominator must be D₁², the inner area. That eliminates (c) and leaves **(b)**.

**Why it matters.** The displaced soil is forced sideways and compresses the surrounding ground, and some drags into the tube along the walls, remoulding the specimen:

| Sampler | Area ratio | Sample |
|---|---|---|
| **Thin-walled Shelby tube** | **≈ 10%** | **Undisturbed** — fit for strength and consolidation tests |
| **Split-spoon (SPT)** | **≈ 110%** | **Disturbed** — classification and index tests only |

So **A_r ≤ 10%** is the requirement for undisturbed sampling, with up to 20% accepted for stiff soils. The companion ratios are **inside clearance** (D₃ − D₁)/D₁ of 0.5 to 3%, and **outside clearance** (D₂ − D₄)/D₄ of 0 to 2%.

**Correction to the circulating key.** The answer sheet keys (a), but its own explanation immediately beneath prints (D₂² − D₁²)/D₁² — which is option (b), not (a). Option (a) would give a negative area ratio and is impossible. The answer is (b).

verification.notes: The circulating key answers (a), but the explanation printed directly beneath it gives (D2²−D1²)/D1² — option (b). Since D2 > D1 always, option (a) yields a negative area ratio, which is impossible. Answer corrected to (b).

examTip.trick: **A_r = (D_o² − D_i²)/D_i² × 100** — the ratio of the soil the sampler wall **displaces** to the soil it **collects**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Under 10% for undisturbed sampling.** A thin-walled Shelby tube achieves it; a **split spoon is around 100%**, which is exactly why an SPT sample is a **disturbed** sample and can never be used for a strength or consolidation test.

questions.stem: Compaction depends on:
questions.solution:
**All of the above.**

Field compaction is the product of how much energy is delivered to the layer and how well that energy is transmitted, and each option controls part of it:

- **Number of passes** — density rises with each pass, steeply at first and then with diminishing returns. Beyond about 8 to 10 passes little further gain is achieved, and over-rolling can begin to break down the aggregate.
- **Weight of roller** — a heavier machine applies greater contact pressure and its influence reaches deeper into the layer.
- **Speed of roller** — the roller must be slow enough for the load to act on each point for long enough. Rolling too fast leaves the layer under-compacted; **2 to 5 km/h** is the usual range.

Since all three govern the result, (d) is the answer.

The other factors that belong on the same list, and are examined alongside:

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Moisture content** | The most important of all — maximum dry density is reached only at the **optimum moisture content** |
| Compactive effort | Higher energy raises the maximum dry density **and lowers** the OMC |
| **Layer thickness** | 150–300 mm loose; a thicker layer will not compact at the bottom |
| Soil type | Well-graded coarse soils reach higher densities than uniform or highly plastic soils |
| Type of roller | **Vibration** for cohesionless soils, **kneading** for cohesive ones |

**The moisture point deserves emphasis** because it dominates everything else. The Proctor test (IS 2720 Parts 7 and 8) establishes the OMC and the maximum dry density in the laboratory; field compaction is then specified as a percentage of that value — typically **95% of MDD** for a subgrade and 98% for a base course — and verified by the core cutter or sand replacement method.

Rolling a soil far from its OMC wastes effort entirely: too dry and the particles will not slip past one another, too wet and the pore water cannot escape fast enough to let them.

examTip.trap: "All of the above" rewards reading every option. Compaction genuinely depends on the water content, the compactive effort, the soil type and the method.
examTip.trick: Two of these have a systematic effect worth knowing: **more compactive energy pushes the curve UP and to the LEFT** (higher dry density at a lower optimum moisture content).
examTip.mnemonic: **More energy: higher and drier.** Standard Proctor to modified Proctor is a 4.5-fold increase in energy, and every compaction curve shifts that way.

questions.stem: C_m is also called:
questions.solution:
**Applied shear stress** — the **mobilised cohesion**.

> C_{m} = c / F_{c}

where c is the soil's available cohesion and F_{c} the factor of safety with respect to cohesion.

The distinction is between what the soil **can** provide and what is actually **being called upon**:

| Quantity | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **c** — cohesion | The soil's **available** strength, a material property from the shear test |
| **C_m** — mobilised cohesion | The portion **actually being used** to resist the applied loading |

Because C_{m} is the part of the strength actually engaged, it equals the **shear stress the soil is being asked to carry** — hence "applied shear stress". Option (a) names the total available cohesion, and option (d) the total shear strength; both are what C_{m} is divided *out of*, not what it is.

**Where the concept is used.** Slope stability analysis by the **friction circle** and φ_{u} = 0 methods works in terms of mobilised strength. The factor of safety can be defined separately for each component:

> F_{c} = c/c_{m}  and  F_{φ} = tan φ / tan φ_{m}

and when the two are made equal the common value is the **factor of safety with respect to strength**:

> F_{s} = (c + σ′ tan φ)/(c_{m} + σ′ tan φ_{m})

A slope is stable when the mobilised strength required for equilibrium is comfortably less than the available strength — with F_{s} of about **1.4 for a permanent slope** and 1.25 for a temporary one.

The related term worth pairing with this is **Taylor's stability number**, S_{n} = C_{m}/(γH), which is precisely mobilised cohesion normalised by unit weight and slope height, and is read from charts against slope angle and φ.

examTip.trick: Read what the symbol represents in the mobilised-strength context — the shear stress actually **applied**, as distinct from the shear **strength** available.
examTip.mnemonic: **Factor of safety = strength AVAILABLE ÷ stress APPLIED.** Keeping those two apart is the whole of stability analysis: the soil's strength does not change with the loading, but the demand on it does.

questions.stem: The active earth pressure of a soil is defined as the lateral pressure exerted by soil:
options: When the retaining wall has no movement relative to the back fill
When the retaining wall tends to move away from the back fill
When the retaining wall moves into the soil
questions.solution:
**When the retaining wall tends to move away from the backfill.**

The direction of wall movement decides which pressure state develops, and this is the whole content of the question:

| Wall movement | State | Coefficient (φ = 30°) | Soil is |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Away from the backfill** | **Active** | **K_a = (1−sin φ)/(1+sin φ) = 1/3** | **Pushing the wall** — soil expands laterally |
| No movement | **At rest** | K_o = 1 − sin φ = 0.5 | In its undisturbed state |
| **Into the soil** | **Passive** | K_p = (1+sin φ)/(1−sin φ) = 3 | **Resisting the wall** — soil compressed laterally |

So **active** is the case where the soil is the *driving* force. As the wall yields outward, the soil behind it expands horizontally, the lateral stress **falls**, and the soil approaches failure with the major principal stress vertical. That minimum lateral pressure is the active pressure — and it is what a retaining wall must be designed to resist.

**Passive** is the reverse: the wall is forced into the soil, the lateral stress **rises** to a maximum, and the soil fails with the major principal stress horizontal. Passive resistance is what holds the toe of a sheet pile or the front of a footing in place.

Note the ordering, always: **K_a < K_o < K_p**, and K_p = 1/K_a.

**The resulting thrust** on a wall of height H in cohesionless backfill:
> P_{a} = ½ K_{a} γ H², acting at **H/3 above the base**

**A practical point examined alongside.** The movement required to develop full active pressure is very small — of the order of **0.1 to 0.5% of the wall height** — so active conditions arise in almost any real wall. Full **passive** resistance, by contrast, needs movement of **2 to 5%** of the height, which is often more than the structure can tolerate; passive resistance is therefore usually reduced by a factor of safety before being relied upon.

examTip.trick: The three states are decided entirely by **movement**: wall moves **AWAY** from the soil → **active** (soil expands, pressure falls to a minimum); wall moves **INTO** the soil → **passive** (maximum); **no movement** → **at rest**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Active is the MINIMUM pressure and needs only 0.1–0.4% of H to mobilise; passive is the MAXIMUM and needs 2–5% of H.** That asymmetry is why passive resistance in front of a wall is usually ignored — it arrives too late to help.

questions.stem: Mat foundation is provided when:
options: Heavy load has to be transferred
Isolated footing covers more than 50% area
questions.solution:
**All of the above** — the three conditions usually arrive together.

A mat (raft) is a single large slab covering most or all of the plan area, carrying every column and wall as one unit. It becomes the right choice when:

- **The soil is weak or compressible.** Spreading the load over the whole footprint keeps the bearing pressure low enough for the ground to carry, and the raft's stiffness distributes it.
- **Isolated footings would cover more than about 50% of the plan area.** Once individual footings grow that large they nearly touch, and the excavation, formwork and reinforcement of one continuous slab costs less than many separate ones. This is the standard economic rule of thumb.
- **Column loads are heavy**, so the required area per column is large — which is simply the same condition arriving from the loading side rather than the soil side.

They are not independent tests but three symptoms of one situation, so (d) is the answer.

The further reasons a raft is chosen:

| Reason | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Reduce differential settlement** | The raft's flexural stiffness makes the structure settle more nearly uniformly |
| Erratic soil, soft pockets | The slab **bridges** local weakness |
| Basement below the water table | A continuous slab resists **uplift and buoyancy**, and can be made watertight |
| **Compensated (floating) foundation** | Weight of excavated soil offsets the building weight, so the **net** pressure increase — and hence settlement — is small or zero |

Types: flat plate; plate thickened under columns; **beam-and-slab**; cellular; and pile-supported raft, which combines shallow and deep action.

Despite its size a raft remains a **shallow** foundation, since its depth of embedment is small relative to its width — the point tested directly in Set 2 Q44.

examTip.trap: "All of the above" again — read every option. A mat suits low bearing capacity, large loaded area, closely spaced heavy columns, and where differential settlement must be controlled.
examTip.trick: The economic threshold: a raft pays when individual footings would cover **more than about half the plan area**.
examTip.mnemonic: **A raft SPREADS the load and TIES the structure together** — the second benefit, cutting **differential** settlement, is often the decisive one, because differential movement is what cracks buildings, not total settlement.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an assumption of Terzaghi's bearing capacity theory?
options: Base of the footing is smooth
Depth of foundation is less than or equal to its width
Load applied is vertical and non-eccentric
questions.solution:
**"Base of the footing is smooth" is the incorrect statement** — Terzaghi assumes the base is **rough**.

The roughness assumption is not incidental; it is central to the whole analysis. A rough base prevents the soil immediately beneath the footing from spreading laterally, so that wedge of soil moves **down with the footing as a rigid body** rather than shearing along its underside. That trapped elastic wedge is what generates the radial shear and Rankine passive zones from which the bearing capacity factors are derived. Assume a smooth base and the failure mechanism — and the factors — would be quite different.

**Terzaghi's full set of assumptions:**
- The soil is **homogeneous, isotropic and weightless** for the purposes of the shear-strength analysis.
- The footing is **shallow**, D_{f} ≤ B.
- The footing is a **strip** (continuous), B/L → 0; shape factors are applied afterwards for square and circular footings.
- The **base of the footing is rough**.
- The failure surface is as assumed, and failure occurs as **general shear**.
- The ground surface is **horizontal**.
- The load is **vertical, concentric and symmetric**.
- The failure zone does not extend above the base of the foundation.
- The **shear resistance of the soil above the base is neglected** — the overburden is treated as a surcharge only.

The resulting equation, for a strip footing:
> q_{u} = cN_{c} + γD_{f}N_{q} + 0.5γBN_{γ}

with N_{c} = 5.7, N_{q} = 1 and N_{γ} = 0 at φ = 0.

**Where the assumptions break down**, which is why later theories exist: **Meyerhof** allows for inclined and eccentric loading, footing shape and depth, and the shear strength of the overburden; **Skempton** refines N_{c} for clay with depth; **Vesic** and **Hansen** give further factors. And in loose sand or soft clay, failure occurs as **local or punching shear** rather than the general shear Terzaghi assumes, so his equation over-estimates capacity there.

examTip.trap: Read the **NOT**. Terzaghi assumed the base is **ROUGH**, not smooth — the roughness is what traps the elastic wedge beneath the footing and gives N_c = 5.7 rather than Prandtl's smooth-base 5.14.
examTip.trick: Terzaghi's real assumptions: **strip footing, shallow (D_f ≤ B), general shear failure, homogeneous soil, ROUGH base, soil above founding level treated as surcharge only, vertical concentric load.**
examTip.mnemonic: **Rough base is Terzaghi's 5.7; smooth base is Prandtl's 5.14.** The difference between the two numbers IS the base assumption.

questions.stem: Relative compaction is given by:
questions.solution:
**RC = γ_d / γ_dmax**, usually expressed as a percentage.

Relative compaction compares the dry unit weight **achieved in the field** with the **maximum dry unit weight** obtained in the laboratory Proctor test on the same soil. It is the standard measure of how well a fill has been compacted, and it is what a specification calls for:

| Layer | Typical requirement |
|---|---|
| Embankment / subgrade | **95% of MDD** (Standard Proctor) |
| Sub-base and base course | 98 – 100% of MDD (Modified Proctor) |
| Earth dam core | 95 – 98%, at controlled moisture content |

Because the field value can never exceed the laboratory maximum by much, RC is at most a little above 100%, and the ratio must have γ_dmax in the **denominator** — which disposes of option (a), an inverted expression that would fall below 1 as compaction improved.

**Do not confuse relative compaction with relative density**, which the γ_dmin in option (b) is drawn from. They are different quantities applied to different soils:

| | **Relative compaction** | **Relative density (density index)** |
|---|---|---|
| Formula | **γ_d/γ_dmax** | **(e_max − e)/(e_max − e_min)** |
| Reference | Laboratory **Proctor** MDD | **Loosest and densest** attainable states |
| Applies to | **All soils**, especially cohesive fills | **Cohesionless** soils — sands and gravels |
| Range | ~90 – 100% | 0% (loosest) to 100% (densest) |

Relative density classifies a sand as very loose (0–15%), loose (15–35%), medium (35–65%), dense (65–85%) or very dense (85–100%), and correlates with the SPT N-value and the angle of internal friction.

**Field measurement of γ_d** for the RC calculation is by the **core cutter** method (cohesive soils), **sand replacement** (any soil), or a nuclear density gauge; the moisture content is determined at the same time, since compaction must be checked at close to the OMC to be meaningful.

examTip.trap: **Relative COMPACTION** (a percentage of maximum dry density, from the Proctor test) is different from **relative DENSITY / density index** (from e_max and e_min, for cohesionless soil). The names are nearly identical and the quantities are not.
examTip.trick: Relative compaction is a **field control** figure — typically 95–100% of the laboratory maximum is specified.
examTip.mnemonic: **Relative compaction = γ_d/γ_dmax (any soil, field control). Relative density = (e_max − e)/(e_max − e_min) (cohesionless only).** Note relative compaction is never zero — even loose soil has some density.

questions.stem: Which of the following water is usable to plants?
questions.solution:
**Capillary water.**

Soil water is classified by how tightly it is held, and only one category is both **present long enough** and **loosely enough held** for roots to take up:

| Form | Held by | Available to plants? |
|---|---|---|
| **Gravitational (free) water** | Nothing — drains under gravity | **No** — it drains away within a day or two |
| **Capillary water** | **Surface tension in the soil pores** | **Yes — this is the plant's water supply** |
| **Hygroscopic water** | Tightly adsorbed as a film on particle surfaces | **No** — held far beyond root suction |
| Chemically combined water | Chemical bonds within the mineral | **No** |

**Capillary water** occupies the pores against gravity after free drainage has ceased, and it is retained at suctions the roots can overcome. It is therefore the whole of the usable reservoir.

The two limits that bound it define the quantity irrigation design actually works with:

| Limit | Meaning | Suction |
|---|---|---|
| **Field capacity** | Water retained after free drainage stops | ~⅓ bar |
| **Permanent wilting point** | Plant can no longer extract water and does not recover | ~15 bar |

> **Available moisture = Field capacity − Permanent wilting point**

Irrigation is scheduled so the soil moisture never falls to the wilting point: water is applied when a permitted fraction of the available moisture has been depleted — the **readily available moisture**, commonly 50 to 75% of the total.

The depth of water to apply at each irrigation follows directly:
> d = γ_{d} × D × (FC − OMC_{before irrigation})

where D is the root-zone depth. That figure, aggregated over the season and divided by the irrigation efficiency, becomes the **gross irrigation requirement** on which the canal is sized.

examTip.trick: Soil water by availability: **gravitational** water drains away and is unavailable; **hygroscopic** water is held too tightly for roots; **capillary** water, held between field capacity and wilting point, is what plants can actually use.
examTip.mnemonic: **Available water = field capacity − permanent wilting point**, and that difference is what irrigation scheduling is built on. Sandy soils hold little of it; loams hold the most.

questions.stem: EGL − HGL gives:
questions.solution:
**Velocity head, v²/2g.**

The two lines plot different parts of the same Bernoulli sum:

| Line | Plots | Equals |
|---|---|---|
| **EGL** — Energy Grade Line | **Total head** | z + p/γ + v²/2g |
| **HGL** — Hydraulic Grade Line | **Piezometric head** | z + p/γ |

Subtracting one from the other leaves exactly the term that distinguishes them:

> **EGL − HGL = v²/2g = velocity head**

The consequences are worth holding, because they let you read a pipeline's behaviour straight off a sketch:

- The **EGL always lies above the HGL** by the velocity head, and the gap **widens where the flow speeds up** — through a contraction, for instance — because v²/2g grows.
- In a pipe of **constant diameter** the velocity is constant, so the two lines run **parallel**.
- The **EGL always falls in the direction of flow** (except across a pump), since friction and minor losses continuously destroy total head. Its slope is the **energy slope**, S_{f} = h_{f}/L — which is option (d), a different quantity: the *gradient* of the EGL, not the gap between the lines.
- The **HGL may rise or fall**: at an enlargement the velocity drops, pressure recovers, and the HGL climbs even though the EGL continues to fall.
- Where the **HGL falls below the pipe axis** the pressure is **sub-atmospheric** — the condition that invites air entry and **cavitation**, and the reason a long siphon or a summit in a pipeline must be checked against the vapour pressure limit.
- For a reservoir at rest, v = 0, so the **EGL and HGL coincide** at the free surface.

A useful sanity check on any pipeline sketch: at the exit into a reservoir the HGL meets the water surface, and the remaining velocity head — the gap that was there just inside the pipe — is precisely the **exit loss**, k = 1.0.

examTip.trick: **EGL = p/γ + z + V²/2g** and **HGL = p/γ + z**. Subtract and the difference is the **velocity head**.
examTip.mnemonic: **EGL always falls in the direction of flow (friction); HGL may RISE where the pipe expands** and the velocity head converts back to pressure. And **HGL below the pipe means NEGATIVE pressure** — which risks air ingress and, in a water main, **contamination being drawn in**.

questions.stem: Thickness of filter media of a slow sand filter is:
questions.solution:
**90 to 110 cm.**

A slow sand filter needs a deep bed of fine sand because its purification is largely **biological**, not merely mechanical. A gelatinous biological layer — the **schmutzdecke** — develops on the surface over a few days, and it is this living mat, together with the long slow passage through fine sand, that removes bacteria and organic matter.

The two filter types compared, which is what the question is really testing:

| | **Slow sand filter** | **Rapid sand filter** |
|---|---|---|
| **Bed depth** | **90 – 110 cm** | **60 – 75 cm** |
| Effective size of sand | 0.2 – 0.3 mm (**finer**) | 0.35 – 0.55 mm |
| Rate of filtration | **100 – 200 L/m²/h** | **3000 – 6000 L/m²/h** |
| Area required | **Large** | Small |
| Cleaning | **Scraping the top 2–3 cm**, every 1–3 months | **Backwashing**, every 1–3 days |
| Pre-treatment | Plain sedimentation only | **Coagulation and flocculation essential** |
| **Bacterial removal** | **98 – 99%** | 80 – 90% |
| Turbidity tolerated | Low (< 30 NTU) | Up to 100 NTU or more |
| Cost | Low capital-intensity but land-hungry; simple to run | Higher capital and skill, less land |

Note the trade-off: the slow filter is far better at removing bacteria and needs no chemicals, but demands **thirty times the area** for the same output. That makes it well suited to **small towns and rural schemes in Nepal**, where land is available and skilled operators and a chemical supply chain may not be — and unsuitable for a large city.

Both types sit on a **graded gravel support layer** of about 30 to 45 cm over an underdrainage system, and both are followed by **disinfection**, since even 99% bacterial removal is not sterilisation.

examTip.trick: Compare the two filters: a **slow sand filter** uses **finer sand in a thicker bed** and works largely by the biological **schmutzdecke** at the surface; a **rapid sand filter** uses coarser sand and works by physical straining and adsorption.
examTip.mnemonic: **Slow sand: 90–110 cm of fine sand, rate 100–200 l/m²/h, cleaned by SCRAPING the top layer. Rapid: 60–75 cm of coarser sand, rate 3000–6000 l/m²/h, cleaned by BACKWASHING.** Slow filters need no coagulation and remove bacteria well; rapid filters need coagulation first.

questions.stem: Trachoma can be avoided by:
questions.solution:
**Providing clean water.**

Trachoma is an eye infection caused by the bacterium *Chlamydia trachomatis*. Repeated infection scars the inner eyelid, which turns the lashes inward to abrade the cornea, and untreated it is a leading cause of **preventable blindness**. It is concentrated in poor and rural communities with limited clean water and sanitation.

The route of transmission is what decides the answer. Trachoma spreads by **contact** — from eye and nose discharge carried on fingers, shared towels and clothing, and by eye-seeking flies. It is a **water-washed** disease, not a water-borne one: the infection is not swallowed in the water, so **treating the water for drinking does nothing to prevent it**. What breaks the cycle is enough clean water available for **face and hand washing**.

That distinction is the examinable point:

| Class | Mechanism | Examples | Control |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Water-borne** | Pathogen **ingested** in the water | Cholera, typhoid, dysentery, hepatitis A | **Treat and disinfect** the water |
| **Water-washed** | Poor hygiene from **insufficient** water | **Trachoma**, scabies, conjunctivitis, skin infections | **Quantity and access** to clean water |
| Water-based | Part of life cycle in water | Schistosomiasis, guinea worm | Avoid contact; control host |
| Water-related vector | Insect breeds in water | Malaria, dengue, filariasis | Eliminate breeding sites |

Since the problem is hygiene rather than contamination of what is drunk, **chlorination (option c) is irrelevant** here — it is the answer for cholera or typhoid.

The WHO control strategy is the **SAFE** approach: **S**urgery for advanced lids, **A**ntibiotics, **F**acial cleanliness, and **E**nvironmental improvement — the last two being where the water supply engineer's contribution lies.

examTip.trick: Trachoma is an **eye infection spread by contact and flies**, strongly associated with a lack of water for **washing** — so the remedy is water **quantity and availability**, not only its quality.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water-washed diseases (trachoma, scabies, skin and eye infections) are prevented by having ENOUGH water; water-borne diseases (cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A) by having CLEAN water.** Two different problems with two different engineering answers.

questions.stem: Grout is a mixture of:
questions.solution:
**Water, cement and sand.**

Grout is a **flowable** cementitious mixture placed to fill voids, gaps and cavities, hardening in place. It is proportioned to be pourable or pumpable rather than workable under a trowel, so its water content is high relative to mortar and its aggregate is fine.

Where grout is used:
- **Pressure grouting** of rock and soil, to seal seepage paths and consolidate ground — as under a dam or around a tunnel.
- Filling the **cavities of hollow blockwork** and embedding reinforcement in masonry walls.
- **Ducts of post-tensioned** members, to bond and protect the tendons.
- Bedding **machine base plates and column baseplates**, where non-shrink grout is specified.
- **Sealing joints** between precast units and between tiles.

The related cementitious mixes, distinguished by what is in them and how stiff they are:

| Mix | Composition | Consistency |
|---|---|---|
| **Cement slurry / neat grout** | Cement + water only | Very fluid — thin cracks, fine fissures |
| **Grout** | **Cement + sand + water** | Flowable / pourable |
| Mortar | Cement + sand + water, less water | Workable — laid with a trowel |
| Concrete | Cement + sand + **coarse aggregate** + water | Placed and compacted |

So the family runs from neat cement paste to concrete simply by adding coarser material and less water. Option (a) describes neat cement slurry, which is used for the finest fissures but is not what "grout" ordinarily means; options (c) and (d) are lime-based mixes belonging to plastering and traditional mortar.

Requirements a good grout must meet: adequate **fluidity** to reach the void, minimal **bleeding and segregation**, low **shrinkage** (non-shrink or expansive admixtures are common), and sufficient strength and durability once set. For prestressing ducts IS 1343 additionally limits the **chloride content**, since the tendons are highly susceptible to corrosion.

examTip.trick: Grout is a **flowable** mixture designed to fill voids and cracks. Neat grout is cement and water; sanded grout adds fine sand for volume and shrinkage control. No coarse aggregate — it would block the void.
examTip.mnemonic: **Grout FLOWS into voids; mortar BEDS units; concrete CARRIES load.** The distinguishing feature is the maximum particle size relative to the space being filled.

questions.stem: Prestress loss results in:
questions.solution:
**All of the above.**

Prestress is a **pre-applied compression** that improves the member's behaviour in several ways at once. Losing part of it therefore degrades all of them together.

| Aspect | What the prestress does | Effect of losing it |
|---|---|---|
| **Flexural / tensile capacity** | Pre-compresses the tension face so applied load must first overcome it before any tension appears | Cracking occurs at a **lower load**; the member loses its crack-free range |
| **Shear capacity** | Axial compression **confines** the concrete and flattens the principal tensile stress trajectories, raising diagonal-tension resistance | Shear strength **falls** |
| **Compressive capacity** | The section works wholly in compression under service load | With tension re-appearing, the effective compressive section is **reduced** |

Add to these the loss of **camber** and the increase in deflection, and reduced fatigue and durability performance, since cracks admit moisture to the tendons.

**The losses themselves**, and their totals per IS 1343:

| Loss | Pre-tensioning | Post-tensioning |
|---|---|---|
| Elastic shortening | **Yes** | No for a single cable; partial for multiple |
| Creep of concrete | Yes | Yes |
| Shrinkage of concrete | Yes (larger — younger concrete) | Yes (smaller) |
| Relaxation of steel | Yes | Yes |
| **Friction / wobble in duct** | No | **Yes** |
| **Anchorage slip** | No | **Yes** |
| **Total** | **≈ 20%** | **≈ 15%** |

The losses divide into **immediate** (elastic shortening, anchorage slip, friction) and **time-dependent** (creep, shrinkage, relaxation).

**How the losses are contained in practice**, which is the design consequence: use **high-strength concrete of grade M30 or above**, which creeps and shrinks less; use **low-relaxation strand**; **over-tension** initially so that the design prestress remains after losses; and delay transfer until the concrete has gained sufficient strength. That is also why prestressed concrete cannot be built with ordinary low-grade materials — the losses would consume too much of the prestress to leave a reliable margin.

examTip.trap: "All of the above" — read every option. Loss of prestress reduces the effective force, and every consequence follows from that.
examTip.trick: Group the losses by when they act: **immediate** (elastic shortening, anchorage slip, friction) and **time-dependent** (creep, shrinkage, relaxation).
examTip.mnemonic: **Total loss 15–20% pre-tensioned, 20–25% post-tensioned.** Note **friction and anchorage slip belong to POST-tensioning only**, and elastic shortening loss is **zero for a single post-tensioned tendon** — because it is stressed against the already-shortened concrete.

questions.stem: Permissible stress in steel is taken as:
questions.solution:
**Working stress.**

In the working stress method of design, the **permissible stress is the working stress** — a safe value obtained by dividing a limiting strength by a factor of safety, so the member stays comfortably within the elastic range under service load:

> Permissible stress = working stress = yield stress / factor of safety

For structural steel the traditional value is
> σ_{permissible} ≈ **0.6 f_{y}**

which corresponds to a factor of safety of about 1.67 against yield.

**Why not the other two.** The **yield stress** (a) is the point at which permanent deformation begins — designing to it would leave no margin at all for overload, variability in the material, or errors in analysis. The **ultimate stress** (b) is the stress at fracture, and reaching it means collapse; it is never a design value.

The wider contrast, since this is really a question about design philosophy:

| | **Working stress method** | **Limit state method** |
|---|---|---|
| Basis | Elastic behaviour under **service** load | Behaviour at **collapse** and at serviceability |
| Safety applied to | **Material** only — one factor of safety | **Loads and materials separately** — partial safety factors |
| Steel design | σ ≤ 0.6 f_y | Design strength f_y/1.15 = **0.87 f_y** |
| Concrete design | σ ≤ 0.33 f_ck | Design strength **0.446 f_ck** |
| Load factor | None — service loads used directly | **1.5 (DL + LL)** |
| Status | Superseded, retained for some checks | **Current practice** (IS 800:2007, IS 456:2000) |

The limit state method is preferred because a single global factor of safety cannot reflect the fact that **dead load is far more predictable than live or wind load**, nor that concrete varies far more than steel. Partial safety factors let each source of uncertainty be treated on its own merits.

Working stress design nevertheless survives in the **serviceability** checks — crack width and deflection — where elastic behaviour under service load is exactly what is being examined.

examTip.trick: The two design philosophies use different language: **working stress** uses **permissible stresses** (a factor of safety applied to the material strength); **limit state** uses **design strengths** (characteristic strength divided by a partial safety factor) and factored loads.
examTip.mnemonic: **Working stress: permissible = strength ÷ FoS, and the structure is checked at SERVICE load. Limit state: design = characteristic ÷ γ_m, and the structure is checked at FACTORED load.** Limit state is the current method; working stress survives for water-retaining structures and for checking serviceability.

questions.stem: The section in which the area of tensile steel is such that at the ultimate limit state the ultimate compressive strain in concrete is reached, however the tensile strain in the reinforcing steel is less than the yield strain, is known as:
questions.solution:
**Over-reinforced section.**

Too much tensile steel means the steel is never fully stressed. The concrete reaches its ultimate compressive strain of **0.0035 first**, while the steel is still elastic and below its yield strain — so the section fails by **crushing of the concrete** with the steel under-utilised.

The three cases, decided by which material reaches its limit first:

| Section | Reaches limit first | x_u vs x_u,max | Failure | Warning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Under-reinforced** | **Steel yields** | x_u < x_u,max | Steel yields, then concrete crushes | **Ductile — ample warning** |
| **Balanced** | **Both together** | x_u = x_u,max | Simultaneous | Marginal |
| **Over-reinforced** | **Concrete crushes** | x_u > x_u,max | Sudden crushing, steel still elastic | **Brittle — no warning** |

**Why over-reinforced sections are prohibited in design.** The failure is **sudden and brittle**: the concrete crushes explosively with little prior cracking or deflection, so occupants get no warning and no chance to evacuate. An **under-reinforced** section, by contrast, yields first — cracks widen visibly and deflections grow long before collapse. IS 456 therefore requires **x_u ≤ x_u,max**, which forces every section to be under-reinforced or at most balanced.

The limiting neutral axis depths, from cl. 38.1:

| Steel grade | x_u,max/d |
|---|---|
| Fe 250 | 0.53 |
| **Fe 415** | **0.48** |
| Fe 500 | 0.46 |

Where the applied moment exceeds what a singly reinforced section can carry within that limit, the correct remedy is not more tension steel but a **doubly reinforced** section — adding compression steel — or a deeper section.

**A note on the source explanation.** The circulating answer sheet keys (b), which is correct, but defines under-reinforced as "concrete fails before the steel yields" — which is the definition of *over*-reinforced. In an under-reinforced section the **steel yields first**. The keyed answer stands; the explanation has been rewritten.

verification.notes: The keyed answer (b) is correct, but the source's explanation describes under-reinforced sections as 'concrete fails before the steel yields', which is backwards — that is the over-reinforced case. The explanation has been rewritten.

examTip.trap: Under- and over-reinforced are easy to reverse under pressure, and the consequences are opposite.
examTip.trick: Ask **which material fails first**. **Over-reinforced:** so much steel that the **CONCRETE crushes before the steel yields** — sudden, brittle, no warning. **Under-reinforced:** the **steel yields first**, giving large deflections and cracking before collapse.
examTip.mnemonic: **Over-reinforced fails suddenly and is PROHIBITED by IS 456** — which is exactly what the x_u,max/d limit (0.48 for Fe415) enforces. Ductility, not economy, is the reason.

questions.stem: Which test is used to measure weathering of aggregate?
questions.solution:
**Soundness test.**

Soundness is an aggregate's resistance to **disintegration under weathering** — the repeated volume changes caused by freeze–thaw cycling and by sulphate crystallisation in the pores. The test simulates that cycling and measures the resulting loss in mass.

**Method (IS 2386 Part 5):** a graded sample is subjected to five cycles of immersion in a saturated solution of **sodium sulphate or magnesium sulphate**, alternating with oven drying. Salt crystals grow in the pores on each drying and exert pressure much as ice does. The percentage loss in mass is reported, and the limits are about **12% for sodium sulphate** and 18% for magnesium sulphate.

The aggregate tests distinguished by the property each measures — the whole point of the question:

| Test | Measures | Typical limit |
|---|---|---|
| **Soundness** | **Resistance to weathering / freeze–thaw** | **12% (Na₂SO₄)** |
| **Impact value** | Resistance to **sudden shock** | 30% for surfacing, 45% for base |
| **Crushing value** | Resistance to gradual **crushing** load | 30% for surfacing, 45% for base |
| Abrasion (Los Angeles) | Resistance to **wear and attrition** | 30% for surfacing |
| Water absorption | Porosity | < 2% |
| Specific gravity | Density | 2.6 – 2.9 |
| Flakiness / elongation index | Particle **shape** | < 25% and < 15% |

So impact and crushing tests both measure **strength**, and only the soundness test addresses **durability under weather**.

**Why it matters in Nepal specifically:** hill and high-altitude roads and structures experience many freeze–thaw cycles each winter, and an unsound aggregate will disintegrate within the concrete or bituminous layer even though it passed every strength test. Frost action on the aggregate is the same mechanism as the frost heave discussed in Q3 of this paper, acting at the scale of a single stone.

examTip.trick: The **soundness test** subjects aggregate to repeated cycles of immersion in sodium or magnesium sulphate solution and drying, simulating the disruptive effect of **freeze–thaw and salt crystallisation**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Soundness = resistance to WEATHERING. Los Angeles abrasion = resistance to WEAR. Impact value = resistance to SHOCK. Crushing value = resistance to gradual LOAD.** Four tests, four different kinds of durability.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the primary raw material in cement manufacturing?
questions.solution:
**Limestone.**

Limestone (calcium carbonate, CaCO₃) supplies the **lime (CaO)** that makes up roughly **60 to 65%** of Portland cement — by far the largest constituent, and the one that forms the calcium silicates responsible for strength. It is quarried and ground with clay or shale, which contribute silica and alumina.

**The manufacturing sequence:**
1. **Crushing and grinding** of limestone with clay, in a ratio of about 3 : 1.
2. **Burning in a rotary kiln** at 1400 to 1500°C. Calcination drives off CO₂ (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂) and the oxides then combine into **clinker**.
3. **Grinding the clinker** with 3 to 5% **gypsum**, which retards the setting — without it the cement would flash-set and be unusable.

The oxide composition of the finished cement:

| Oxide | % | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **CaO (lime)** | **60 – 65** | **Limestone** |
| SiO₂ (silica) | 17 – 25 | Clay, shale |
| Al₂O₃ (alumina) | 3 – 8 | Clay |
| Fe₂O₃ | 0.5 – 6 | Clay, iron ore |
| MgO, SO₃, alkalis | small | — |

And the four principal compounds — the Bogue compounds — formed in the clinker:

| Compound | Contribution |
|---|---|
| **C₃S** (tricalcium silicate) | **Early strength**; high heat of hydration |
| **C₂S** (dicalcium silicate) | **Later strength**; low heat |
| C₃A (tricalcium aluminate) | Flash set; highest heat; vulnerable to **sulphate attack** |
| C₄AF | Little strength contribution |

Why the other options are wrong: **coal** is the kiln **fuel**, not a raw material entering the cement; **mica** is an undesirable impurity; and **aluminium** enters only as the oxide alumina from clay, in a minor proportion.

Note that **low-heat cement** is made by reducing C₃S and C₃A and raising C₂S — useful in mass concrete — while **sulphate-resisting cement** works by limiting C₃A specifically.

examTip.trick: Cement is about **60–65% CaO**, and only limestone can supply that much calcium. Clay is the **secondary** material, supplying silica and alumina.
examTip.mnemonic: **Roughly 3 parts limestone to 1 part clay.** The kiln then produces the four compounds: **C₃S** (early strength), **C₂S** (late strength), **C₃A** (flash set — restrained by gypsum), **C₄AF** (colour only).

questions.stem: How many wind zones are there in Nepal?
questions.solution:
**Two.**

Nepal is divided into two wind zones for structural design, separated by the **3000 m** elevation contour:

| Zone | Region | Basic wind velocity |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | Terai plains, hills and the **Kathmandu Valley** — generally **below 3000 m** | **47 m/s** |
| **2** | The **mountains** — areas **above 3000 m** | **55 m/s** |

The higher velocity at altitude reflects both the exposure of high ridges and the reduced sheltering, though note that the **air density also falls** with altitude, so the resulting pressure does not rise in proportion to the square of the velocity alone.

**How basic wind speed becomes a design pressure**, following IS 875 Part 3, which Nepal's code adopts:

> V_{z} = V_{b} · k₁ · k₂ · k₃
> p_{z} = **0.6 V_{z}²**  (in N/m², with V_{z} in m/s)

where the modifying factors are:
- **k₁** — risk coefficient, from the design life and importance of the structure.
- **k₂** — terrain, height and structure size factor. Wind speed **increases with height** above ground and is lower in built-up terrain.
- **k₃** — **topography factor**, which matters greatly in Nepal: wind accelerates over ridges and escarpments, and k₃ can reach 1.36.

The design wind force then follows as F = (C_{pe} − C_{pi}) · A · p_{z}, using external and internal pressure coefficients.

**Why wind often governs light structures.** On a steep roof or a light truss the wind acts largely as **suction**, and it can **reverse** the member forces — putting into tension what was designed for compression, and lifting a roof off its supports. That reversal must be checked separately, and it is why roof sheeting fixings and holding-down bolts are so often the critical detail. For heavier buildings in Nepal, **seismic** load usually governs instead.

examTip.trick: Nepal's building code divides the country into wind zones based on the basic wind speed, and the number is small because the topography rather than the zone dominates local wind at most sites.
examTip.mnemonic: **Basic wind speed is then modified by k₁ (risk/life of structure), k₂ (terrain, height and structure size) and k₃ (topography).** On a Nepali ridge or escarpment the **topography factor k₃ can be decisive** — a hilltop site sees far higher wind than the zone map alone suggests.

questions.stem: Stiffness matrix method is also called:
questions.solution:
**Displacement method.**

The two families of matrix analysis differ in **what is taken as the unknown**, and every other difference follows from that choice:

| | **Stiffness method** | **Flexibility method** |
|---|---|---|
| Also called | **Displacement method** | **Force method** |
| Unknowns | **Joint displacements** | **Redundant forces** |
| Equations written | **Equilibrium** at joints | **Compatibility** of displacements |
| Number of unknowns | **Kinematic** indeterminacy (degrees of freedom) | **Static** indeterminacy |
| Governing relation | **{P} = [K]{Δ}** | {Δ} = [F]{P} |
| Suits | **Highly indeterminate** structures | Structures with few redundants |
| Computer implementation | **Standard** — all modern software | Rare |

So the stiffness method solves for displacements first and recovers forces afterwards; the flexibility method does the reverse. Options (a) and (b) are two names for the *other* method, which is why (d) cannot be right.

**Why the stiffness method won.** Its number of unknowns is the kinematic indeterminacy, which is fixed by the **geometry** of the structure and can be counted mechanically, joint by joint, without judgement. The flexibility method requires the analyst to *choose* which redundants to release — a decision that cannot be automated and that changes the difficulty of the arithmetic. The stiffness matrix is also **symmetric, banded and assembled additively** from standard element matrices, which suits a computer perfectly.

Every structural analysis package — STAAD, ETABS, SAP2000, and the finite element method generally — is built on the stiffness method.

The classical hand methods sit in the same two families: **slope-deflection** and **moment distribution** are displacement (stiffness) methods, working in terms of joint rotations; the **method of consistent deformation** and the **three-moment equation** are force (flexibility) methods, working in terms of redundant reactions.

examTip.trick: Two families, distinguished by what is treated as unknown: **FORCE (flexibility) methods** solve for redundant **forces**; **DISPLACEMENT (stiffness) methods** solve for unknown **joint displacements**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Force methods: consistent deformation, column analogy, three-moment. Displacement methods: slope-deflection, moment distribution, MATRIX STIFFNESS.** Every commercial analysis package is a stiffness solver — because the method is **systematic and programmable**, with no case-by-case choice of redundants.

questions.stem: Moment of inertia of a rectangle about its CG with axis parallel to the X-axis is:
questions.solution:
**bd³/12**, where b is the width (the dimension parallel to the axis) and d the depth (perpendicular to it).

The pattern to hold: the dimension **perpendicular to the axis is cubed**, because the moment of inertia weights each element of area by the *square* of its distance from the axis, and integrating across the depth raises the power to three.

> I_{xx} = ∫y² dA = **bd³/12** about the centroidal axis

The related values for the same rectangle:

| Axis | Moment of inertia |
|---|---|
| **Centroidal, parallel to width b** | **bd³/12** |
| Centroidal, parallel to depth d | **db³/12** |
| **Along the base** (edge) | **bd³/3** |
| Polar (about centroid) | bd(b² + d²)/12 |

The base value follows from the **parallel axis theorem**:
> I_{base} = I_{G} + A·h² = bd³/12 + bd(d/2)² = bd³/12 + bd³/4 = **bd³/3** ✓

which is where options (c) and (d) come from — they are correct expressions, but about the **base**, not the centroid.

Other sections worth carrying as a set:

| Section | I about centroid |
|---|---|
| Rectangle | bd³/12 |
| Circle (diameter d) | **πd⁴/64** |
| Hollow circle | π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64 |
| Triangle (base b, height h) | **bh³/36** |
| Semicircle | 0.11 r⁴ |

**Why it matters.** I governs both bending stress (σ = My/I) and stiffness (deflection ∝ 1/EI), and buckling load (P_cr = π²EI/l_e²). The d³ term is why a beam is turned on edge: doubling the depth increases I **eightfold**, whereas doubling the width only doubles it. That single fact explains most of the shape of structural sections — and why an I-section concentrates material in flanges as far from the neutral axis as possible.

examTip.trick: **bd³/12 about the centroid; bd³/3 about the base** — and they differ by exactly the parallel-axis term bd(d/2)² = bd³/4.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rectangle: 12 at the centre, 3 at the base. Triangle: 36 at the centroid, 12 at the base, 4 at the vertex.** Note the **cube on the depth** — doubling a beam's depth multiplies its stiffness by eight.

questions.stem: The load beyond which a body will have a permanent set is:
questions.solution:
**Proof load.**

The **proof load** is the maximum load a member can carry and still return **completely** to its original dimensions when the load is removed. Exceed it and some deformation is retained — a **permanent set**.

Proof load testing is a practical acceptance test: a load somewhat above the working load is applied for a short period, then removed. If no measurable permanent set remains, the member has passed. It is used routinely on chains, slings, lifting tackle, anchor bolts and precast units.

The distinctions the options are probing — note that the question asks for a **load**, not a stress:

| Term | Quantity | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Proof load** | **Force** | **Maximum load leaving no permanent set** |
| Proof stress | **Stress** | Stress producing a specified small permanent strain, usually **0.2%** |
| Rigidity | — | Resistance to deformation; the modulus of rigidity G relates shear stress to shear strain |
| Proof resilience | **Energy** | Maximum strain energy stored **up to the elastic limit** |

So **proof stress** is the near miss: it is the same idea expressed per unit area, and it is defined by *accepting* a small permanent strain rather than none. Proof stress matters for materials such as aluminium, high-strength steel and cold-worked bars that show **no distinct yield point** — the stress–strain curve bends gradually, so a 0.2% offset is used as a substitute for a yield stress.

The related energy terms, since proof resilience appears here:
- **Resilience** — strain energy stored in a body under load.
- **Proof resilience** — strain energy at the elastic limit; the area under the stress–strain curve up to that point.
- **Modulus of resilience** — proof resilience per unit volume, a measure of a material's ability to absorb energy elastically (important in springs).
- **Toughness** — the total area under the whole curve to fracture, which is the ability to absorb energy including plastic deformation.

examTip.trick: Distinguish the points on the stress–strain curve: **proportional limit** (Hooke's law ends), **elastic limit** (permanent set begins), **yield point**, **ultimate**, **fracture**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Beyond the elastic limit the strain no longer fully recovers — that is a PERMANENT SET.** For high-strength steel with no defined yield, the equivalent is the **0.2% proof stress**: the stress at which a line of slope E, offset by 0.2% strain, meets the curve.

questions.stem: Influence line diagram for bending moment in a simply supported beam is a:
questions.solution:
**A triangle.**

For a **fixed section** C at distance a from support A (with b = L − a) on a simply supported span L, the influence line for bending moment at C is made of two straight segments meeting at a peak **directly under C**:

> Peak ordinate = **ab/L**, occurring when the unit load stands at C

The ordinate falls linearly to **zero at both supports**, since a unit load standing over a support produces no moment anywhere. Two straight lines from zero, rising to a single apex — a triangle.

**Why the sides are straight.** With the unit load between A and C, the moment at C is R_{B}·b, and R_{B} varies linearly with the load's position. The same argument applies on the other side. Only the *slope* changes as the load crosses C, which is what creates the apex.

A useful check: the peak is greatest when a = b = L/2, giving **L/4** at mid-span — the familiar maximum influence ordinate for a simply supported beam.

The influence lines for the other quantities on the same beam:

| Function | Shape | Peak |
|---|---|---|
| Reaction R_A | Straight line | 1.0 at A, 0 at B |
| **BM at section C** | **Triangle** | **ab/L at C** |
| **Shear at section C** | **Two parallel straight lines with a unit step at C** | +b/L and −a/L |

**Do not confuse the ILD with the bending moment diagram.** The BM diagram for a *single* point load on a simply supported beam is also triangular, but it plots the moment at *every section* for a *fixed* load. The influence line plots the moment at *one section* as the load *moves* — a distinction tested directly in Set 2 Q53.

The BM diagram for a **UDL** is parabolic, which is where option (b) comes from — and the influence line for BM is never parabolic on a simply supported beam.

**Muller-Breslau's principle** gives the shape without algebra: release the restraint corresponding to the function and impose a unit displacement. Cutting the beam at C and imposing a unit relative rotation produces exactly this triangle.

examTip.trick: The influence line for **moment at a section** of a simply supported span is **triangular**, peaking at **ab/L** under the section. The influence line for **shear** is two parallel lines with a **unit step**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Moment ILD triangular; shear ILD a step.** Do not confuse the moment ILD with the bending moment diagram — they happen to share a triangular shape here, which is exactly why the confusion persists, but they answer different questions.

questions.stem: What will be the deflection of a cantilever beam subjected to a point load W at its free end?
questions.solution:
**WL³/3EI.**

**Derivation by double integration.** With x measured from the free end, the bending moment is M_{x} = −Wx, so

> EI d²y/dx² = Wx
> EI dy/dx = Wx²/2 + C₁
> EI y = Wx³/6 + C₁x + C₂

Applying the boundary conditions at the fixed end (x = L): y = 0 and dy/dx = 0 gives C₁ = −WL²/2 and C₂ = WL³/3. Hence

> EI y(x) = Wx³/6 − WL²x/2 + WL³/3

At the **free end**, x = 0:
> **δ = WL³/(3EI)** ✓

The corresponding end **slope** is θ = WL²/(2EI).

The standard deflection results, worth holding as one table since the denominators are what get confused:

| Beam and loading | Maximum deflection (total load W) |
|---|---|
| **Cantilever, point load at end** | **WL³/3EI** |
| Cantilever, UDL | WL³/**8**EI |
| Cantilever, moment M at end | ML²/**2**EI |
| Simply supported, central point load | WL³/**48**EI |
| Simply supported, UDL | 5WL³/**384**EI |
| Fixed both ends, UDL | WL³/**384**EI |
| Fixed both ends, central point load | WL³/**192**EI |

Note the enormous range: a cantilever deflects **16 times** as much as a simply supported beam of the same span under the same central load (3 against 48), and **128 times** as much as a fixed-ended beam. That is why cantilevers are kept short and deep, and why continuity is so valuable.

**Dimensional check**, which eliminates wrong-form options instantly: W·L³/(E·I) has units N·m³/(N/m²·m⁴) = m ✓. Any expression with L⁴ alongside a *total* load W would give m², not a length — the trap set in Set 2 Q48.

examTip.trick: Learn the four cantilever standards: **end load W → WL³/3EI; UDL w → wL⁴/8EI; end couple M → ML²/2EI**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cantilever end load WL³/3EI against simply supported central load WL³/48EI — SIXTEEN times more.** A cantilever is structurally expensive, which is why its span/depth limit (7) is a third of a simply supported beam's (20), and why **deflection almost always governs**.

questions.stem: A moment M is acting at the free end of a cantilever beam. What will be the maximum moment developed in the beam?
questions.solution:
**M** — the applied moment is transmitted unchanged along the whole beam.

Take any section at distance x from the free end and sum moments of the forces to the left of it. The **only** action on that side is the applied couple M itself; there is no transverse load, so no force–distance term arises. Therefore

> M_{x} = **M** for every x, from the free end to the fixed end

The bending moment diagram is a **rectangle** of constant ordinate M, and the shear force is **zero throughout** — which is consistent with S = dM/dx, since a constant moment has zero slope.

This is the condition of **pure bending**: the beam curves uniformly, with the same curvature at every section, because M/EI is constant. The curvature is 1/R = M/EI, so the beam bends into a circular arc.

The associated deformations at the free end:
> Slope θ = **ML/EI**
> Deflection δ = **ML²/2EI**

Both follow immediately from the moment–area method, since the M/EI diagram is simply a rectangle of area ML.

**Why the distractors are there.** A factor of 2 (option a) would arise if the moment were somehow amplified — it never is, in a determinate cantilever. Halving or quartering (c, d) would imply the moment dissipates along the beam, which no equilibrium argument supports.

A useful contrast: a **point load W** at the free end gives a moment that varies **linearly** from zero at the tip to WL at the support. A **moment** applied at the tip gives a moment that is **constant** at M everywhere. The two loadings look similar in a sketch but produce entirely different diagrams — and the constant-moment case is why the middle third of a four-point bending test (Set 2 Q10) is used for flexure testing.

examTip.trick: A couple applied at the free end of a cantilever produces a **CONSTANT bending moment M along the entire length** — there is no other load to vary it.
examTip.mnemonic: **A couple gives constant moment and ZERO shear.** That is the general rule: an applied couple **steps the BMD** and leaves the SFD untouched, the exact reverse of a point load. It is a standard examination discriminator.

questions.stem: Coefficient of friction for laminar flow is:
questions.solution:
**16/Re.**

This question turns on a definition that trips up almost everyone, because **two different quantities are both written f** and they differ by a factor of 4.

| Quantity | Symbol | Head loss written as | Laminar value |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Darcy friction factor** | f | h_f = **f**LV²/(2gD) | **64/Re** |
| **Coefficient of friction** | f′ (Fanning) | h_f = **4f′**LV²/(2gD) | **16/Re** |

The two are related by **f = 4f′**, so 64/Re ÷ 4 = **16/Re**.

The question asks for the **coefficient of friction**, so the answer is **16/Re**. Had it asked for the *friction factor*, the answer would be 64/Re — which is exactly why option (d) is there.

**Where the values come from.** For laminar flow the Hagen–Poiseuille result gives
> h_f = 32μVL/(γD²)

Equating this to fLV²/(2gD) and substituting Re = ρVD/μ yields f = 64/Re directly.

The practical consequences of that inverse dependence:
- In **laminar** flow, h_f ∝ **V** (first power), because f ∝ 1/V cancels one power of V².
- In **turbulent** flow, h_f ∝ **V²** approximately, since f varies only weakly with Re. For smooth pipes, f ≈ 0.316/Re^{0.25} (Blasius).
- Laminar friction is **independent of pipe roughness** — the viscous sublayer covers the wall entirely. Roughness matters only in turbulent flow, which is why the Moody diagram has a single laminar line but a family of turbulent curves.

Flow regimes by Reynolds number: **laminar below 2000**, transitional 2000 to 4000, **turbulent above 4000**.

When reading any friction problem, check which form of the head-loss equation is intended — the presence or absence of the 4 tells you which f is meant.

verification.notes: Both 16/Re and 64/Re are correct under their respective definitions. The question asks for the coefficient of friction (the Fanning form, used with the 4fLV²/2gD expression), giving 16/Re. Option (d), 64/Re, is the Darcy friction factor.

examTip.trap: **64/Re is the DARCY friction factor; 16/Re is the FANNING coefficient.** Both are correct in their own convention, and mixing them costs a factor of four.
examTip.trick: The tell is which form of the head-loss equation is being used: **h_f = fLV²/2gD** goes with 64/Re; **h_f = 4f′LV²/2gD** goes with 16/Re.
examTip.mnemonic: **Darcy 64, Fanning 16, and f = 4f′.** In laminar flow the **roughness is irrelevant** in either convention — the fluid moves in orderly layers and never feels the wall texture.

questions.stem: What are the sediments that are rolling, sliding and bouncing called?
questions.solution:
**Bed load.**

Bed load is the coarser sediment that travels **in contact with, or very close to, the river bed**, moving by three distinct mechanisms:

| Mechanism | Motion |
|---|---|
| **Rolling** | Grains roll along the bed |
| **Sliding** | Grains slide without rotating |
| **Saltation** | Grains **bounce** in short hops, briefly leaving the bed |

Because the particles are supported by the bed rather than by the turbulence of the flow, bed load consists of the **larger** material — sand, gravel and cobbles.

The total sediment load of a river divides as:

| Component | Supported by | Material | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bed load** | **The bed itself** | Sand, gravel, cobbles | **Rolling, sliding, saltating** |
| **Suspended load** | **Turbulence** of the flow | Silt, clay, fine sand | Usually the **largest** fraction by mass |
| **Dissolved load** | Chemically in solution | Ions | Not a mechanical sediment |
| **Wash load** | Turbulence | Finest fraction | Not exchanged with the bed |

**Why the distinction matters in practice.** Bed load is what shapes the channel — it forms the ripples, dunes and bars of an alluvial bed (Q34 of this paper) and drives **scour** at bridge piers and guide banks. Suspended load is what fills reservoirs and abrades turbine runners, which is why a **settling basin** is placed at a hydropower intake.
