Sediment concentration is greatest near the bed, and that gradient is exactly what a **silt excluder** exploits, skimming the dirty bottom layer away from the canal.

Bed load transport is estimated by formulae such as **Meyer-Peter–Müller, Einstein and Shields**, all built on the idea of a **critical shear stress** below which grains do not move. Because it is so hard to measure directly, bed load is often taken as a percentage — commonly 10 to 20% — of the measured suspended load.

For Himalayan rivers all these quantities are exceptionally high, which is why sediment management dominates the design of Nepali headworks.

examTip.trick: Sediment moves in two modes: **BED load** rolls, slides and saltates along the bed; **SUSPENDED load** is carried within the flow by turbulence.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bed load rolls; suspended load floats along; wash load is the very fine fraction that never settles.** Bed load is what **fills reservoirs and abrades turbines**; suspended load is what makes the water brown. Total load = bed + suspended.

questions.stem: Which is not a formation seen in an alluvial channel with sediment motion?
questions.solution:
**Meandered.**

The question is about **bed forms** — the small-scale features sculpted into the bed by sediment in motion. Meandering is not a bed form at all: it is a **plan-form** characteristic, the sinuous path the whole channel takes across its flood plain, developed over long periods by erosion of the outer bank and deposition on the inner bank.

The genuine bed forms, in the order they appear as flow intensity rises:

| Regime | Bed form | Froude number | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Lower** | Plane bed, no motion | — | Below threshold of movement |
| Lower | **Ripples** | Fr < 1 | Small wavy forms, height < 40 mm |
| Lower | **Dunes** | Fr < 1 | Larger, crescent-shaped; **gentle upstream slope, steep downstream face** |
| Transition | Washed-out dunes, plane bed | Fr ≈ 1 | Bed forms flatten |
| **Upper** | **Antidunes** | **Fr > 1** | In phase with the surface waves; **migrate upstream** |
| Upper | Chutes and pools | Fr > 1 | Steep, high-energy |

So ripples, dunes and antidunes are all bed forms, and only meandering is the odd one out.

**Antidunes are the distinctive case** and worth remembering: they occur only in **supercritical** flow, the water surface waves are in phase with the bed waves, and the forms travel **upstream** even though the water and sediment move downstream — which is what gives them the name.

**Why bed forms matter.** They dominate the channel's **roughness**. A rippled or duned bed has a far higher effective Manning's n than a plane bed, so the same discharge requires a greater depth. That makes the stage–discharge relation of an alluvial river non-unique — the same depth can carry different discharges depending on which regime the bed is in — and it is a real difficulty in gauging Himalayan rivers.

**Meandering**, by contrast, is characterised by its own parameters: the **meander length, belt width and sinuosity** (channel length ÷ valley length, above about 1.5 for a meandering stream). It is controlled by river training works — guide banks, spurs and revetments — rather than by anything to do with bed form.

examTip.trap: Read the **NOT**. Ripples, dunes, antidunes and plane beds are **bed forms** within a channel; **meandering** is a **planform** — the shape of the channel in plan, not a bed configuration.
examTip.trick: Bed forms progress with increasing flow: **plane bed → ripples → dunes → washed-out dunes → plane bed → antidunes**, and the resistance changes dramatically along the way.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bed forms are what the BED does; meandering is what the CHANNEL does.** The distinction matters because bed forms change the **effective roughness** with discharge — which is why a river's Manning's n is not a constant.

questions.stem: Which element of a hydroelectric power plant prevents the penstock from the water hammer phenomenon?
questions.solution:
**Surge tank.**

When the turbine gates close suddenly, the momentum of the water column cannot vanish instantly and a pressure wave — **water hammer** — travels back up the conduit. Unrelieved, it can burst the penstock or damage the runner and spiral casing.

A surge tank is an open-topped shaft placed at the junction of the low-pressure headrace tunnel and the high-pressure penstock, and it works in both directions:

- **On sudden closure**, it accepts the rejected water. The level in the shaft rises, converting the pressure surge into a harmless change of water level, and confining the water-hammer pressure to the **short length of penstock below the tank** rather than the whole tunnel.
- **On sudden opening**, it supplies water immediately from its own storage while the flow in the long tunnel accelerates, preventing negative pressure and cavitation.

Why the other options are wrong: **valves and gates** (a) are what *cause* the surge when they operate; a **draft tube** (b) sits downstream of the runner and recovers residual kinetic energy; a **spillway** (c) passes flood water over the dam and has nothing to do with the pressure conduit.

Types of surge tank: simple, **restricted orifice**, **differential (Johnson)**, and inclined. The restricted-orifice and differential types throttle the flow into the shaft and so damp the oscillation faster.

**When is a surge tank needed?** Where the pressure conduit is long relative to the head. Where one is impractical, a **pressure relief valve** serves instead.

The quantitative link, tested in Set 1 Q63 and Set 2 Q66:
> Closure time **< 2L/c** → sudden closure, Δh = **CV/g** (very large)
> Closure time **> 2L/c** → gradual closure, Δh = **VL/(gt)** (much smaller)

The surge tank effectively shortens the L that matters, which is precisely how it reduces the pressure rise.

examTip.trick: The surge tank gives the decelerating water column a **free surface** to rise into, turning a destructive pressure wave into a slow rise and fall of level.
examTip.mnemonic: **It protects only what is UPSTREAM of it** — the long low-pressure headrace tunnel. The short penstock **below** the tank still takes the full water hammer and is built strong enough for it. Place the tank as close to the turbine as the topography allows.

questions.stem: The discharge passing over an ogee weir is proportional to:
questions.solution:
**H^(3/2).**

The discharge over any weir with a horizontal crest — ogee, broad-crested or sharp-crested rectangular — follows

> **Q = C · B · H^(3/2)**

where B is the crest length and H the head over the crest. Hence **Q ∝ H^(3/2)**.

**Where the 3/2 power comes from.** Discharge is velocity × area. The velocity over the crest scales as √H (from Torricelli, v ∝ √(2gH)), and the flow **area** also grows with head, scaling as H. Multiplying:

> Q ∝ √H × H = **H^(3/2)** ✓

That reasoning also reveals why the exponent differs for a V-notch: there the width of flow grows *with* the depth, so the area scales as H² and

> Q ∝ √H × H² = **H^(5/2)** — option (d), the triangular weir result

The exponents worth carrying:

| Device | Q proportional to |
|---|---|
| **Rectangular / broad-crested / ogee weir** | **H^(3/2)** |
| **Triangular (V-notch) weir** | **H^(5/2)** |
| Trapezoidal (Cipolletti) weir | H^(3/2) |
| Orifice, siphon spillway (running full) | **H^(1/2)** |
| Venturi flume | H^(3/2) |

Note that **√H (option b) is the orifice law**, not a weir law — it applies when the opening is fully submerged and the area is fixed, as in the siphon spillway of Set 1 Q4.

The practical consequence of the 3/2 power: a **small rise in head passes a large increase in discharge**, which is what makes a weir an effective flood-passing structure and also a good flow-measuring device. It is the same relation used in Set 2 Q71 to find the head over a broad-crested weir from a known discharge.

**Correction to the circulating key.** The answer sheet keys (b), √H, and its accompanying note claims the discharge is "proportional to the cube root of the upstream water head" — but then prints the Francis formula **Q = C·B·H^(3/2)**, which contradicts both the keyed letter and the note. Neither √H nor a cube root is correct; the exponent is 3/2, so the answer is (c).

verification.notes: The circulating key answers (b) √H and describes the relation as a 'cube root', yet prints the Francis formula Q = C·B·H^(3/2) immediately beneath. The correct exponent is 3/2. √H is the orifice law, not a weir law, and H^(5/2) applies to a V-notch. Answer corrected to (c).

examTip.trick: Integrating the velocity **√(2gh)** over the depth of the nappe gives **h^(3/2)** — velocity varies as √h and the flow area as h.
examTip.mnemonic: **All weirs of constant width give H^(3/2); a V-notch gives H^(5/2)** because its width grows with depth too. That higher exponent is exactly why a **V-notch suits SMALL flows** — a small discharge still produces a readable head.

questions.stem: Which of the following expressions is correct?
questions.solution:
**GM = I/V − BG.**

For a floating body, the three points on the centreline are B (centre of buoyancy), G (centre of gravity) and M (metacentre). The distance from B up to M is

> **BM = I/V**

where I is the second moment of area of the **water-plane section** about the axis of tilt, and V the **displaced volume**. The metacentric height then follows from the geometry BM = BG + GM:

> **GM = BM − BG = I/V − BG** ✓

**Note that option (b) is algebraically the same statement rearranged**, so it is not *false* as an identity — but the question asks for the standard expression for the quantity that matters, and it is GM that is wanted, since GM is what decides stability. Read the options as "which is the correct formula", and (a) is the intended and conventional form.

**Why GM is the quantity of interest:**

| GM | Equilibrium |
|---|---|
| **Positive (M above G)** | **Stable** — a righting couple restores the body |
| Zero | Neutral |
| Negative (M below G) | **Unstable** — the body capsizes |

**Experimental determination:**
> GM = (w · x)/(W · tan θ)

by shifting a known weight w a distance x across the deck and measuring the resulting angle of tilt θ.

**A design tension worth knowing.** A large GM gives strong stability but a short, violent roll, since the period of oscillation is
> T = 2π √(k²/(g · GM))

so GM is chosen as a compromise rather than simply maximised — a "stiff" vessel is uncomfortable and hard on its structure, a "tender" one has little margin.

Contrast the **fully submerged** body, where the displaced shape does not change on tilting: there the metacentre concept does not apply, and stability requires only that **B lie above G**.

examTip.trick: **GM = BM − BG** with **BM = I/V**, so **GM = I/V − BG** ✓. I is the second moment of the **waterline plane** about the axis of tilt.
examTip.mnemonic: **I ∝ beam³**, which is why a wide raft is very stable and a log rolls. Design tension: a **large GM is stable but rolls harshly**; a small positive GM is comfortable but leaves little margin. GM is measured in practice by the **inclining experiment**.

questions.stem: What is the detention time for a septic tank?
questions.solution:
**24 hours.**

A septic tank is a watertight settling and digestion chamber for the on-site treatment of household sewage. A detention time of about **24 hours** is provided so that the solids have time to settle and the retained sludge can undergo **anaerobic digestion**.

Standard design features, all commonly examined:

| Feature | Value |
|---|---|
| **Detention time** | **24 hours** (12–24 h in some codes for larger tanks) |
| Length : breadth | **2 : 1 to 4 : 1** |
| **Minimum width** | **750 mm** |
| Minimum liquid depth | 1.0 to 1.8 m |
| Free board | 300 mm |
| Compartments | **Two**, the first about ⅔ of the length |
| **Sludge removal interval** | **2 to 3 years** |
| Sludge allowance | ~30 L per person per year |

**How it works.** Sewage entering the tank separates into three layers: a floating **scum** of grease and light matter, a clear middle **liquid** zone, and a bottom **sludge** blanket. Anaerobic bacteria digest the sludge, reducing its volume and converting organics to gases — methane, carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulphide — which are vented.

The two-compartment arrangement matters: most settlement occurs in the first chamber, and the second polishes the effluent and guards against carry-over of solids if the first is disturbed. **Baffles or T-pipes** at inlet and outlet keep the scum layer from escaping.

**The critical limitation, and the reason septic tanks are so often mis-specified.** A septic tank removes only about **30 to 50% of BOD**; its effluent is anaerobic, foul and still dangerous. It **must** be followed by secondary disposal — a **soak pit, dispersion trench or leach field** — sized from the soil's percolation rate. Discharging septic tank effluent directly to a drain or watercourse is a public health hazard, and treating the tank as complete treatment is the commonest error in practice.

Septic tanks suit **unsewered areas** — much of Nepal outside the larger municipalities — and require permeable soil and a water table well below the disposal field.

examTip.trick: A septic tank must hold sewage long enough for **solids to settle and anaerobic digestion to begin** — a day is the conventional design figure for domestic use.
examTip.mnemonic: **Detention 24 hours; sludge removed every 1–2 years.** The **effluent is NOT treated** — it still carries pathogens and BOD, which is why it must go to a **soak pit or drain field**, never to a watercourse. That second stage is the part most often omitted or undersized.

questions.stem: Which pipe is strong in resisting inside stress but weak when stressed from outside?
questions.solution:
**Steel.**

A steel pipe is thin-walled and made of a material of very high tensile strength, so it resists **internal** pressure extremely well: the hoop tension is carried easily, and steel penstocks routinely operate at heads of hundreds of metres.

The same thinness makes it weak against **external** pressure. Loading from outside — earth pressure, traffic, or an internal vacuum during rapid drawdown or a closed valve — puts the wall into **compression**, and a thin shell in compression **buckles (collapses inward)** long before the material yields. Buckling depends on stiffness and geometry, not strength, so the high yield stress of steel does not help.

The pipe materials compared:

| Material | Internal pressure | External pressure | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Steel** | **Excellent** | **Poor — buckles** | Light, long lengths, weldable; needs protection against corrosion |
| Cast iron | Good | Good | Heavy, brittle; life ~100 years; being superseded |
| Ductile iron | Very good | Good | Stronger and tougher than CI; needs internal and external protection |
| Concrete / RCC | Moderate | **Very good** | Heavy, low corrosion, little maintenance; not for small diameters |
| PVC / HDPE | Moderate | Moderate | Light, corrosion-free, cheap; low temperature and UV limits |

**Design consequences for steel pipe:**
- Wall thickness from the hoop stress relation **t = pD/(2σ)**, using the pressure *including* the water-hammer rise.
- A separate **check against external collapse**, and **stiffener rings** where buried deep or under vacuum.
- **Air valves** at summits, so the pipe cannot draw a vacuum when drained.
- Protection against corrosion — lining, coating, wrapping, or cathodic protection — since a thin wall has little corrosion allowance.

This is why steel is the standard for **penstocks and pumping mains** under high internal pressure, while large gravity mains and culverts under deep fill are often concrete.

examTip.trick: A **thin steel pipe** is excellent in **hoop tension** (internal pressure) but has almost no resistance to **buckling under external pressure** — the shell simply collapses inward.
examTip.mnemonic: **Internal pressure puts the wall in TENSION (strong); external pressure puts it in COMPRESSION and it BUCKLES (weak).** Which is exactly why a main being drained needs a **large-orifice air valve** to admit air — otherwise the vacuum collapses the pipe. It is a real maintenance failure mode.

questions.stem: Why is an air gap left at the top of sewers?
options: To meet the fluctuation of sewage inflow
To maintain open channel flow condition
To provide space over sewage for ventilation
questions.solution:
**All of the above.**

Sewers are deliberately designed to run **part full** — commonly half to three-quarters full at the design peak — and the void above the flow serves three purposes at once:

- **Absorbing fluctuation.** Sanitary flow varies widely through the day and grows over the design period. The spare capacity accommodates the peaks without surcharging, and gives room for the growth the sewer was sized for.
- **Maintaining open channel flow.** A part-full sewer flows under **gravity at atmospheric pressure**, so it can be designed by Manning's equation with a free surface. Once it runs full it becomes a pressure conduit, the hydraulics change entirely, and any surcharge can back sewage up into house connections.
- **Ventilation.** This is the most important of the three. Sewage decomposes anaerobically and generates **hydrogen sulphide, methane, carbon dioxide and ammonia**. The air space lets these gases move along the sewer to ventilating columns and manhole covers instead of accumulating.

Since all three are genuine reasons, (d) is the answer.

**Why ventilation is critical, not merely desirable.** Hydrogen sulphide is the central problem. It is **toxic** — and it deadens the sense of smell, so its rotten-egg odour is no reliable warning to anyone entering a manhole. It is also **corrosive by an indirect route**: H₂S released into the air space is oxidised by bacteria on the damp crown of the pipe into **sulphuric acid**, which attacks cement concrete. The resulting **crown corrosion** destroys sewers from the inside top downward, and is the reason ventilation and adequate velocity matter so much. **Methane** adds an explosion risk.

The companion design requirement is velocity: a **self-cleansing velocity of 0.6 to 0.9 m/s** at minimum flow keeps solids moving so they cannot settle and decompose in the first place, with a maximum of about 2.4 to 3.0 m/s to avoid eroding the invert.

A useful hydraulic fact that makes part-full design work well: in a circular pipe the **velocity is maximum at 0.81D** depth and the **discharge maximum at 0.95D** — so a sewer flowing part full performs nearly as well as one flowing full, and rather better in places.

examTip.trap: "All of the above" — read every option. The air space serves ventilation, surge capacity, and access at once.
examTip.trick: The critical reason is **ventilation**: sewer gases must escape. A sealed sewer accumulates **H₂S**, which bacteria on the moist crown oxidise to **sulphuric acid**.
examTip.mnemonic: **CROWN CORROSION destroys concrete sewers from the inside within decades.** The defences are ventilation, maintaining **self-cleansing velocity** (so the sewage does not go septic), and acid-resistant linings on large sewers.

questions.stem: 1 TCU is equivalent to:
options: The colour produced by 1 g of platinum cobalt
The colour produced by 1 mg of platinum cobalt
The colour produced by 1 mg of platinum cobalt in 1 L of distilled water
The colour produced by 1 mg of platinum cobalt in 1 mL of distilled water
questions.solution:
**The colour produced by 1 mg of platinum cobalt in 1 litre of distilled water.**

A colour unit must specify **both a mass and a volume** — a concentration — because colour intensity depends on how much colouring matter is present per unit volume of water. That immediately rules out options (a) and (b), which name a mass with no volume at all.

Between the remaining two, the standard is **1 mg per litre**, not per millilitre. A milligram in a millilitre would be a thousand times more concentrated, an absurdly strong reference.

> **1 TCU = colour of 1 mg/L of platinum, as the chloroplatinate ion, in distilled water**

The unit is also called the **Hazen unit**, and the scale the **platinum–cobalt scale**. Measurement is by comparison against calibrated standards in a **tintometer** (Lovibond) or by spectrophotometer.

**Standards:** drinking water should ideally be **5 TCU**, with **15 TCU** the permissible limit where no alternative source exists.

**True versus apparent colour** — a distinction the definition depends on:

| | Caused by | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| **True colour** | **Dissolved** substances — humic acid, tannins, iron, manganese | After **filtering out** suspended matter |
| Apparent colour | True colour **plus suspended solids** | On the unfiltered sample |

TCU is a measure of **true** colour, which is why the sample is filtered or centrifuged first.

The companion aesthetic parameters, each with its own unit and instrument: **turbidity** in NTU by nephelometer (limit 5 NTU), **taste and odour** by the threshold odour number, and **pH** by pH meter (6.5 to 8.5). Colour is not in itself a health hazard, but it makes water unacceptable to consumers — and consumers who reject a treated supply will return to an unsafe one, which is why aesthetic quality is treated as a genuine engineering requirement.

examTip.trick: The colour unit is defined against a **platinum-cobalt standard** — 1 mg of platinum per litre produces 1 True Colour Unit (also called 1 Hazen unit).
examTip.mnemonic: **Colour ≤ 5 TCU and turbidity ≤ 5 NTU (ideally 1) for drinking water.** They measure different things: **colour is DISSOLVED matter, turbidity is SUSPENDED matter** — which is why the sample is filtered before a true colour reading.

questions.stem: Spot welding is used when two plates are placed:
options: At right angles to each other
questions.solution:
**One below the other** — that is, **overlapping**.

Spot welding, properly **resistance spot welding**, clamps two **overlapping** sheets between a pair of copper electrodes and passes a heavy current through them. The electrical resistance at the interface generates intense local heat, the metal fuses at that point, and the electrode pressure forges the joint. The result is a discrete **spot** of weld, and a row of such spots forms the joint.

The geometry is essential to the process: the current must pass **through both thicknesses in series**, so the sheets have to lie face to face. Plates butted edge to edge, side by side, or at right angles offer no such path and cannot be spot welded.

**Characteristics:** no filler metal, no flux, no shielding gas; very fast, and readily automated. It suits **thin sheets**, typically up to about 3 mm, which is why it dominates automobile body assembly and sheet-metal fabrication rather than heavy structural work.

The welding processes and the joints they suit:

| Process | Joint geometry | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **Spot welding** | **Overlapping (lap) joint** | **Thin sheets**, sheet metal, car bodies |
| Butt weld | Plates **in the same plane**, edge to edge | Main tension members; develops full plate strength |
| **Fillet weld** | Plates **at right angles** or lapped | Connections, brackets, cleats — the structural workhorse |
| Seam welding | Overlapping | A continuous line of spots — tanks, drums |
| Plug / slot weld | Overlapping | Where access permits only one side |

So option (d) describes a **fillet** weld and option (b) a **butt** weld.

Recall from Set 2 Q92 that a fillet weld's effective throat is only **0.7 × the size**, whereas a full-penetration **butt weld** is taken at the **full thickness** of the thinner plate — which is why butt welds are specified where the connection must be as strong as the member itself.

examTip.trick: Spot welding fuses **overlapping** sheets at discrete points by passing current through electrodes clamped either side — so the plates must be **lapped**, one on top of the other.
examTip.mnemonic: **Spot and seam welding need a LAP; butt welding needs plates edge to edge.** Spot welding suits thin sheet and is a production process; structural steelwork uses fillet and butt welds instead.

questions.stem: What is ponding?
options: Hold back of water to form pond
Storing water for long period of time
Storing water for using in peak period
questions.solution:
**All of the above.**

Ponding — or **pondage** — is the provision of a limited body of stored water behind a diversion structure, and each option describes one aspect of it:

- **Holding back water to form a pond** is the physical arrangement.
- **Storing water** is what the pond does, though for a limited period.
- **Storing water for the peak period** is the operational purpose: releasing it when demand is highest.

Since all three describe the same provision, (d) is the answer.

**Where it matters in hydropower.** A pure run-of-river plant generates whatever the river happens to be carrying at that moment, so it cannot follow the daily demand curve. Adding **pondage** — a small forebay or pond holding a few hours to a day of flow — lets the plant store water through the night when demand is low and release it at a higher rate during the **evening peak**. The plant becomes a daily peaking station without needing a large reservoir.

The distinction from **storage** is one of timescale, and it is the examinable point:

| | **Pondage** | **Storage** |
|---|---|---|
| Period regulated | **Hours to a day (or a week)** | **Seasonal — months** |
| Structure | Small pond, forebay, barrage | Large dam and reservoir |
| Purpose | Follow the **daily** demand peak | Carry monsoon flow into the **dry season** |
| Land, cost, resettlement | Small | Large |

**For Nepal this is a real design lever.** Most schemes are run-of-river because the terrain gives high head over short distances and large reservoirs bring severe environmental, resettlement and sedimentation problems. Pondage is therefore added wherever the topography allows, so that the plant can at least meet the evening peak, even though it cannot solve the **seasonal** deficit between monsoon and winter flows. Only genuine storage projects can do that.

Note that pondage also **traps sediment**, so a pond needs flushing arrangements — which is why a settling basin and a flushing regime are designed alongside it.

examTip.trap: "All of the above" — the word **ponding** has several legitimate meanings in civil engineering, and the question is testing whether you know more than one.
examTip.trick: It can mean a **curing method** for concrete slabs (retaining water on the surface), **water accumulating** on a flat roof or pavement, and a **progressive roof failure** where deflection collects water, which adds load, which increases deflection.
examTip.mnemonic: **The dangerous meaning is the PROGRESSIVE one** — on a flat roof, ponding can be self-amplifying and cause collapse, which is why flat roofs are given a positive fall and an overflow.

questions.stem: Extra widening is:
questions.solution:
**Both psychological and mechanical widening.**

Extra widening is the additional carriageway width provided on a **horizontal curve** over and above the width needed on a straight. IRC treats it as the sum of two independent components:

> **W_e = W_m + W_ps**

**Mechanical widening** accounts for the geometry of the vehicle itself. A vehicle negotiating a curve tracks a wider path than its own width, because the **rear wheels follow a shorter radius than the front wheels** — the phenomenon of off-tracking. It depends on the wheelbase:

> W_m = **n l² / (2R)**

with n the number of lanes, l the wheelbase (6.1 m for a truck) and R the curve radius.

**Psychological widening** accounts for driver behaviour. Drivers instinctively keep further from the edge and from oncoming vehicles on a curve, so extra width is needed for comfort and safety quite apart from the vehicle's geometry. It depends on **speed**, not on the wheelbase:

> W_ps = **V / (9.5 √R)**

with V the design speed in km/h.

Note how the two components differ in what governs them — vehicle dimensions against driver psychology — which is why both must be computed and added rather than one being taken as a proxy for the other.

**Practical points:**
- Both terms vary as **1/R** or 1/√R, so extra widening matters most on **sharp** curves and becomes negligible on flat ones. IRC requires it only for radii below about 300 m.
- On a **single-lane** road the psychological component is omitted, since there is no oncoming vehicle in the same carriageway.
- Extra widening is introduced **progressively along the transition curve**, reaching its full value at the start of the circular arc — applied on the **inner** edge of the curve, or split between both edges.

Option (d) is simply the location where widening is applied, not a component of it.

examTip.trick: Extra widening on a horizontal curve has **two components**: **mechanical** (the rear wheels track inside the front wheels, so the vehicle occupies more width) and **psychological** (drivers keep further from the edge on a curve).
examTip.mnemonic: **W_e = nl²/2R + V/(9.5√R)** — the first term mechanical, the second psychological. Both grow as the radius falls, which is why tight curves on hill roads need substantial widening.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of providing free board?
options: Stability against overturning and safety against gully erosion
Stability against overturning and safety against frost crack
questions.solution:
**Option (b)** is the keyed answer.

**What freeboard actually does.** Freeboard is the vertical distance between the design water level and the top of the structure — the crest of a canal bank, an embankment or a dam. Its purposes are:

- **Preventing overtopping**, which is the primary reason. The margin absorbs wave action, wind set-up, surges from sudden gate operation, and the simple uncertainty in the estimated design flood.
- **Protecting the embankment.** Overtopping of an earth bank causes erosion of the crest and downstream face, and can breach it entirely within minutes. The freeboard keeps the saturation line and the water surface below the crest, which preserves the **stability** of the section — the sense in which the keyed option's "stability against overturning" can be read.
- Allowing for **settlement** of the embankment over time, and for silting of the bed which raises water levels.

Typical values: **0.3 m** for a small canal discharging under 1 m³/s, rising to **0.75 to 1.0 m** for a main canal; for a dam, computed from wave run-up using the fetch and design wind.

**Flagged for review.** None of the four printed options states the real purpose of freeboard — preventing overtopping. The keyed option (b) pairs a defensible idea (stability) with **frost cracking**, which has little to do with freeboard and is a marginal concern in most of Nepal's canal systems; option (a) pairs the same idea with **gully erosion**, which is a surface-drainage problem on slopes rather than a freeboard issue. The two differ only in that second clause, and neither clause is the reason freeboard is provided. The keyed answer is retained so the paper matches the original sitting, but the question is poorly framed and the owner may prefer to replace it. What a candidate should carry forward is the correct principle stated above, not the choice between these options.

verification.notes: None of the printed options states the actual purpose of freeboard, which is to prevent overtopping by waves, surges and flood uncertainty. Options (a) and (b) differ only in a second clause (gully erosion vs frost crack), neither of which is a freeboard consideration. The keyed answer (b) is retained to match the original sitting, but the question is poorly framed and should be reviewed or replaced before use in a paid set.

examTip.trick: A retaining structure's toe or base projection serves stability, and depth serves protection — so a single feature can address both **overturning** and **frost** at once.
examTip.mnemonic: **A retaining wall is checked for FOUR things: overturning (FoS 2.0), sliding (1.5), bearing (3.0), and OVERALL slope stability (1.5).** The fourth is the one most often skipped — and on a Nepali hillside it frequently governs. The commonest actual cause of failure, though, is **blocked drainage**.

questions.stem: The method which uses dead furrows on cropped farms for drainage of excess irrigation or rain water is called:
questions.solution:
**Bedding.**

The **bedding method** is a **surface** drainage technique for flat, poorly drained cropland. The field is ploughed into a series of raised **beds** separated by shallow channels called **dead furrows**. Crops grow on the crowned beds, while excess surface water runs off the bed slopes into the dead furrows and is carried away to a field drain or collector ditch.

It is simple, needs no buried pipework, and is well suited to **heavy, slowly permeable soils** where sub-surface drainage would be ineffective because water cannot percolate downward fast enough to reach a buried drain.

Typical dimensions: beds **10 to 30 m wide** with a crown height of 0.2 to 0.4 m, laid out so the dead furrows run down the prevailing land slope.

The drainage methods distinguished:

| Method | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Bedding** | **Surface** | **Raised beds with dead furrows between them** |
| Surface inlet | Surface | A grated inlet admitting ponded surface water into a sub-surface drain |
| **Tile drainage** | **Sub-surface** | Buried perforated pipe (clay tile or perforated PVC) lowering the water table |
| French drain | Sub-surface | A trench filled with **coarse stone**, no pipe; intercepts seepage |
| Open ditch | Surface | Open channels collecting run-off |
| Vertical drainage | Sub-surface | **Tube wells** pumping to lower the water table |

The **surface versus sub-surface** distinction is the organising idea: surface methods remove **ponded water from the ground surface**, while sub-surface methods **lower the water table** below the root zone.

**Why agricultural drainage matters.** It is the remedy for **waterlogging** — the condition in which a high water table saturates the root zone, displaces soil air and suffocates the crop, and then draws salts to the surface as the shallow water evaporates. Nepal's Terai canal commands are vulnerable precisely because canal seepage raises the water table in flat terrain with impervious subsoil. As Set 2 Q96 noted, canal **lining** removes the cause; drainage removes the effect, and both are usually needed.

examTip.trick: **Bedding** shapes the field into broad, gently crowned strips separated by **dead furrows** that act as shallow surface drains.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bedding is SURFACE drainage for flat, slowly permeable land** — cheap and shallow. Compare **subsurface (tile) drainage**, which lowers the water table itself and is what waterlogging and salinity actually require.

questions.stem: What are cross drainage works carrying a canal over a natural drain called?
questions.solution:
**Aqueduct and syphon aqueduct.**

Cross-drainage works are classified by **which watercourse passes over which**, and — for the canal-over-drain cases — whether the lower one flows under pressure. Two questions therefore settle the name:

| Canal is | Drain flows | Structure |
|---|---|---|
| **Above** the drain | Freely, at atmospheric pressure | **Aqueduct** |
| **Above** the drain | **Under pressure** through a barrel | **Syphon aqueduct** |
| **Below** the drain | Canal flows freely | **Super passage** |
| **Below** the drain | **Canal flows under pressure** | **Canal syphon** |

So the two structures carrying the **canal over the drain** are the **aqueduct** and the **syphon aqueduct** — option (a).

The distinction between them is the available headroom. In an **aqueduct** there is enough clearance for the drain to pass beneath as **open channel flow**. Where the drain bed cannot be lowered enough and the canal must be kept high, the drainage is forced through a **barrel under pressure** — a syphon aqueduct — with the floor of the drain depressed and then raised again on the far side.

The other two are the mirror images: a **super passage** carries the drain over the canal with the canal flowing freely below, and a **canal syphon** (or level crossing where they meet) carries the canal under the drain in a pressurised barrel.

**How the choice is made in practice:** compare the **canal bed level with the drain's high flood level**. If the canal bed is well above the drain HFL, an aqueduct serves. If the drain HFL is above the canal bed but the canal must still cross over, a syphon aqueduct is needed. If the drain is much higher, a super passage or canal syphon is used.

Design considerations common to all: adequate **waterway for the design flood**, protection of the barrel floor and the transitions against scour, and — for the pressurised types — a **self-cleansing velocity** through the barrel so that silt does not deposit where it cannot be removed.

examTip.trap: The four cross-drainage works are easy to scramble, and the naming is not intuitive.
examTip.trick: Name them by **which one goes over**: **AQUEDUCT** — canal over drain, drain flows free. **SYPHON AQUEDUCT** — canal over drain, drain runs **under pressure**. **SUPER PASSAGE** — drain over canal, canal free. **CANAL SYPHON** — drain over canal, canal under pressure.
examTip.mnemonic: **"Aqueduct" always means the CANAL is on top. Add "syphon" when the thing underneath is pressurised.**

questions.stem: What can't you provide at a head regulator?
questions.solution:
**A canal aqueduct.**

A head regulator is the control structure at the **head of a canal**, where it takes off from a river, barrage or reservoir. Its job is to regulate the discharge entering the canal, exclude silt, and shut the canal off when required.

An **aqueduct** is something else entirely: a **cross-drainage work** carrying a canal over a natural drain at some point **along its length**. It belongs where the canal meets a stream, not at the offtake — so it cannot be a component of the head regulator. That is the whole of the question.

The genuine components of a barrage headworks and head regulator:

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **Head regulator gates** | Control the discharge entering the canal |
| **Divide wall** | Separates the **canal intake pocket** from the main river channel, creating still water in which silt can settle |
| **Under sluice** | Low-crested bays adjacent to the regulator that **scour out** the deposited silt and pass it downstream |
| **Fish ladder** | Lets fish **migrate upstream** past the obstruction |
| **Silt excluder** | Tunnels in the pocket floor that skim the bottom, silt-laden layer away from the canal |
| Guide banks, aprons, cut-offs | Training the approach flow and protecting against scour and seepage |

So options (b), (c) and (d) are all standard parts of the works, and only the aqueduct is out of place.

**Why the divide wall and under sluices work together**, since they are examined as a pair: the divide wall creates a **quiet pocket** in front of the canal intake so that suspended sediment settles rather than entering the canal; the **under sluices** then flush that accumulated deposit back into the river. Without the sluices the pocket would silt up and the wall would become useless.

This is the same principle as the **silt excluder** of Set 2 Q33 — exploiting the fact that sediment concentration is greatest near the bed, and arranging the works so the dirty bottom layer goes downstream while the cleaner upper layer enters the canal.

examTip.trick: A **head regulator** controls flow from the river into the canal, at the very start of the canal. A **canal aqueduct** carries a canal over a drainage line — a structure of the canal's route, not of its head.
examTip.mnemonic: **At the head you find: the head regulator, the SILT EXCLUDER, and the divide wall.** Cross-drainage works belong further down the alignment, wherever the canal meets a natural drain.

questions.stem: Which is not a fixed component?
questions.solution:
**Railway locomotive.**

Transportation infrastructure divides into **fixed** and **mobile** components, and the test is simply whether the item is permanently attached to a location:

| Fixed components — the **way** and its facilities | Mobile components — the **vehicles** |
|---|---|
| **Airport** — runways, taxiways, terminal, control tower | Aircraft |
| **Harbour** — docks, piers, quays, breakwaters | Ships |
| **Railroad track** — rails, sleepers, ballast, formation, signals | **Locomotives, wagons, coaches** |
| Roads, bridges, tunnels | Cars, buses, trucks |

A **locomotive moves along** the fixed track; it is not part of it. The other three options are all permanent works forming part of the way, so only (d) is mobile.

**Why the distinction matters to the engineer**, which is the point of teaching it:

| | Fixed components | Mobile components |
|---|---|---|
| Capital cost | **Very high**; long-lived assets | Lower per unit |
| Design life | Decades to a century | 15 – 40 years |
| Provided by | Usually the **State** or a public authority | Often operators, sometimes private |
| Engineer's role | **Design, construction, maintenance** | Specifying the design vehicle |
| Flexibility | Effectively **permanent** — location cannot be changed | Freely relocated |

The fixed components are what the civil engineer designs, and the mobile ones enter that design as **loading and geometric requirements** — the axle load and gauge that fix the rail section and sleeper spacing, the design aircraft that fixes runway length and pavement thickness, the design vessel that fixes berth depth, and the design vehicle whose wheelbase and dimensions fix the extra widening and turning radii of a road.

So the mobile component is not irrelevant to the design; it is the **input** to it. But it is not itself part of the fixed works.

examTip.trap: Read the **NOT**. The question is asking which item is **not** a fixed cost.
examTip.trick: **Fixed costs** do not vary with output — depreciation, insurance, taxes, permanent staff. **Variable costs** rise with use — fuel, consumables, operating labour, maintenance from running hours.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fixed costs accrue whether the plant runs or sits idle.** That distinction is what makes **break-even analysis** work, and what determines whether a plant should be run at all when prices fall.

questions.stem: For the BEIRI settling basin, which of the following statements is false?
options: It is used in Middle Marsyangdi
Plant needs to be closed during flushing operation
questions.solution:
**"It is continuous type" is the false statement** — the BEIRI basin is **discontinuous** (intermittent).

Settling basins are classified by how the accumulated sediment is removed:

| Type | Flushing | Plant operation during flushing |
|---|---|---|
| **Continuous** | Sediment removed **continuously** while the plant runs | Uninterrupted |
| **Intermittent / discontinuous** | Sediment allowed to accumulate, then **flushed periodically** | **Plant must be shut down or the basin isolated** |

The **BEIRI** (Bureau of Electricity and Irrigation Research Institute) design is of the **intermittent** type: sediment collects in the hopper, and when the deposit reaches a set level the basin is flushed. That is precisely why option (d) — the plant needing to be closed during flushing — is a **true** statement about it, and consistent with it being discontinuous.

So options (b), (c) and (d) are all true of the BEIRI basin: it is instrumented with **sensors** to detect the sediment level and trigger flushing, it is used at **Middle Marsyangdi**, and its flushing requires the plant to be taken off line. Only the claim that it is continuous is false.

**Why settling basins matter so much in Nepal.** Himalayan rivers carry very high loads of hard, angular quartz and feldspar — minerals harder than the steel of a turbine runner. Passed through the machine at high velocity, that sediment abrades buckets and guide vanes, destroys the designed profile and drives efficiency down; repair means dismantling the unit, so generation is lost as well as money spent.

A settling basin therefore widens the section so that velocity falls to about **0.2 to 0.4 m/s**, giving particles time to settle out before the water reaches the headrace and turbine. Target particle sizes are around **0.2 mm** for a Francis turbine and **0.1 mm or finer** for a high-head Pelton, since abrasion damage rises steeply with head.

The trade-off between the two types is straightforward: **continuous** basins avoid shutdowns but are more complex and costly; **intermittent** basins are simpler but sacrifice generation during each flush. The choice depends on the sediment load and on the value of the lost energy.

examTip.trap: Read the **FALSE**. Three statements will be true of the basin and one will not.
examTip.trick: Settling basins split into **continuous flow** (silt removed while the plant runs, by a flushing duct) and **intermittent** (the basin is taken out of service and emptied). Which type a given basin is, is a design fact to be checked, not assumed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Continuous flushing keeps the plant running but wastes water; intermittent saves water but interrupts generation.** For a Himalayan run-of-river scheme with heavy monsoon sediment, continuous flushing is usually worth the water it costs.

questions.stem: Which method is mostly adopted by business enterprises?
questions.solution:
**IRR** — the internal rate of return.

IRR is the discount rate at which a project's net present value is zero:

> NPV = Σ [C_t/(1 + IRR)^t] = 0

Businesses favour it because it expresses profitability as a **single percentage** that can be compared directly against the cost of capital, against the hurdle rate (MARR), and against other investment opportunities — including projects of quite different size and duration. A rate is intuitive to managers in a way that an absolute NPV figure is not.

The decision rule: **accept if IRR ≥ MARR**.

The alternatives and why they are weaker:

| Method | Basis | Time value of money? | Main weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Payback period** | Time to recover the initial outlay | **No** | **Ignores all cash flows after payback**; ignores discounting |
| Discounted payback | Same, on discounted flows | Yes | Still ignores flows beyond the payback point |
| **IRR** | Rate at which **NPV = 0** | **Yes** | Multiple IRRs possible; can misrank alternatives |
| ARR (accounting rate of return) | Average profit ÷ average investment | **No** | Uses accounting profit, not cash flow; no discounting |

So payback and ARR are popular for their simplicity but are not sound investment criteria — payback's fatal flaw is that a project which recovers its cost quickly and then earns nothing scores better than one which recovers slowly and then earns for decades.

**Two real limitations of IRR** worth knowing, since they are examined:
1. A cash flow with **several sign changes** can have **multiple IRRs**, none of them meaningful.
2. IRR can **rank mutually exclusive alternatives wrongly**, because a small project with a spectacular rate may leave most of the available capital idle. The remedy is **incremental analysis** — ranking by increasing investment and testing each increment against the MARR, as in Set 1 Q15 and Set 2 Q23.

For those reasons **NPV** is theoretically the superior criterion, and in practice firms compute both: NPV to decide, IRR to communicate.

examTip.trick: IRR is popular because it reports a **single percentage** that can be compared directly against the cost of capital, with no discount rate needing to be assumed first.
examTip.mnemonic: **IRR is the rate at which NPV = 0.** Its weaknesses matter though: it can give **multiple values** when cash flows change sign more than once, and it can **rank mutually exclusive projects wrongly**. For choosing *between* alternatives, **NPV is the safer criterion**.

questions.stem: Which is the first stage in a project formulation?
questions.solution:
**Setting objectives.**

Nothing else can sensibly begin until it is settled **what the project is for**. Objectives define what the project must achieve, and they are the reference against which every later step is judged — alternatives are compared against them, the plan is built to deliver them, and performance is measured against them.

The project formulation sequence:

| Stage | Content |
|---|---|
| 1. Identification of needs and opportunities | Recognising the problem the project would address |
| **2. Setting objectives** | **Defining clear, measurable goals** |
| 3. Identifying alternative solutions | Exploring different ways of meeting those goals |
| 4. Evaluation and selection | Comparing alternatives on technical, financial, economic, social and environmental criteria |
| 5. Preparation of the project proposal | Detailing the chosen option — schedule, budget, resources |

**Why planning cannot come first.** A plan is a route to a destination. Planning before the objectives are fixed means scheduling work whose purpose has not been agreed — the commonest cause of scope creep and of projects that finish on time and on budget while failing to solve anything.

**Controlling and evaluating** belong to the later phases of the project **cycle**, not to formulation at all:

> **Formulation → Appraisal → Implementation → Monitoring and control → Evaluation**

Control is exercised *during* execution, comparing progress against the plan; evaluation happens *after*, judging whether the objectives were met.

**What makes an objective usable** is worth knowing, since "setting objectives" is easy to state and hard to do: it must be **specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound**. "Improve irrigation" is not an objective; "deliver a dependable supply to 1,200 ha of command area by 2030" is — because it can be designed for, and afterwards it can be checked.

In Nepal's public sector this discipline is formalised through the **logical framework (logframe)** approach used by the National Planning Commission and by donor-funded projects, which requires goals, purpose, outputs and activities each to carry **verifiable indicators**.

examTip.trick: Everything downstream depends on the objective — you cannot generate alternatives, screen them, or appraise them until you know what the project is for.
examTip.mnemonic: **Objectives → identification of alternatives → screening → feasibility → detailed formulation → appraisal → implementation.** A project that skips the first step is usually a solution looking for a problem, and it shows up later as scope creep.

questions.stem: Salvage value is defined as:
options: Value of dismantled materials of a property at the end of its utility period
Estimated value of a built-up property at the end of its useful life without being dismantled
Value of the property shown in the account book in that particular year
Present value of a property considering it to be replaced at the current market rates
questions.solution:
**The estimated value of a property at the end of its useful life, without being dismantled.**

Salvage value is what an asset is still worth when the owner has finished with it — sold **as it stands**, still assembled and potentially still usable by someone else. It is also called **disposal**, **residual** or **terminal** value, and it appears as the final cash inflow in an economic analysis.

The critical distinction is from **scrap value**, which option (a) describes:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Salvage value** | Value at the end of useful life, **sold intact / not dismantled** |
| **Scrap value** | Value of the **dismantled materials** — the metal, timber and rubble |
| **Book value** | Cost **less accumulated depreciation**, as recorded in the accounts |
| **Replacement value** | Cost of providing an equivalent new asset at **current market rates** |
| Market value | What it would actually fetch today |

So options (c) and (d) name **book value** and **replacement value** respectively — all four options are real valuation terms, and the question is testing whether they are kept apart.

**Where salvage value enters the calculation.** It reduces the net cost of ownership, and it appears in every depreciation formula:

> **Straight line:** annual depreciation = (C − S)/n
> **Declining balance:** a fixed percentage of the reducing book value each year
> **Sinking fund:** a uniform annual deposit accumulating to (C − S) over n years

where C is the initial cost, S the salvage value and n the useful life. In present-worth analysis the salvage value is discounted back as a single receipt at year n.

A point worth noting: salvage value can be **negative** where disposal costs money — demolition, decommissioning, site restoration or safe disposal of hazardous material. A cost of that kind must be included as an outflow at the end of the study period, and for some infrastructure it is substantial.

examTip.trap: **Scrap value** is the near-miss: scrap is the value of the **dismantled materials**; salvage is the value of the property **without being dismantled**.
examTip.trick: The question's phrase "without being dismantled" is the discriminator — it rules out scrap explicitly.
examTip.mnemonic: **Salvage = still standing and usable. Scrap = the value of the rubble** (typically about 10% of original cost, and it is the S in the depreciation formula (C − S)/n).

questions.stem: Speed at a particular place at different times is:
questions.solution:
**Time mean speed (TMS).**

The two mean speeds differ in **what is held fixed** — a place or an instant — and the question specifies a fixed **place** observed over **different times**:

| | **Time mean speed** | **Space mean speed** |
|---|---|---|
| Measured at | **A point**, over a period of **time** | Over a **length** of road, at a given instant |
| Averaging | **Arithmetic** mean of spot speeds | **Harmonic** mean |
| Formula | **v̄_t = Σv_i / n** | **v̄_s = n / Σ(1/v_i)** |
| Obtained from | Radar, enoscope, loop detector at a point | Travel time over a known length |

So "a particular place at different times" is a point measurement accumulated over time — the **arithmetic** average of the individual spot speeds, which is the **time mean speed**.

Space mean speed is the opposite arrangement: a **length** of road at a **given time**, obtained by dividing the distance by the average travel time.

**The relationship between them**, which is examined:
> **v̄_s ≤ v̄_t** always

Space mean speed is the lower of the two, and the gap widens as the speeds become more variable — because the harmonic mean weights slow vehicles more heavily. A slow vehicle occupies the test length for longer, so it contributes more to the space average than to the point average.

**Which one to use.** Space mean speed is the correct one for the fundamental traffic relation
> **q = k × v̄_s**

(flow = density × space mean speed), and for computing travel time over a route. Time mean speed is what a fixed speed-measuring device naturally reports, and it is what the percentile analysis for speed limits is based on.

**Correction to the circulating key.** The answer sheet keys (c), space mean speed, yet the explanation printed with it defines space mean speed as the "average speed of vehicles over a certain length of road at a given time" and time mean speed as the "average speed at a point over a period of time" — the second of which is exactly what the question describes. The key contradicts its own definitions; the answer is (b).

verification.notes: The circulating key answers (c), space mean speed. The question describes measurement at a fixed place over different times, which is the definition of time mean speed — and the source's own printed explanation says exactly that of TMS while keying SMS. Answer corrected to (b).

examTip.trap: **Time mean** and **space mean** speed are constantly swapped, and space mean is always the smaller of the two.
examTip.trick: **Time mean** = average of speeds of vehicles passing **one point over time** (arithmetic mean). **Space mean** = average speed over a **length of road at one instant** (harmonic mean).
examTip.mnemonic: **Time mean at a POINT over time; space mean over a LENGTH at an instant.** Space mean speed is what appears in **q = k × v_s**, the fundamental traffic relation — using time mean speed there is wrong.

questions.stem: With increase in temperature, viscosity of a liquid:
questions.solution:
**Decreases** (for a liquid).

The direction of the effect is opposite in liquids and gases, because viscosity arises from a different mechanism in each:

| Fluid | Viscosity arises from | Effect of rising temperature |
|---|---|---|
| **Liquid** | **Cohesive forces** between closely packed molecules | Cohesion weakens → **viscosity falls** |
| **Gas** | **Molecular momentum transfer** between layers | Molecules move faster → transfer increases → **viscosity rises** |

In a liquid the molecules are close together and held by intermolecular attraction. Heating gives them more thermal energy, they slip past one another more easily, and the resistance to shear falls. This is the everyday observation that hot oil pours more freely than cold.

In a **gas** the molecules are far apart and cohesion is negligible; viscosity comes from molecules crossing between adjacent layers and carrying momentum with them. Heating speeds that exchange up, so gas viscosity **increases** with temperature.

**Magnitudes for water**, to fix the scale:

| Temperature | Dynamic viscosity μ |
|---|---|
| 0°C | 1.79 × 10⁻³ Pa·s |
| **20°C** | **1.00 × 10⁻³ Pa·s** |
| 100°C | 0.28 × 10⁻³ Pa·s |

So the viscosity of water falls by a factor of more than six between freezing and boiling — not a small correction.

**Why it matters in practice.** Viscosity enters the Reynolds number, Re = ρVD/μ. A fall in μ **raises** Re, so warming a flow can push it from laminar into turbulent, changing the friction factor and the head loss. It also affects the settling velocity of sediment (through Stokes' law), the permeability of soil to water, and the workability of bituminous mixes — which is why bitumen viscosity is specified at 60°C and 135°C, and why paving temperature is controlled on site.

Note also that **pressure** has almost no effect on the viscosity of a liquid over ordinary ranges, so temperature is the variable that matters.

examTip.trick: A liquid's viscosity comes from **cohesion** between closely packed molecules, and heat weakens it. A **gas's** viscosity comes from **molecular momentum exchange** and therefore **increases** with temperature — the opposite behaviour.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hot oil runs; hot air drags.** Practical consequence in soil mechanics: since **k = Kγ/μ**, laboratory permeability results are corrected to **27 °C** before use — a real correction, not a formality, since μ nearly halves between 10 °C and 30 °C.

questions.stem: What is used in rainwater gutter in roof?
questions.solution:
**Steel sheet** — galvanised iron (GI) sheet in ordinary practice.

A gutter is a shallow channel fixed along the eaves of a roof to collect rainwater from the roof surface and lead it to a downpipe, keeping the discharge away from the walls and foundation. What it needs is a material that is:

- **Thin and light**, so it can be supported on brackets at intervals without a heavy structure;
- **Impervious** and able to be formed into a watertight channel with soldered or lapped joints;
- Readily **bent or pressed** into shape on site;
- **Corrosion-resistant**, since it is permanently exposed and repeatedly wetted.

Galvanised steel sheet meets all four, which is why it is the standard material for gutters and downpipes on ordinary buildings in Nepal.

Why the others fail: **cement and sand** (a, b) are constituents of mortar or concrete — far too heavy and brittle for a thin suspended channel, and prone to cracking. **Bitumen** (c) is a waterproofing material applied *to* a surface; it cannot form a self-supporting channel of its own.

The alternatives in use:

| Material | Note |
|---|---|
| **GI / galvanised steel sheet** | **The usual choice** — cheap, formable, adequately durable |
| Aluminium | Lighter, better corrosion resistance, costlier |
| Copper, lead | Very durable, expensive; heritage and high-end work |
| **uPVC / PVC** | Corrosion-free, light, snap-fit joints; **now very common** |
| Cast iron | Traditional, heavy, durable |
| Precast concrete / RCC channel | Only for large parapet gutters, integral with the structure |

**Design points examined alongside:** gutters must be laid to a **slope** of about 1 in 100 to 1 in 200 towards the outlet; the cross-sectional area follows from the roof catchment area and the design rainfall intensity; downpipes are provided at roughly one per 40 m² of roof; and the outlet must be screened to stop leaves blocking it.

Rainwater from the roof is also the source for **rainwater harvesting**, increasingly required in urban Nepal — in which case the first flush is diverted and the remainder led to a storage tank or recharge pit rather than to the drain.

examTip.trick: A gutter must be **impervious, formable into a channel section, and durable in continuous wetting** — which suits thin sheet metal (galvanised steel, aluminium) or uPVC.
examTip.mnemonic: **Size the gutter and downpipe from the ROOF AREA and the rainfall INTENSITY, not from habit.** In Nepal's monsoon intensities, undersized gutters overflow and the water runs down the wall — which is a damp problem, not a drainage inconvenience.

questions.stem: What is the process dealing with vertical curves and gradients?
questions.solution:
**Vertical alignment.**

A road's geometry is designed as two separate projections, and each has its own set of elements:

| | **Vertical alignment** | **Horizontal alignment** |
|---|---|---|
| Concerns | The **longitudinal profile** — the road seen from the side | The **plan** — the road seen from above |
| Elements | **Gradients, vertical curves (summit and valley)**, sight distance on grade | Straights, **circular curves, transition curves, superelevation, extra widening** |

So gradients and vertical curves belong to the **vertical alignment**, which is exactly what the question names.

**Gradients** — the rates of rise and fall — are classified as:

| Gradient | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Ruling gradient** | The design gradient, normally adopted |
| **Limiting gradient** | Steeper, used where the terrain makes the ruling gradient uneconomical |
| **Exceptional gradient** | Steeper still, only in short unavoidable stretches |
| **Minimum gradient** | Needed for **drainage** in a lined side drain, about 1 in 200 to 1 in 500 |

In mountainous terrain — most of Nepal — the ruling gradient is commonly about **5%**, with limiting and exceptional values of 6% and 7%. A **grade compensation** is applied on curves, where the curve resistance adds to the grade resistance.

**Vertical curves** are **parabolic**, giving a constant rate of change of grade:
- A **summit (crest) curve** is governed by **sight distance** — the driver must see far enough over the crest to stop, so the curve length follows from SSD or OSD.
- A **valley (sag) curve** is governed by **headlight sight distance at night** and by **passenger comfort**, since centrifugal force acts downward and adds to gravity.

Why the other options are wrong: **levelling** (d) is a *surveying operation* for determining elevations — it provides the data from which the profile is drawn, but it is not the design process. **Vertical control** (a) likewise refers to the network of benchmarks establishing reduced levels. Both are means of measurement rather than design of the alignment.

examTip.trick: Highway geometry splits into three: **horizontal alignment** (curves, superelevation, extra widening, transitions), **vertical alignment** (gradients, summit and valley curves), and **cross section** (camber, width, shoulders, side slopes).
examTip.mnemonic: **Gradient and vertical curves = vertical alignment. Camber and width = cross section.** Confusing gradient with the cross section is a standard trap — gradient runs *along* the road, camber *across* it.

questions.stem: In which of the following is scoping not required?
questions.solution:
**Option (c) is the keyed answer, but the key is at odds with the environmental legislation.**

**What the law actually requires.** Under Nepal's Environment Protection Act 2076 and Rules 2077, the environmental study tiers and their procedural requirements are:

| Level | Scope of project | Scoping required? | ToR required? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BES** — Brief Environmental Study | Small, minor impacts | **No** | No |
| **IEE** — Initial Environmental Examination | Moderate impacts | **No** | **Yes** |
| **EIA** — Environmental Impact Assessment | Major, significant impacts | **Yes** | **Yes** |

So **scoping is a defining requirement of the EIA process**, not something absent from it. Scoping is the stage at which the significant issues, the study boundaries and the alternatives to be examined are identified, and the approved **Terms of Reference** is then prepared from it. An EIA cannot proceed without both.

It follows that EIA is the **one option where scoping *is* required** — so it cannot be the answer to a question asking where it is not.

**What the source itself says.** The answer sheet keys (c) and annotates it "ToR: BES/IEE, Scoping: EIA". That note states plainly that scoping belongs to **EIA** — which contradicts the keyed letter. The key appears to answer the question "in which is scoping *required*", not the question as printed.

**Why this is flagged rather than simply corrected.** Read as printed, the question has **two defensible answers**: scoping is not required for either **BES** or **IEE**. Since the item cannot be resolved to a single correct option, it is marked for review rather than re-keyed to an arbitrary one of the two. Option (d), ToR, is not a study type at all but a document produced within one.

The knowledge a candidate should carry forward is the table above, and the standard EIA sequence: **screening → scoping and ToR approval → baseline study → impact prediction → mitigation → environmental management plan → monitoring and auditing**, with public consultation throughout.

verification.notes: The key answers (c) EIA, but scoping is a mandatory step of the EIA process — the source's own note says so. As printed, the question has two defensible answers (BES and IEE both lack a scoping requirement), so it cannot be re-keyed to a single option and is flagged for review. Owner should replace or reword this item before use in a paid set.

examTip.trick: **Scoping** determines which impacts a study must examine, and it is required for the fuller assessment, not for the preliminary screening-level one.
examTip.mnemonic: **IEE (Initial Environmental Examination) is the shorter study for smaller projects; EIA is the full one for large or sensitive projects.** The sequence for an EIA runs **screening → scoping → terms of reference → study → report → review → approval → monitoring**.

questions.stem: The cracking of concrete occurs first in:
questions.solution:
**All of the above.**

Cracking is governed by the **tensile strength of the concrete**, not by how the steel is arranged. Concrete is weak in tension — its flexural tensile strength is only about **0.7√f_ck** — so as soon as the tensile stress at the extreme fibre reaches that value, a crack forms. That happens in **every** reinforced section, whatever its reinforcement layout, and it happens on the **tension face** in each case.

Why the arrangement of steel makes no difference to the onset:

| Section | Steel arrangement | Where the first crack forms |
|---|---|---|
| **Singly reinforced** | Tension steel only | **Tension face** |
| **Doubly reinforced** | Tension **and** compression steel | **Tension face** — the compression steel is on the other side and cannot prevent it |
| **Balanced** | Proportioned so steel and concrete reach their limits together | **Tension face** |

The reinforcement's role begins *after* cracking: the steel carries the tension across the crack and controls its **width and spacing**, keeping the member serviceable. It does not prevent the crack from forming.

**The important consequences**, which is where this question leads:

- Cracking in RCC is **normal and expected**, not a defect in itself. What matters is **crack width**. IS 456 limits it to **0.3 mm** in ordinary conditions, and **0.2 mm or 0.1 mm** in aggressive or marine exposure, because wide cracks admit moisture and chlorides that corrode the reinforcement.
- Crack width is controlled by **bar spacing and cover**, and by using **more, smaller-diameter bars** rather than fewer large ones for the same area of steel — many fine cracks are far better than a few wide ones.
- **Minimum reinforcement** is required precisely so that when the concrete cracks, the steel can carry the released tension without itself yielding: IS 456 sets A_st,min/bd = **0.85/f_y** for beams.
- Where cracking must be avoided altogether, the answer is **prestressing** — pre-compressing the tension face so that applied load must first overcome that compression before any tension appears, as in Q20 of this paper.

Other causes of cracking that have nothing to do with load: **plastic shrinkage** while the concrete is fresh, **drying shrinkage**, **thermal** movement, and **settlement** of the formwork or the foundation.

examTip.trap: "All of the above" — read every option. Concrete cracks first wherever the **tensile** stress reaches its modest tensile strength.
examTip.trick: Concrete's tensile strength is only about **10% of its compressive strength** (roughly 0.7√f_ck), so cracking is essentially inevitable in any member carrying tension.
examTip.mnemonic: **Reinforced concrete design ASSUMES the concrete is cracked in tension** — the steel carries all of it. The design question is therefore not whether it cracks but whether the **crack WIDTH** stays within limits (0.3 mm normally, 0.2 mm in aggressive exposure).

questions.stem: Positive bending moment causes members to be:
questions.solution:
**Convex downward.**

A **positive (sagging)** bending moment bends the member so that it dips in the middle — the shape a simply supported beam takes under a downward load. Viewed from below, the underside bulges outward, so the member is **convex downward** (equivalently, concave upward).

The stress distribution follows directly, and this is the part that matters:

| | **Positive (sagging)** | **Negative (hogging)** |
|---|---|---|
| Deflected shape | Dips in the middle — **convex downward** | Arches up — **convex upward** |
| **Tension** on | **Bottom fibres** | **Top fibres** |
| Compression on | Top fibres | Bottom fibres |
| **Main steel goes** | **Bottom** | **Top** |
| Occurs at | **Mid-span** of a simply supported or continuous beam | **Supports** of a continuous beam; over the whole of a **cantilever** |

**The design consequence is the reason this is examined.** Concrete is weak in tension, so the reinforcement must be placed where the tension is. In a continuous beam the moment **changes sign**, so the main steel has to migrate: **bottom steel at mid-span, top steel over the supports.** Get that the wrong way round and the beam has no tensile capacity where it needs it most.

The crossover happens at the **point of contraflexure**, where the bending moment passes through zero while changing sign. Because the moment is zero there, it is the natural place to **curtail reinforcement** or locate a splice — the point tested in Set 1 Q89.

A **cantilever** is entirely in hogging, which is why its steel runs along the **top** throughout — a detail that is easy to get wrong on site, and one of the more common causes of cantilever failures.

The sign convention itself is arbitrary but universal: sagging positive, hogging negative. What is not arbitrary is the physical fact that tension develops on the **convex** face, whichever way the member bends.

examTip.trick: **Positive (sagging) moment** means **compression on top, tension at the bottom**, so the beam curves with its concave side upward — that is, **convex downward**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sagging holds water; hogging sheds it.** The detailing consequence is what matters: **sagging → main steel at the BOTTOM; hogging → main steel at the TOP.** Getting that reversed in a cantilever or over a continuous support is a real and dangerous site error.

questions.stem: If an irrigation channel has a side slope of 1 : S, bed width B, depth y and length L, then the total area of the side slopes is:
questions.solution:
**2Ly√(1 + S²).**

**Step 1 — sloping length of one side.** With a side slope of 1 vertical to S horizontal, a rise of y is accompanied by a horizontal run of Sy. By Pythagoras the sloping length is

> l = √(y² + S²y²) = **y√(1 + S²)**

**Step 2 — area of one side over the channel length:**
> A₁ = l × L = Ly√(1 + S²)

**Step 3 — both sides:**
> **A = 2Ly√(1 + S²)** ✓

Two checks eliminate the wrong options at once. The factor **2** is needed because a channel has two banks, which rules out (c) and (d). And the sloping length must be built from the **depth y**, not the bed width B, since the slope rises through the depth — which rules out (b) and (d).

**Why this quantity is wanted.** It is the area to be **lined**, so it feeds straight into the quantity and cost estimate. The total lined area of a trapezoidal channel is

> A_{lining} = L × (B + 2y√(1 + S²))

the bracket being the **wetted perimeter** P. So the question is really asking for the sloping part of the wetted perimeter multiplied by the length — and that same P is what appears in the hydraulic radius R = A/P used in Manning's equation.

The companion relations for the same trapezoidal section, worth keeping together:

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| Cross-sectional **area** of flow | A = By + Sy² |
| **Wetted perimeter** | P = B + 2y√(1 + S²) |
| Hydraulic radius | R = A/P |
| **Area of both side slopes over length L** | **2Ly√(1 + S²)** |

Note carefully whether a question writes the slope as **1 : S** (vertical : horizontal, as here) or **S : 1** (horizontal : vertical, as in Set 1 Q71). Reversing them is the commonest error in canal problems, and it changes the answer.

examTip.trick: The two sloping sides each have length **y√(1 + S²)** (from Pythagoras on a rise y and a run Sy), so the two together give **2y√(1 + S²)**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Wetted perimeter P = B + 2y√(1 + S²); area A = By + Sy².** With S = 0 these reduce to the rectangle's B + 2y and By ✓ — always check a channel formula against the rectangular case.

questions.stem: If D₁₀ of the particle is 2 mm with a discharge of 2 m³/s, then the longitudinal slope is:
questions.solution:
**1 in 820.**

Since a particle size and a discharge are given and a **bed slope** is asked for, this is Lacey's regime theory.

**Step 1 — Lacey's silt factor**, with the particle size in millimetres:
> f = 1.76 √d
> f = 1.76 × √2 = 1.76 × 1.4142 = **2.489**

**Step 2 — Lacey's regime slope:**
> S = f^{5/3} / (3340 · Q^{1/6})

**Step 3 — evaluate the two powers:**
> f^{5/3} = 2.489^{1.6667} = **4.570**
> Q^{1/6} = 2^{0.1667} = **1.1225**

**Step 4 — substitute:**
> S = 4.570/(3340 × 1.1225) = 4.570/3749 = 1.219 × 10⁻³
> S = **1 in 820** ✓

Note how weakly the slope depends on discharge — the **one-sixth power** means that doubling Q changes S by only about 11%. The silt factor, raised to the 5/3 power, dominates: a coarser bed material demands a much steeper regime slope.

The family of Lacey's regime equations, which are used together and are worth memorising as a set:

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Silt factor** | **f = 1.76 √d** (d in mm) |
| **Regime perimeter (waterway)** | **P = 4.75 √Q** |
| **Regime scour depth** | **R = 0.47 (Q/f)^{1/3}** |
| **Regime slope** | **S = f^{5/3}/(3340 Q^{1/6})** |
| Regime velocity | V = (Qf²/140)^{1/6} |
| Regime area | A = P × R |

These are the standard tools for designing a **stable (non-silting, non-scouring) channel in alluvium**, and for estimating the scour depth that fixes the foundation level of a bridge pier or the launching apron of a guide bank — as used in Set 2 Q74 for the weir length and Set 2 Q34 for the apron.

Lacey's theory assumes the channel has attained **regime**: flowing steadily in incoherent alluvium of the same character as the material it transports, with a stable width, depth and slope. Where those conditions do not hold — a rocky bed, a lined channel, or a river in flood — the equations do not apply.

examTip.trick: This is a **regime / tractive force** slope problem. **Lacey's silt factor f = 1.76√d** (d in mm), then **S = f^(5/3)/(3340 Q^(1/6))**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lacey's regime equations: P = 4.75√Q, R = 0.473(Q/f)^⅓, S = f^(5/3)/(3340 Q^(1/6)).** A channel "in regime" carries both its water **and its sediment load** without net scour or deposition — a stricter criterion than hydraulic efficiency alone.

questions.stem: Maximum bending moment in a three hinged arch under a point load occurs on either side of its crown at:
questions.solution:
**L/2√3 on either side of the crown.**

**Outline of the derivation.** For a three-hinged parabolic arch of span L and rise h carrying a point load W at distance x from the left support:

> R_{A} = W(L − x)/L,  R_{B} = Wx/L

Taking moments about the crown hinge gives the horizontal thrust H = Wx/(2h), and the arch axis is y = 4hx(L − x)/L². The bending moment at any section is the beam moment less the thrust moment:

> M = R_{A}x − Hy = (WL²x − 3WLx² + 2Wx³)/L²

Setting dM/dx = 0:
> L² − 6Lx + 6x² = 0
> x²  − Lx + L²/6 = 0

Solving the quadratic:
> x = L/2 ∓ **L/(2√3)**

So the two stationary points sit symmetrically at a distance **L/2√3 ≈ 0.2887 L** on either side of the crown, which is at mid-span.

**What this means physically.** A three-hinged arch has **zero moment at all three hinges** — the two springings and the crown. Between them the moment rises to a maximum and falls again, so there must be a peak on each side of the crown, and the derivation locates it at 0.289 L from the centre.

That is the real value of arch action: the horizontal thrust **subtracts** from the free-span beam moment everywhere, so an arch carries the same load with far smaller bending moments than a beam of equal span. The price is the **horizontal thrust** at the abutments, which must be resisted by massive foundations or a tie.

A further consequence worth noting from H = Wx/(2h): the **thrust is inversely proportional to the rise**. A shallow arch develops enormous thrust — which is why flat arches need heavy abutments, and why the three-hinged arch of Set 2 Q62 with only 8 m of rise over a 40 m span produced a thrust of 30 kN from an 80 kN load.

Being **statically determinate**, the three-hinged arch needs no compatibility condition — unlike the two-hinged arch of Set 2 Q28, which requires H = ∫(My ds/EI)/∫(y² ds/EI).

examTip.trick: For a three-hinged parabolic arch under a point load, the maximum moment occurs at a characteristic fraction of the span from the crown, and the **L/2√3** form is the standard result.
