examTip.mnemonic: **A three-hinged arch is DETERMINATE** — the crown hinge supplies the extra equation, so H = M_crown(as simple beam)/rise. Being determinate, it develops **no self-stress from settlement or temperature**, which is exactly why the form is used on compressible ground.

questions.stem: One litre of sewage, when allowed to settle for 30 minutes, gives a sludge volume of 27 cm³. If the dry weight of this sludge is 3.0 grams, then its sludge volume index will be:
questions.solution:
**9 mL/g.**

The **sludge volume index** is the volume occupied by one gram of dry sludge after 30 minutes of settling:

> **SVI = settled sludge volume (mL/L) / suspended solids concentration (g/L)**

**Substituting:**
> Settled volume = 27 cm³/L = **27 mL/L**
> Solids concentration = 3.0 g/L
> SVI = 27/3.0 = **9 mL/g**

Expressed in the more usual units, SVI = (V × 1000)/MLSS with MLSS in mg/L: (27 × 1000)/3000 = 9 — the same figure.

**What SVI tells the operator.** It measures the **settleability** of activated sludge, which is the crux of the process: the biology may work perfectly, but if the sludge will not settle in the secondary clarifier it escapes with the effluent and the plant fails.

| SVI (mL/g) | Settling character |
|---|---|
| **< 100** | **Good** — dense, compact, settles readily |
| 100 – 150 | Satisfactory |
| **> 150** | **Poor — bulking sludge** |

A value of 9 is exceptionally low, indicating a very dense, well-settling sludge.

**Sludge bulking** — a high SVI — is the classic operational problem of the activated sludge process. It is caused by the proliferation of **filamentous organisms** such as *Sphaerotilus*, and is provoked by a low food-to-microorganism ratio, nutrient deficiency (nitrogen or phosphorus), low dissolved oxygen, or a low pH. The sludge becomes light and fluffy, refuses to compact, and carries over into the final effluent.

Remedies: adjust the **F/M ratio** and sludge age, raise the dissolved oxygen, correct the nutrient balance, or dose chlorine or hydrogen peroxide to the return sludge to selectively kill the filaments.

The related control parameters of the process: **MLSS** (2000–4000 mg/L), **F/M ratio** (0.2–0.4), **sludge age** or mean cell residence time (5–15 days), and the **recirculation ratio**.

examTip.trick: **Sludge Volume Index SVI = (settled volume in ml/l × 1000)/(MLSS in mg/l)** — but read carefully what the question gives and what units it uses.
examTip.mnemonic: **SVI below 100 settles well; above 150 indicates SLUDGE BULKING** — filamentous organisms that will not settle, so solids escape over the final weir. Bulking is the classic operational failure of an activated sludge plant.

questions.stem: The kor depth for rice is 190 mm and the kor period is 14 days. The outlet factor for this will be:
questions.solution:
**637 hectares per cumec.**

The **outlet factor** is another name for the **duty** of water, and it is related to delta and base period by

> D = 8.64 B / Δ

where B is the period in **days** and Δ the depth in **metres**.

**Substituting the kor values:**
> Δ = 190 mm = **0.19 m**
> B = 14 days
> D = 8.64 × 14 / 0.19
> D = 120.96/0.19 = **636.6 ≈ 637 hectares/cumec**

**What "kor" means**, since the question depends on it. The **kor period** is the short critical spell, soon after sowing, when the crop needs its first and most important watering. The **kor depth** is the depth of water required in that single watering. Because it is the peak demand of the season, the **capacity of the outlet and the distributary is fixed by the kor requirement**, not by the seasonal average — which is exactly why the duty computed from kor figures is called the **outlet factor**.

Typical kor values:

| Crop | Kor depth | Kor period |
|---|---|---|
| **Rice** | **190 mm** | **14 days** |
| Wheat | 135 mm | 4 weeks |
| Sugarcane | 165 mm | 4 weeks |
| Cotton | 100 mm | 3 weeks |

**Where the 8.64 comes from:** 86 400 seconds in a day divided by the 10 000 m² in a hectare. The constant carries the unit conversion, so Δ must be in metres and D emerges in hectares per cumec.

Note the **inverse relationship**: a high duty means a low delta, because one cumec is then irrigating more land and applying less depth to each hectare. Rice, with its large delta, has a correspondingly low duty — 637 ha/cumec against several thousand for a light crop.

This is the same relation used in Set 1 Q95, worked in the other direction to find delta from a given duty.

examTip.trick: **Outlet discharge factor (duty) = 8.64 B/Δ**, with B in days and Δ in metres. Here: **8.64 × 14/0.19 = 636.6 ≈ 637 hectares per cumec** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Kor depth is the water needed at the CRITICAL growth stage, and the kor period is how long it must be delivered** — so it sizes the **peak** canal capacity, not the seasonal total. Note the inverse relation: **higher duty means LESS water per hectare**, so a high duty signals an efficient system.

questions.stem: How many members are selected by the Nepal Engineering Council itself?
questions.solution:
**Two.**

Section 3 of the **Nepal Engineering Council Act, 2055** lists the composition of the Council, and it distinguishes carefully between members **nominated by the Government**, members **elected by the Nepal Engineers' Association**, and members **nominated by the Council itself**. Only the last category answers the question, and it contains **two engineers**.

The full composition:

| Position | How appointed |
|---|---|
| **Chairman** | Nominated by the Government — bachelor's degree, **15 years'** experience |
| **Vice-chairman** | Nominated by the Government — bachelor's degree, **10 years'** experience |
| Five engineers | **Nominated by the Government** |
| President, Nepal Engineers' Association | Ex officio |
| Five engineers | **Elected by the Nepal Engineers' Association** |
| One Campus Chief | Nominated by the Government from among engineering college campus chiefs |
| One representative | Institute of Engineering, Tribhuvan University |
| **Two engineers** | **Nominated by the Council itself** ← the answer |
| Registrar | **Member-Secretary** |

Note the balance the Act strikes: the Government nominates the two senior officers and five members, the professional association elects five, the academic institutions are represented, and the Council itself co-opts two — so no single body controls the whole membership.

A further requirement worth knowing: nominations and elections to the two five-member groups must be made **subject-wise**, drawing from different branches of engineering, so that the Council is not dominated by one discipline.

The **Registrar** is the Council's chief executive and serves as Member-Secretary; the post is not one of the nominated memberships.

The Council's statutory functions, examined alongside its composition: registering engineers in **categories A (General), B (Professional) and C (Foreign)**; conducting the **registration examination**; recognising engineering qualifications and accrediting programmes; and regulating professional conduct, with power to suspend or cancel registration for misconduct.

examTip.trick: Read the question precisely: it asks how many members the **Council itself** nominates, as distinct from those nominated by the Government or elected by the engineers' association.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two nominated by the Council itself.** The rest of the composition: **chairman (15 years' experience) and vice-chairman (10 years)** nominated by the Government, **five engineers** nominated by the Government, plus the president of the Nepal Engineers' Association and other ex-officio members.

questions.stem: If the dew point is above 0°C, then:
questions.solution:
**Dew will form.**

The **dew point** is the temperature at which air becomes saturated and its water vapour begins to condense. What the condensate *is* depends on whether that temperature lies above or below freezing:

| Dew point | Condensate | Process |
|---|---|---|
| **Above 0°C** | **Dew** — liquid droplets | Condensation |
| Below 0°C | **Frost** — ice crystals | Deposition (vapour straight to solid) |

So with a dew point above zero, the vapour condenses as **liquid dew** on grass, leaves and cool surfaces — typically on a clear, still night when the ground radiates heat away and its surface cools to the dew point.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Frost** (a) requires a dew point **below** 0°C — the case tested in Q3 of this same paper.
- **Vapour** (b) is the *starting* state; condensation is precisely the loss of vapour, not its formation.
- **Hailstones** (d) form by an entirely different mechanism — supercooled droplets freezing in layers as they are carried repeatedly up and down inside a **cumulonimbus** thunderstorm by strong updraughts. They have nothing to do with a surface dew point.

**Related quantities worth keeping straight:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Dew point** | Temperature at which air becomes saturated |
| **Relative humidity** | Actual vapour pressure ÷ saturation vapour pressure, as a % |
| Absolute humidity | Mass of vapour per unit volume of air |
| Specific humidity | Mass of vapour per unit mass of moist air |

When air is **saturated**, the temperature equals the dew point and relative humidity is 100%. The closer the two temperatures, the more humid the air feels.

**Why this matters in civil engineering.** Dew point governs **surface condensation** — on cold walls, glazing, and inside roof spaces, where it causes damp, mould and corrosion — so insulation and vapour barriers are designed to keep surface temperatures above the dew point. It also matters for **painting and coating**: applying paint to a surface at or below the dew point traps moisture and causes the film to fail, which is why specifications require the substrate to be at least 3°C above the dew point.

examTip.trick: **Dew point** is the temperature at which air becomes saturated. If it is **above 0 °C**, the condensate forms as **liquid dew**; if below, it deposits directly as **frost**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dew point above zero → dew; below zero → frost.** In building physics the same idea governs **interstitial condensation** — moisture condensing inside a wall wherever the temperature falls below the dew point of the air within it, which is why vapour barriers go on the warm side.

questions.stem: What is the value of distribution factor for a 4 lane road in Nepal?
questions.solution:
**0.4 for both directions** — that is, a four-lane single carriageway carrying traffic both ways.

The **lane distribution factor (D)** is the proportion of the total commercial vehicle traffic that is assumed to use the **most heavily loaded lane**. It is needed because pavement thickness is designed for the worst-loaded lane, not for the average across the carriageway.

The values in IRC 37, which the Nepali guidelines follow:

| Carriageway | Road | Distribution factor |
|---|---|---|
| **Single carriageway** (both directions) | Single lane | **1.0** |
| | Two lane | 0.75 |
| | **Four lane** | **0.4** |
| **Dual carriageway** (one direction each) | Two lane | 0.75 |
| | Three lane | 0.6 |
| | Four lane | 0.45 |

So for a **four-lane single carriageway**, D = **0.4** — matching option (c).

**The pattern to understand rather than memorise:** the more lanes there are, the more the traffic spreads out, so the share taken by the worst lane falls. A single-lane road has D = 1.0 because every vehicle must use the one lane. Note also that a dual carriageway gives a **higher** factor per lane than a single carriageway of the same total width, because each direction's traffic is confined to its own half.

**Where D enters the design.** Flexible pavement thickness is designed for the cumulative standard axles over the design life:

> **CSA = 365 × A × [(1 + r)^n − 1]/r × F × D**

where A is the initial commercial vehicle count per day, r the annual growth rate, n the design life in years, **F the vehicle damage factor** (equivalent standard axles per commercial vehicle) and **D the lane distribution factor**.

The CSA, together with the **subgrade CBR**, then fixes the pavement composition from the IRC 37 design catalogue. Getting D wrong by the factor of 2.5 between a single-lane and a four-lane road would change the design traffic — and hence the pavement thickness — very substantially.

examTip.trick: The **lane distribution factor** apportions the total commercial traffic to the **critical lane** for pavement design — not all vehicles use all lanes equally.
examTip.mnemonic: **More lanes, smaller factor per lane — but never 1/n, because traffic distributes unevenly.** The design traffic in **msa** then follows: **N = 365 × A × D × F × [(1+r)ⁿ − 1]/r**, where D is this distribution factor and F the vehicle damage factor.

questions.stem: In which of the following is the minimum value taken?
questions.solution:
**Backward pass.**

Network analysis makes two sweeps through the diagram, and each uses the opposite rule at a junction:

| | **Forward pass** | **Backward pass** |
|---|---|---|
| Direction | Start → finish | **Finish → start** |
| Computes | **Earliest** event times (E) | **Latest** event times (L) |
| At a junction take the | **MAXIMUM** of the incoming values | **MINIMUM** of the outgoing values |
| Starting value | E = 0 at the start event | L = E at the final event |

**Why maximum on the forward pass.** An activity cannot start until **every** predecessor is finished, so where several paths converge on an event, the earliest it can occur is governed by the **longest** of them. Taking the maximum is what makes the critical path emerge as the longest path through the network.

**Why minimum on the backward pass.** Working back, an event's latest permissible time must not delay **any** of the activities that follow it. Where several paths leave an event, the latest allowable time is fixed by the **most demanding** — the smallest of the values computed back along each path. Taking the minimum is what preserves the project completion date.

A memory hook: **forward for the largest, backward for the smallest** — or, put another way, both passes take the value that is **most restrictive** in their direction of travel.

**What the two passes then give you.** The floats follow immediately:

> Total float = L_j − E_i − duration
> Free float = E_j − E_i − duration

and the **critical path** is the chain of activities on which **E = L at every event**, so the total float is zero. Any delay on that chain delays the whole project — which is the single most useful output of the exercise.

A useful check on your arithmetic: at the **final event** the two passes must agree, L = E; and at the **start event** likewise, both being zero. If they do not, the passes have been computed wrongly.

examTip.trap: Forward and backward pass are easy to reverse. **Forward pass takes the MAXIMUM** (an activity cannot start until all its predecessors finish); **backward pass takes the MINIMUM**.
examTip.trick: Reason it out rather than memorise: going forward you must wait for the **slowest** predecessor; going backward you must not delay the **earliest** successor.
examTip.mnemonic: **Forward = earliest times = MAXIMUM. Backward = latest times = MINIMUM.** Then **total float = LST − EST**, and a **critical activity has ZERO total float** — which is how the critical path is identified.

questions.stem: Which of the following is incorrect for a settling basin?
questions.solution:
**"1H : 5V for vertical direction" is the incorrect statement.**

A settling basin must widen and deepen gradually from the approach conduit, and then contract again at the outlet. Those **transitions** are what the ratios describe, and they are governed by one requirement: the expansion must be gentle enough that the flow does not **separate** from the boundary. A separated, eddying flow re-suspends the sediment the basin exists to remove, defeating its purpose.

The ratios the source gives:

| Transition | Ratio |
|---|---|
| **Inlet expansion** | **1H : 2V** — about 27° |
| Outlet contraction | 1H : 1V |

The keyed option, **1H : 5V**, is not one of these, and a 5:1 flare would be far too abrupt to keep the flow attached — hence it is the incorrect statement.

Why the other three options are **true** of a settling basin:
- **Removing silt** (c) is exactly its purpose.
- **Near-laminar, tranquil flow** (d) is the design intent — velocity reduced to about **0.2 to 0.4 m/s** so that turbulence cannot hold particles in suspension.
- The **1H : 2V inlet expansion** (a) is the standard gentle flare.

**How a settling basin is designed.** Widen the section so the horizontal velocity falls, and make it long enough that a particle of the target size, settling at its own velocity, reaches the floor before the flow carries it out:

> Length ≈ (depth × flow velocity) / (settling velocity of the design particle)

with the settling velocity from **Stokes' law** for fine material.

Target particle sizes are about **0.2 mm** for a Francis turbine and **0.1 mm or finer** for a high-head Pelton, since abrasion damage rises steeply with head. Himalayan rivers carry hard quartz and feldspar — minerals harder than runner steel — so this is not a marginal refinement but central to a Nepali scheme's economics.

Basins are classified by how the deposit is removed: **continuous** flushing (uninterrupted generation, more complex) or **intermittent** flushing, as in the BEIRI type of Q50 of this paper, where the plant must be taken off line while the basin is cleaned.

verification.notes: The transition ratios are taken from the source answer key, which states 1H:2V at the inlet and 1H:1V at the outlet. The keyed incorrect option, 1H:5V, matches neither and would be too abrupt to avoid flow separation.

examTip.trap: Read the **INCORRECT**. Three statements about the basin will be right and one will not.
examTip.trick: A settling basin's proportions follow from the **settling velocity** of the target particle: the transition slopes must be gentle enough that the flow does not **separate** and re-suspend the sediment.
examTip.mnemonic: **Inlet transitions can be relatively steep (accelerating flow never separates); OUTLET transitions must be gentle (decelerating flow does).** That asymmetry governs every hydraulic transition, from a venturi to a settling basin.

questions.stem: After reaching the yield point, strain in a test sample …… than stress.
questions.solution:
**Increases heavily.**

Up to the yield point the material behaves elastically: stress and strain rise together in fixed proportion, and the slope of that line is the modulus of elasticity, σ = Eε.

Beyond yield the behaviour changes completely. The material begins to deform **plastically** — dislocations move, the internal structure begins to rearrange — and strain increases **rapidly for very little further increase in stress**. In mild steel there is even a short **yield plateau** where the strain grows at essentially constant stress. The stress–strain curve flattens dramatically, which is precisely the statement that strain increases heavily relative to stress.

The full stress–strain curve for mild steel, and the points that get examined:

| Point | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Proportional limit** | Last point where σ ∝ ε; Hooke's law holds up to here |
| **Elastic limit** | Last point from which the specimen fully recovers |
| **Upper and lower yield point** | Onset of appreciable plastic flow; the yield plateau |
| **Ultimate tensile strength** | **Maximum stress** the specimen sustains; necking begins |
| Breaking point | Fracture, at a nominal stress **below** the ultimate |

Note the counter-intuitive last row: after the ultimate point the cross-section **necks** locally, so the load falls even though the true stress in the reduced section is still rising. Nominal stress is computed on the *original* area, which is why the curve turns downward.

**Why this matters structurally.** The large plastic strain beyond yield **is** ductility, and it is what makes steel structures safe. It allows:
- **Visible warning** — cracking and deflection long before collapse;
- **Redistribution of moments** in indeterminate structures, so an overloaded section sheds load to its neighbours;
- **Energy absorption** in an earthquake, which is the entire basis of ductile seismic design.

That is why structural steel and reinforcement are kept to **low carbon** content, and why IS 1786 specifies a minimum elongation with each grade — 23% for Fe 250 falling to 12% for Fe 500. It is also why an **over-reinforced** concrete section is prohibited: it fails by concrete crushing while the steel is still elastic, forfeiting all of this warning and ductility.

examTip.trick: At the **yield plateau**, strain increases greatly at **essentially constant stress** — the defining feature of a ductile material and the source of its warning before failure.
examTip.mnemonic: **The yield plateau IS ductility, and ductility is the most valuable property a structural material can have** — it gives warning, permits moment redistribution, and absorbs earthquake energy. High-strength steels have **no plateau**, which is why their yield is defined by the **0.2% proof stress** instead.

questions.stem: A rod of area 1000 mm² has an axial pull of 2 kN. What is the shear stress on a plane at 30° inclined to the horizontal axis?
questions.solution:
**0.866 N/mm².**

**Step 1 — axial (normal) stress.**
> σ_x = P/A = 2000/1000 = **2 N/mm²**

The bar carries only axial load, so σ_y = 0 and τ_xy = 0 — this is a state of **uniaxial stress**.

**Step 2 — shear stress on an inclined plane.** The transformation equation is
> τ_θ = −[(σ_x − σ_y)/2] sin 2θ + τ_xy cos 2θ

Substituting σ_y = τ_xy = 0 and θ = 30°:
> τ_θ = −(2 − 0)/2 × sin 60°
> τ_θ = −1 × 0.866
> **|τ| = 0.866 N/mm²**

The negative sign only indicates the sense of the shear; the magnitude is what the options give.

**The general result for uniaxial stress**, worth carrying because it answers this whole family of questions:

> σ_θ = σ_x cos²θ,  **τ_θ = (σ_x/2) sin 2θ**

From which the important special cases follow:

| θ | Normal stress | Shear stress |
|---|---|---|
| 0° | **σ_x** (maximum) | 0 |
| **45°** | σ_x/2 | **σ_x/2 — MAXIMUM shear** |
| 30° | 0.75 σ_x | 0.433 σ_x |
| 90° | 0 | 0 |

**The key structural fact:** maximum shear stress occurs on planes at **45°** to the axis, and equals **half** the axial stress:

> **τ_max = σ_x/2 = 1 N/mm²** here

That is why a ductile material in a tension test fails along a cone at roughly 45° — it yields in **shear**, not in tension — and why the **cup-and-cone** fracture is the signature of ductile failure. A brittle material, weak in tension rather than shear, instead breaks square across the bar on the plane of maximum normal stress.

Note that option (a), 2 N/mm², is the axial stress itself, and option (d), 1 N/mm², is the *maximum* shear stress at 45° — both placed to catch a candidate who does not carry the calculation through to the stated angle.

examTip.trick: The shear stress on a plane at angle θ to the axis is **τ = (σ/2)sin 2θ**, and it is **maximum at θ = 45°** where τ = σ/2. Here σ = 2000/1000 = 2 N/mm², so the maximum shear is 1 N/mm² — check what angle the question asks for.
examTip.mnemonic: **Maximum shear is HALF the axial stress, on a plane at 45°.** That is why a **ductile** tensile specimen fails on a **45° cone** (shear) while a **brittle** one fails square across (direct tension) — same stress state, different weakest mode.

questions.stem: Nepal Government handed over the fast-track project to the Nepal Army. After handing in, what type of contract was it?
options: Build, Design, Procurement, Subcontracting and all works
questions.solution:
**BOOT** — **Build, Own, Operate and Transfer.**

The delivery models in this family differ in **whether ownership passes during the concession**, and that single distinction is what the question tests:

| Model | Expansion | Ownership during concession |
|---|---|---|
| **BOT** | Build – Operate – Transfer | Remains with the **public authority**; the concessionaire only operates |
| **BOOT** | **Build – Own – Operate – Transfer** | **Vested in the concessionaire**, then transferred back at the end |
| BOO | Build – Own – Operate | **No transfer** — retained permanently |
| BOLT | Build – Operate – Lease – Transfer | Leased back to the authority |
| DBFO | Design – Build – Finance – Operate | Concessionaire also arranges the finance |
| EPC / turnkey | Engineer – Procure – Construct | Contractor builds only; no operation |

So in **BOT** the asset stays in public ownership throughout and the private party merely runs it; in **BOOT** the private party **owns** the asset for the concession period, recovers its investment from tolls or charges, and then hands ownership back.

**How such a concession works.** The concessionaire finances and constructs the works, then operates them for an agreed period — commonly 20 to 30 years — recovering capital, operating costs and a return from user charges. At the end the asset transfers to the government, normally at no cost and in a specified condition.

**Why governments use these models:** the capital cost is met without immediate public borrowing; construction and operating risk transfer to the private party; and private management may bring efficiency. **The costs:** users pay tolls for decades, the government's contingent liabilities can be large, and the contractual arrangements are complex and hard to renegotiate.

Options (c) and (d) are not recognised contract types at all — merely lists of activities.

In Nepal these arrangements fall under the **Public Private Partnership and Investment Act 2075** and the Public Procurement Act 2063, and have been used for hydropower and road projects. Note that a **build-only** arrangement — a construction contract with no operating concession — is an EPC or item-rate contract, not a BOT variant, whatever the identity of the contractor.

examTip.trick: Read the letters: **B-O-O-T = Build, Own, Operate, Transfer**. The distinguishing feature against BOT is the **ownership** during the concession period.
examTip.mnemonic: **BOT: build, operate, transfer (no ownership). BOOT: build, OWN, operate, transfer. BOO: never transfers.** The concession model matters for who carries the **construction, operating and revenue risk**, and for how the asset appears on the public balance sheet.

questions.stem: A jar of height 1 m, fully filled, is placed 1 m above the floor. A tap at the bottom of the jar is opened and the water jet strikes the floor at a horizontal distance of 1.8 m. What would be the coefficient of velocity?
questions.solution:
**0.90.**

The jet leaving the orifice is a **projectile**, and tracking its trajectory gives the actual velocity, which is then compared with the theoretical value.

**Step 1 — the trajectory relations.** With x the horizontal distance and y the vertical fall:
> x = v·t  and  y = ½gt²

Eliminating t:
> v = x √(g/2y)

**Step 2 — the theoretical velocity** from Torricelli, under head h:
> v_th = √(2gh)

**Step 3 — the coefficient of velocity** is the ratio, and the g's cancel to give the standard form:

> **C_v = x / √(4yh)**

**Step 4 — substitute** y = 1 m (the fall to the floor) and h = 1 m (the head in the jar):
> C_v = 1.8/√(4 × 1 × 1)
> C_v = 1.8/2 = **0.90** ✓

The **C_v = x/√(4yh)** relation is worth memorising outright: it turns a measurement of the jet's landing point into the coefficient, with no timing required, and it is the standard laboratory method.

**The three orifice coefficients** and how they relate:

| Coefficient | Definition | Typical value |
|---|---|---|
| **C_v** — velocity | Actual velocity ÷ theoretical velocity | **0.95 – 0.99** |
| **C_c** — contraction | Area at **vena contracta** ÷ orifice area | 0.61 – 0.69 |
| **C_d** — discharge | Actual discharge ÷ theoretical discharge | **0.61 – 0.65** |

and they are linked by
> **C_d = C_v × C_c**

C_v is slightly less than 1 because of **friction** at the orifice edge; C_c is well below 1 because the streamlines converge and the jet **contracts** to a minimum section — the vena contracta — a short distance downstream of the opening. It is the contraction, not the friction, that dominates the loss of discharge.

Note that the value obtained here, 0.90, is somewhat low for a well-formed orifice, which the question's rounded figures account for. In the same family of measurements, the coefficient of resistance C_r = (1/C_v²) − 1 expresses the loss as a fraction of the kinetic head.

examTip.trick: This is a **jet trajectory** problem: water issues at **V = √(2gh)** and then behaves as a **projectile**, so horizontal distance x = V t with t from the fall height.
examTip.mnemonic: **x = 2√(h × y)** where h is the head above the orifice and y the fall to the floor — a clean result worth carrying. Maximising it: for a jar of height H standing at height Y, the range is greatest for an orifice at **mid-height of the total**.

questions.stem: Increase in permissible stress in design of a wall subjected to eccentric load with eccentricity ratio > 1/24 is:
questions.solution:
**25%.**

IS 1905 permits an increase in the allowable compressive stress in masonry where the load is applied **eccentrically** beyond a threshold eccentricity. Where the eccentricity ratio e/t exceeds **1/24**, the permissible stress may be increased by **25%**.

**Why an increase is allowed at all, rather than a reduction.** It looks counter-intuitive, but it follows from how the stress is *calculated*. An eccentric load is analysed by combined direct and bending stress:

> σ_max = P/A + M/Z = (P/A)(1 + 6e/t)

That expression gives the **peak** stress at the extreme fibre of the section, on the assumption of a linear elastic stress distribution. In reality masonry is not linearly elastic at high stress: it **yields locally** and the stress **redistributes** across the section, so the true peak is lower than the calculation predicts. The 25% allowance is a code recognition of that reserve — the calculated peak stress is conservative, and it may be permitted to exceed the nominal allowable value.

The related provisions of IS 1905 that govern load-bearing masonry:

| Provision | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Slenderness ratio** | ≤ **27** for a load-bearing wall |
| **Effective thickness**, cavity wall (both leaves loaded) | **Greater of ⅔(t₁+t₂) and the thicker leaf** |
| Stress reduction factor | Applied as slenderness increases |
| Shape modification factor | Depends on the height-to-width ratio of the masonry unit |
| Eccentricity allowance | **+25% for e/t > 1/24** |

The effective-thickness rule is the one this series has already corrected: **Set 1 Q38's circulating key gave only the thicker leaf**, whereas IS 1905 cl. 4.5.3 requires the greater of the two values.

**Where eccentric loading arises in practice:** a slab or beam bearing on only part of the wall thickness, a floor framing into one face, a change of wall thickness at a storey, or a wall carrying lateral load in addition to vertical. In each case the resultant does not pass through the centroid, and both the eccentricity and the slenderness must be checked.

examTip.trick: The permissible stress is increased because an **eccentric load within the middle third** still keeps the whole section in compression — the masonry is not being asked to do anything it cannot.
examTip.mnemonic: **Middle third rule: e ≤ t/6 keeps the entire section in COMPRESSION.** Beyond that, part of the section lifts off, the contact area shrinks, the resultant moves further toward the edge — and the process is **progressive**, which is why the limit is enforced rather than merely recommended.

questions.stem: A quantum of discharge with high enough magnitude and frequency to bring about changes to the river boundary and surrounding area is:
questions.solution:
**Dominant discharge.**

The dominant (or **channel-forming**) discharge is the flow that does the most **cumulative** work in shaping the channel over the long term. It is defined by the product of two competing factors:

| Factor | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Magnitude** of the flow | Larger flows move more sediment per event |
| **Frequency** of occurrence | Larger flows occur more rarely |

The **product** of the two peaks at an intermediate flow. A **very large flood** transports enormous quantities of sediment but occurs perhaps once in fifty years, so its total contribution over a century is modest. A **small everyday flow** occurs constantly but moves almost nothing. The channel's form is therefore set by the flow in between — big enough to do work, frequent enough to do it repeatedly.

In practice the dominant discharge is commonly taken as the **bankfull discharge**, corresponding to a return period of about **1 to 2 years** (often quoted as the 1.58-year flow), or in Indian and Nepali practice as roughly **half to two-thirds of the maximum flood discharge**.

Why the other options are different quantities:

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Maximum flood discharge** | The **extreme** event — governs waterway size, freeboard and structural safety |
| **Design discharge** | The flow a structure is **designed** for, chosen from a return period and the acceptable risk |
| **Median discharge** | The flow **exceeded 50% of the time** — a statistical middle, unrelated to sediment work |
| **Dominant discharge** | The flow that **shapes the channel** |

**Where it is used.** Lacey's regime theory, and river training design generally, is built on the dominant discharge — it is the Q that goes into the regime relations for **waterway P = 4.75√Q**, **scour depth R = 0.47(Q/f)^(1/3)** and **slope S = f^(5/3)/(3340 Q^(1/6))**, as computed in Q62 of this paper. Using the extreme flood instead would predict a channel far wider and flatter than the river actually maintains.

So the two discharges serve different purposes and both are needed: the **maximum flood** for structural safety and freeboard, the **dominant discharge** for the stable geometry the river will settle into. Guide banks, spurs and revetments are proportioned from the second while being checked against the first.

examTip.trick: The **dominant (channel-forming) discharge** is not the biggest flood — a rare flood does great work but too seldom to shape the channel. It is the flow whose **magnitude × frequency product** is greatest.
examTip.mnemonic: **Roughly the 1 to 2 year flood, close to BANKFULL discharge.** The channel a river maintains is the one that suits this flow, not the flood of record — which is why bankfull width is such a good predictor of a river's regime dimensions.

questions.stem: Which is not a professional engineering body?
options: Society of Public Health Engineers Nepal (SOPHEN)
Society of Consulting Architectural & Engineering Firms (SCAEF)
questions.solution:
**Society of Electrical & Electronics Association (SEEN)** — as keyed by the source.

The other three are recognised professional bodies in Nepal:

| Body | Character |
|---|---|
| **NEA** — Nepal Engineers' Association | The principal **membership body** for engineers of all disciplines; promotes the profession and represents engineers' interests |
| **SOPHEN** — Society of Public Health Engineers Nepal | A **discipline-specific** society for public health engineering — water supply, sanitation, waste management |
| **SCAEF** — Society of Consulting Architectural & Engineering Firms | An association of **consulting firms**, promoting ethical practice and quality in consultancy |

Note what the three have in common: each is an association **of professionals or professional firms**, with a defined membership, a code of conduct and a role in representing its members.

**The distinction that matters most here**, and which is examined repeatedly, is between a professional association and the **statutory regulator**:

| | **Nepal Engineers' Association (NEA)** | **Nepal Engineering Council (NEC)** |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | **Voluntary** professional membership body | **Statutory regulator**, created by the NEC Act 2055 |
| Joining | By choice | **Registration is mandatory** to practise |
| Powers | Advocacy, networking, professional development | **Licensing**; conducts the registration examination; can **suspend or cancel** registration for misconduct |
| Membership of the other | The NEA President and five NEA-elected engineers sit on the **NEC** | — |

So the NEA promotes the profession while the **NEC regulates** it, and a Nepali engineer must be registered with the Council — not merely a member of the Association — in order to practise lawfully. That is the point of the license examination this syllabus prepares for.

A related caution on abbreviations: **NEA** in this context is the Nepal *Engineers'* Association, not the **Nepal Electricity Authority**, which is the state power utility and not a professional body at all. The two share initials and are frequently confused.

examTip.trap: Read the **NOT**. Three of the four will be genuine professional bodies and one will be invented or mis-titled.
examTip.trick: The recognised bodies in Nepal include the **Nepal Engineers' Association (NEA)** as the professional membership body and the **Nepal Engineering Council (NEC)** as the statutory regulator.
examTip.mnemonic: **Association versus Council: the NEA represents engineers; the NEC REGULATES them.** Membership of an association is voluntary; **registration with the Council is a legal requirement to practise.**

questions.stem: What is the direction of closing error?
questions.solution:
**tan δ = ΣD / ΣL.**

The closing error of a traverse is a vector with two components:
- **ΣL** — the algebraic sum of the **latitudes** (the north–south, or Y, component);
- **ΣD** — the algebraic sum of the **departures** (the east–west, or X, component).

Its **magnitude** follows from Pythagoras:
> e = √[(ΣL)² + (ΣD)²]

and its **direction** — a bearing measured from the north–south axis — follows from the tangent:
> **tan δ = ΣD / ΣL**

**Why departure over latitude.** In surveying, bearings are measured **clockwise from north**, so the tangent of a bearing is the easting component divided by the northing component — departure over latitude. That convention is the reverse of the mathematical habit of taking tan θ = y/x, which is exactly what option (a) is placed to catch.

Options (b) and (d) can be dismissed immediately: squaring both components destroys the sign information that identifies the quadrant, and a ratio of squares is always positive, so it could never distinguish NE from SW.

**What the result is used for.** The relative precision of the traverse is
> e / perimeter

compared against the permissible limit for the class of survey (say 1 in 5000). If acceptable, the error is **distributed** among the legs:

| Rule | When used | Correction proportional to |
|---|---|---|
| **Bowditch's rule** | Angular and linear precision **comparable** (compass traverse) | **Length** of each leg |
| **Transit rule** | Angles measured **more precisely** than lengths (theodolite traverse) | Latitude / departure of each leg |

**A distinction worth carrying**, because it is the trap in Set 1 Q76: the **closing error** vector and the **closing line** point in **opposite** directions. The closing error runs from the true starting point to the plotted end point; the closing line is the correction that closes the traverse, running the other way. A closing error in the NW quadrant means a closing line in the SE quadrant.

examTip.trick: The closing error has two components — **ΣL** (latitudes) and **ΣD** (departures) — and its direction is **tan δ = ΣD/ΣL**, with the quadrant taken from the two signs.
examTip.mnemonic: **Magnitude = √(ΣL² + ΣD²); direction from tan δ = ΣD/ΣL.** The **relative** error (closing error ÷ perimeter) is what judges the survey: 1 in 1000 for ordinary work, 1 in 5000 or better for precise. Then balance by **Bowditch** or **Transit**.

questions.stem: Find the porosity if specific gravity is 2.6 and water content is 45% for a fully saturated condition of soil.
questions.solution:
**0.55.**

**Step 1 — find the void ratio** using the fundamental phase identity:
> **S · e = w · G_s**

For a **fully saturated** soil, S = 1, so
> e = w · G_s = 0.45 × 2.6 = **1.17**

**Step 2 — convert void ratio to porosity:**
> **n = e/(1 + e)**
> n = 1.17/(1 + 1.17) = 1.17/2.17 = 0.5392
> **n ≈ 0.55**

**The identity Se = wG_s is the single most useful relation in soil phase problems** and is worth committing outright: given any three of S, e, w and G_s, it delivers the fourth. It follows directly from the definitions — write the weight of water two ways, as w·W_s and as S·V_v·γ_w, and the identity drops out.

The conversions between the volumetric ratios:

| From | To | Relation |
|---|---|---|
| e | n | **n = e/(1 + e)** |
| n | e | **e = n/(1 − n)** |

Note that **porosity is always less than 1** (voids as a fraction of *total* volume) while **void ratio can exceed 1** (voids relative to *solids* only) — as it does here, at 1.17. Confusing the two is the commonest error, and a quick check that n came out below 1 while e came out above it confirms the calculation is the right way round.

The other relations in the same family:

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| Degree of saturation S | V_w/V_v |
| Void ratio e | V_v/V_s |
| Porosity n | V_v/V |
| Air content a_c | V_a/V_v |
| Water content w | **W_w/W_s** (a *weight* ratio) |
| Saturated unit weight | γ = γ_w(G_s + e)/(1 + e) |
| Dry unit weight | γ_d = G_s γ_w/(1 + e) |

A water content of 45% with G_s = 2.6 describes a **soft, highly compressible saturated clay** — a void ratio of 1.17 means the volume of voids exceeds that of the solids, which is why such soils settle so much under load and why consolidation analysis matters for them.

examTip.mnemonic: **eS = wG is the master phase relation — with S = 1 it becomes simply e = wG.** Then convert with **n = e/(1+e)** and **e = n/(1−n)**. Note void ratio can exceed 1; **porosity never can**, which is a useful check on the answer.

questions.stem: What is the formula for overall efficiency of a two-stage high rate trickling filter?
questions.solution:
**E = E₁ + E₂(1 − E₁).**

The two filters act **in series**, so the second one works on what the first left behind — not on the original load. That is the whole logic of the formula.

**Derivation.** Take the influent BOD as 1 unit.
- The first stage removes E₁, leaving **(1 − E₁)** to pass on.
- The second stage removes its efficiency E₂ of *that remainder*, so it removes **E₂(1 − E₁)**.
- Total removed = **E₁ + E₂(1 − E₁)** ✓

**Worked example** — two filters each 80% efficient:
> E = 0.80 + 0.80(1 − 0.80) = 0.80 + 0.16 = **0.96, or 96%**

Note what this shows: the overall efficiency is **not** 160% (option a, which is nonsense once the sum exceeds 1) and not the 80% average (option d). Efficiencies in series **never add**, and the result always stays below 100% however many stages are used — each stage can only work on a diminishing remainder. That is the general principle worth carrying.

Equivalently, the fraction **remaining** is the product of the individual remainders:
> 1 − E = (1 − E₁)(1 − E₂)

which rearranges to exactly the same expression.

**Why two stages are used at all.** A single high-rate trickling filter achieves only about 65 to 85% BOD removal, which is often insufficient to meet the effluent standard. Adding a second stage lifts the total to about 90 to 95% at far less cost than building one very large low-rate filter.

The filter types compared:

| | **Low rate (standard)** | **High rate** |
|---|---|---|
| Hydraulic loading | 1 – 4 m³/m²/day | **10 – 40 m³/m²/day** |
| Organic loading | Low | High |
| **Recirculation** | **None** | **Essential** |
| BOD removal | 80 – 90% | 65 – 85% per stage |
| Nitrification | Good | Limited |

**Recirculation** is the defining feature of the high-rate filter: part of the effluent is returned to the filter inlet, which dilutes the incoming strength, keeps the medium continuously wetted, improves distribution, and suppresses fly nuisance and odour. The recirculation ratio is typically 0.5 to 3.

examTip.trick: The second stage treats only what the **first stage left behind**, so its efficiency applies to the **remaining** fraction (1 − E₁) — hence **E = E₁ + E₂(1 − E₁)**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Stages combine on what REMAINS, never by simple addition.** Two 80% stages give 80 + 80(0.2) = **96%**, not 160%. The same logic governs any multi-stage treatment train — and it is why the last few percent of removal are always the most expensive.

questions.stem: A defect in timber caused by a longitudinal separation of the fibres along the annual rings is called:
questions.solution:
**Shake.**

A **shake** is a longitudinal split or separation of the wood fibres, occurring **along the annual rings** or radially across them. It forms while the tree is standing or during felling and seasoning, and it interrupts the continuity of the fibres — which is exactly why it weakens the timber, and why it lets moisture into the heart of the section.

The common defects of timber, and what each is:

| Defect | Description | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Shake** | **Longitudinal separation of fibres**, along or across the rings | Reduces strength; admits moisture |
| **Knot** | The base of a branch embedded in the trunk | Interrupts grain; **weakens in tension**; hard to work |
| **Wane** | Bark or want of wood on an edge of a converted section | Reduces the effective section |
| Twisted fibre | Fibres spiralling round the trunk (wandering heart) | Timber unsuitable for sawing into straight members |
| **Check** | A crack **not** extending through the full thickness | Reduces strength locally |
| Split | A crack extending **right through** the piece | Serious loss of strength |
| Rind gall | Curved swelling from an improperly cut branch | Weak, unsuitable |

The types of shake worth distinguishing:
- **Cup shake** — separation following one annual ring, caused by sap frost.
- **Heart shake** — radial cracks starting at the pith, from decay at the heart of an over-mature tree.
- **Star shake** — radial cracks from the bark inward, usually from severe frost or from too-rapid drying.

**Why defects matter for design.** IS 883 grades structural timber and sets limits on the size and location of knots, shakes and checks; the permissible stresses are then reduced from the clear-specimen values accordingly. A knot in the **tension** face of a beam is far more damaging than the same knot in the compression face, so grading rules restrict defects by position as well as by size.

The distinction to carry: defects arise from **natural causes** (knots, shakes, twisted fibres), from **conversion** (wane, sawing defects), from **seasoning** (checks, splits, warping, cup and bow), or from **attack** by fungi and insects. Proper **seasoning** — reducing the moisture content to 10 to 12% for interior work — prevents most of the seasoning group, which is why it is done before the timber is worked, as noted in Set 2 Q50.

examTip.trick: Timber defects by cause: **shake** (separation along the grain, from growth stresses or felling), **knot** (a branch base), **check** (a crack across the rings, from drying), **wane** (missing edge), **twist and cup** (seasoning distortions).
examTip.mnemonic: **Shakes follow the annual rings; checks cut across them.** Both are separations, and the direction is what names them. Shakes are a **natural (growth) defect**; checks are a **seasoning defect** — which matters, because one can be avoided by better drying and the other cannot.

questions.stem: The minimum bearing of a lintel on each side of an opening in a masonry wall is generally taken as:
questions.solution:
**200 mm** on each side, or the thickness of the wall, whichever is greater in ordinary practice.

A lintel spans an opening — a door or window — and carries the masonry above it down onto the piers at each side. The **bearing** is the length by which the lintel sits on the wall beyond the clear opening, and it has to be long enough to do three things:

- Keep the **bearing stress** on the masonry within its permissible value, since the whole reaction is delivered over that small area.
- Provide **anchorage** for the tension reinforcement, so the bars can develop their force at the support.
- Guard against the lintel **slipping or rotating** off its seating, and accommodate inaccuracy in setting out on site.

The **effective span** of a lintel is therefore taken as the lesser of: the clear span plus the effective depth, or the centre-to-centre distance of the bearings — the same rule IS 456 applies to any simply supported member.

Related dimensions for lintels and openings, examined alongside:

| Item | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **Bearing each side** | **200 mm**, or the wall thickness |
| Lintel depth | Span/12 to span/15, commonly 150–230 mm |
| Minimum cover to reinforcement | 20 mm (moderate exposure) |
| Sill and lintel band thickness (seismic) | 75 mm, with 2 bars top and bottom |

**Why the lintel does not carry the whole wall above it.** Masonry above an opening tends to arch: the load spreads outward at roughly 45°, so a **triangle of masonry** discharges its weight to the piers rather than onto the lintel. The lintel therefore carries only the masonry within that triangle plus any concentrated load bearing directly on it — which is why lintels are far shallower than a beam carrying the full wall height would need to be. Where a **relieving arch** is built above the lintel, that arching action is made explicit.

**Seismic detailing in Nepal** adds an important requirement: NBC 202 and NBC 203 call for **continuous RC bands** at plinth, sill, lintel and roof level, running right round the building and tying the walls together. A lintel band is not merely a set of individual lintels over openings — it is a continuous horizontal tie, and that continuity is what holds masonry walls together in an earthquake. Discontinuous lintels were a common failure mode in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake.

examTip.trick: The lintel must bear far enough onto the masonry to spread its reaction without crushing the wall or spalling the edge — and the conventional minimum is the **wall thickness or 200 mm**, whichever is greater.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bearing at least 200 mm each end.** The load a lintel actually carries is usually taken from the **triangular arching action** above it (a 60° triangle), not the full wall height — masonry above the opening arches over and carries itself, provided there is enough wall above and either side.

questions.stem: In rate analysis, the contractor's profit is usually taken as:
questions.solution:
**10%.**

Rate analysis builds up the rate for one unit of an item of work — one cubic metre of brickwork, one square metre of plaster — from its constituent costs. The contractor's profit is added at the end as a percentage of the accumulated cost, and **10%** is the figure conventionally allowed.

The full build-up of a rate:

| Component | Typical allowance |
|---|---|
| **Material cost** | Quantity × rate, including wastage |
| **Labour cost** | From the task work / output constants |
| Tools and plant (T&P) | **1 – 2%** of labour cost |
| Water charges | **1.5%** of the cost of work |
| Overheads / establishment | 3 – 5% |
| **Contractor's profit** | **10%** |
| = **Rate per unit** | |

**Why each element is needed.** Material and labour are the direct costs. **T&P** covers small tools, mixers and vibrators. **Water charges** cover the water for mixing and curing — a real cost that is easily forgotten. **Overheads** cover the site office, supervision, insurance and the contractor's head-office cost. And profit is the return for taking the commercial risk.

**Where the wastage allowances sit**, since they belong to the material line and are frequently asked:

| Material | Wastage allowance |
|---|---|
| Bricks | 5% |
| Cement | 2 – 3% |
| Sand and aggregate | 5 – 10% |
| Steel reinforcement | 3 – 5% |

**Where the rates and constants come from.** Material rates are taken from the **District Rate** published annually by each District Development Committee in Nepal, and labour outputs from the **Norms** (the standard schedule of rates and task work). Using the published district rate is what makes a public-sector estimate defensible and auditable.

The estimate that results feeds the whole procurement chain: the **detailed estimate** fixes the cost ceiling, the **bill of quantities** priced at these rates becomes the tender document, and the same rates govern **interim payments** measured on site. That is why the measurement conventions of IS 1200 — the 0.1 m² deduction limit for brickwork, the 0.5 m² limit for plaster, as in Set 2 Q83 — matter as much as the arithmetic: a bill prepared by one engineer must describe the same work when priced by another.

examTip.trick: Rate analysis builds a unit rate from **materials + labour + plant + overheads + profit**. Profit is a percentage on the whole.
examTip.mnemonic: **Contractor's profit 10–15%; contingencies in the estimate 3–5%; work-charged establishment 1.5–2%.** Three different allowances that serve three different purposes — profit belongs to the contractor's rate, contingencies to the employer's estimate.

questions.stem: According to Darcy's law, the coefficient of permeability k has the same units as:
questions.solution:
**Velocity** — k is expressed in m/s, cm/s or m/day.

Darcy's law for laminar flow through a soil:

> **v = k · i**

where v is the discharge (or superficial) velocity and **i = h/L** is the hydraulic gradient. Since the hydraulic gradient is a **ratio of two lengths and therefore dimensionless**, k must carry the whole of the dimension of v. So k has the units of **velocity**.

Equivalently, in terms of discharge:
> **q = k · i · A**

Typical values, spanning about ten orders of magnitude — which is why permeability dominates so much of soil behaviour:

| Soil | k (m/s) | Drainage |
|---|---|---|
| Clean gravel | > 10⁻² | Very good |
| Clean sand | 10⁻² – 10⁻⁵ | Good |
| Silty sand, silt | 10⁻⁵ – 10⁻⁷ | Poor |
| **Clay** | **< 10⁻⁹** | **Practically impervious** |

**How k is measured:**

| Method | Suits |
|---|---|
| **Constant head permeameter** | **Coarse** soils — sand and gravel |
| **Falling head permeameter** | **Fine** soils — silt and clay |
| Consolidation test (indirect) | Clay, from c_v |
| **Pumping test in the field** | Large-scale, in situ value — most reliable |

The laboratory value is often far below the field value, because in the ground **fissures, root holes, sand lenses and layering** create preferential paths that a small remoulded specimen cannot represent. In layered ground the equivalent permeability is the **weighted arithmetic mean parallel to the layers** and the **weighted harmonic mean perpendicular** to them, so horizontal permeability usually exceeds vertical, sometimes by an order of magnitude.

**Why k matters.** It governs the **rate** of every water-related process in soil: seepage discharge under a dam (q = kH·N_f/N_d from the flow net of Set 2 Q84), the **time** for consolidation settlement, the drawdown achievable by dewatering, and the risk of **piping**. Note the important distinction: permeability controls the *rate* of consolidation, while compressibility controls its *magnitude* — which is why a clay settles as much as a sand of the same compressibility, but takes years rather than days to do it.

Darcy's law holds only for **laminar** flow, which covers essentially all natural seepage; it breaks down in very coarse rockfill where the flow becomes turbulent.

examTip.trick: **v = ki**, and the hydraulic gradient **i is dimensionless** (length over length). So k must carry the same units as v — a **velocity**, m/s.
examTip.mnemonic: **k is a velocity, not a volume rate** — specifically, the discharge velocity at unit hydraulic gradient. And remember **v is NOT the real water speed**: the seepage velocity **v_s = v/n** is 2–3 times faster, which is what governs contaminant travel times.

questions.stem: The shear test in which both drainage and pore water pressure can be controlled and measured is the:
questions.solution:
**Triaxial compression test.**

The triaxial apparatus encloses a cylindrical specimen in a rubber membrane inside a pressure cell. That arrangement gives control of everything the other tests cannot reach:

- **Drainage** can be opened or closed at will, through porous stones at the ends.
- **Pore water pressure** can be measured directly at the base of the specimen.
- The **cell (confining) pressure** σ₃ is applied independently of the axial load.
- **Consolidation** can be completed before shearing.

Because drainage and pore pressure are controllable, three distinct test conditions can be run — and each models a different real situation:

| Test | Drainage | Models |
|---|---|---|
| **UU** (unconsolidated undrained) | Closed throughout | **Rapid loading** on saturated clay — end of construction |
| **CU** (consolidated undrained) | Consolidated, then sheared undrained | Loading after the soil has consolidated under its own weight |
| **CD** (consolidated drained) | Open throughout, sheared slowly | **Long-term** stability; gives effective-stress parameters c′ and φ′ |

That distinction between **total-stress (c_u, φ_u)** and **effective-stress (c′, φ′)** parameters is the whole reason the triaxial test matters: a clay slope may be stable immediately after excavation and fail years later as pore pressures equalise, and only a drained or pore-pressure-measured test can predict that.

Why the other tests cannot do this:

| Test | Limitation |
|---|---|
| **Direct shear (box shear)** | Failure plane is **forced** to be horizontal; drainage cannot be controlled; pore pressure not measurable; stress distribution non-uniform |
| **Vane shear** | In-situ, gives **c_u only** with φ = 0; no drainage control |
| **Unconfined compression** | A special case with **σ₃ = 0**; undrained only; suits soft clay, gives c_u = q_u/2 |

The **direct shear test** remains useful for sand, where drainage is so rapid that the distinction hardly arises, and it is simpler and quicker. But for clay, and for any problem where the timing of loading matters, the triaxial test is the reference method.

A further advantage worth noting: the triaxial specimen fails on its **own weakest plane**, wherever that lies, rather than on a plane imposed by the apparatus — so the strength measured is genuinely the soil's own.

examTip.trick: The triaxial cell is **sealed**, so the drainage line can be opened or closed at will and the **pore pressure measured** through a transducer. A shear box is open and can do neither.
examTip.mnemonic: **Triaxial: drainage controlled, pore pressure measured, failure plane free to find itself. Shear box: cheap, quick, and blind.** That is why the shear box is acceptable for a drained sand test and useless whenever pore pressure matters — which is whenever clay is involved.

questions.stem: Reynolds number represents the ratio of:
options: Inertial force to surface tension force
questions.solution:
**Inertial force to viscous force.**

> **Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν**

A large Reynolds number means inertia dominates and the flow is **turbulent**; a small one means viscosity dominates and the flow is **laminar**. The number is dimensionless, which is what allows model tests to be scaled to full size.

The flow regimes in a pipe:

| Re | Regime |
|---|---|
| **< 2000** | **Laminar** |
| 2000 – 4000 | Transitional |
| **> 4000** | **Turbulent** |

The family of dimensionless numbers, each the ratio of inertia to a *different* competing force — this is the set the options are drawn from, and they are worth learning together:

| Number | Ratio | Governs | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Reynolds, Re** | Inertia / **viscous** | Viscous flows | **Pipe flow**, submerged bodies, laminar–turbulent transition |
| **Froude, Fr** | Inertia / **gravity** | Free-surface flows | **Open channels**, spillways, hydraulic jump, ship resistance |
| **Weber, We** | Inertia / **surface tension** | Very small scales | Capillary waves, droplets, sprays |
| **Mach, M** | Inertia / **elastic** | Compressible flow | High-speed gas flow, water hammer |
| **Euler, Eu** | **Pressure** / inertia | Pressure-driven flow | Cavitation, pressure distribution |

**Which number governs which problem** is the practically important point. A **pipe flow** problem is a Reynolds problem, because there is no free surface for gravity to act on. An **open channel** problem is a Froude problem, because gravity controls the surface profile — which is why the hydraulic jump, the choice between subcritical and supercritical flow, and spillway design all turn on Fr rather than Re.

For **model testing** the relevant number must be kept the same in model and prototype — **dynamic similarity**. A spillway model is run at the same Froude number as the real structure; a pipe or aerofoil model at the same Reynolds number. Satisfying both at once in a scaled model is generally impossible, which is why the engineer must decide which force actually dominates the phenomenon being studied.

Note also that Re appears directly in the friction relations: **f = 64/Re** for laminar flow (or the coefficient of friction 16/Re, as in Q32 of this paper), whereas in turbulent flow f depends on both Re and relative roughness through the Moody diagram.

examTip.trick: **Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν** — inertia over viscosity. At low Re viscosity damps every disturbance; at high Re inertia lets disturbances grow into turbulence.
examTip.mnemonic: **Re < 2000 laminar, > 4000 turbulent in a pipe** (500 in an open channel, since R = D/4). Its companion is the **FROUDE number** = inertia/gravity, which governs **free-surface** flow — and it is Froude, not Reynolds, that a spillway model is scaled on.

questions.stem: For a given discharge in a rectangular channel, the minimum specific energy occurs at:
questions.solution:
**Critical depth.**

**Specific energy** is the energy per unit weight measured from the channel bed:

> **E = y + v²/2g = y + Q²/(2gA²)**

Plotting E against depth y for a fixed discharge gives the **specific energy curve** — a curve with two limbs and a single minimum. The depth at which E is least is by definition the **critical depth y_c**, and at that point the **Froude number equals 1**.

**The two limbs**, and what they mean:

| Limb | Depth | Fr | Regime |
|---|---|---|---|
| Upper | y > y_c | **< 1** | **Subcritical** — deep, slow; gravity dominant |
| — | y = y_c | **= 1** | **Critical** — minimum specific energy |
| Lower | y < y_c | **> 1** | **Supercritical** — shallow, fast; inertia dominant |

For any specific energy **above** the minimum there are **two** depths that carry the same discharge with the same energy — one subcritical and one supercritical. These are the **alternate depths** (option c), and they are the reason the curve has two limbs.

**Results for a rectangular channel**, with q = Q/b the discharge per unit width:

> **y_c = (q²/g)^(1/3)**
> **E_min = 1.5 y_c**  — so the critical depth is exactly **two-thirds** of the minimum specific energy
> v_c = √(g y_c)

Why the other options are different quantities:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Normal depth** | The depth of **uniform flow**, set by the bed slope and roughness through Manning's equation |
| **Alternate depths** | The **two** depths having the **same specific energy** for a given discharge |
| **Sequent (conjugate) depths** | The two depths across a **hydraulic jump**, having the same **momentum** — not the same energy, since energy is lost in the jump |

The normal-versus-critical comparison classifies the channel slope: a **mild** slope has y_n > y_c, a **steep** slope y_n < y_c, and a **critical** slope y_n = y_c. That classification determines which surface profiles (M1, M2, S1 …) can occur, and hence where a hydraulic jump will form.

**Why critical flow matters practically.** Because the depth–discharge relation is unique at critical flow, a deliberately created critical section becomes a **flow-measuring device** — this is the principle of the **broad-crested weir, Venturi flume and Parshall flume**. And a transition from supercritical to subcritical flow can only occur through a **hydraulic jump**, which is what stilling basins are designed to contain.

examTip.trick: Setting **dE/dy = 0** for E = y + q²/(2gy²) gives **y_c³ = q²/g** — the depth of minimum specific energy, by definition the critical depth.
examTip.mnemonic: **y_c depends ONLY on q — not on slope, not on roughness.** That independence is exactly why critical-flow structures (broad-crested weir, Parshall flume) make reliable permanent gauges: their calibration does not drift as the channel silts or grows weed. Also **E_c = 1.5 y_c**.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, the minimum period of curing for concrete made with ordinary Portland cement is:
questions.solution:
**7 days** for ordinary Portland cement, and **at least 10 days** where mineral admixtures or blended cements are used.

IS 456 cl. 13.5 requires exposed surfaces to be kept **continuously in a damp or wet condition** for at least seven days from the date of placing. In hot and dry weather, or with blended cements, the period is extended — to **10 to 14 days** — because hydration is slower or moisture is lost faster.

**What curing actually does.** Cement gains strength by **hydration**, a chemical reaction that consumes water. If the concrete is allowed to dry, the reaction stops in the surface zone and cannot be restarted by wetting later. The consequences of poor curing are all concentrated where they matter most — at the surface:

| Consequence | Why |
|---|---|
| **Low strength**, particularly in the surface zone | Hydration incomplete |
| **Plastic and drying shrinkage cracking** | Rapid moisture loss while the concrete is weak |
| **High permeability** | Coarse, discontinuous pore structure |
| **Poor durability** — carbonation, chloride ingress, **corrosion of reinforcement** | A permeable cover offers little protection to the steel |
| Dusting and low abrasion resistance | Weak surface paste |

Note that durability, not strength, is usually the real casualty: the cover concrete is the reinforcement's only defence, and it is precisely the part that suffers when curing is skimped.

**Methods of curing:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Ponding** | Best for slabs and pavements |
| Wet covering — hessian, gunny bags, straw | Must be kept **continuously** damp, not allowed to dry between wettings |
| **Sprinkling / fogging** | Suits vertical surfaces |
| Membrane curing compounds | Where water is scarce; seals the surface |
| **Steam curing** | Precast work — accelerates early strength |
| Formwork left in place | Provides some protection but not moisture |

**A related figure worth pairing with this**, since the two are often confused: the **striking time for formwork** is a different requirement, governed by the strength the member has gained rather than by hydration of the surface. Vertical formwork may be removed after **16 to 24 hours**, but slab and beam **props** stay for 7 to 21 days depending on span — as tabulated in Set 2 Q38. Removing the shuttering does not end the obligation to cure.

Curing is the cheapest operation in concrete construction and the one most often neglected, which is why it appears so regularly in the examination.

examTip.trick: Curing keeps water available for **hydration**, which continues for months but is fastest in the first week. Seven days captures most of it for OPC.
examTip.mnemonic: **7 days for OPC, 10–14 days for blended cements and in hot weather** — mineral admixtures react more slowly, so they need longer. Inadequate curing is one of the commonest and most damaging site failures: it costs strength, and far more importantly it costs **surface durability**, where the cover concrete is exactly what protects the steel.

questions.stem: The self-weight of the structure and all permanently attached finishes constitute the:
questions.solution:
**Dead load.**

Dead load is the **permanent, stationary** load of the structure itself together with everything fixed to it: slabs, beams, columns and walls, plus floor finishes, plaster, ceilings, permanent partitions, fixed services and cladding.

Its defining feature is **predictability**. Because the dimensions and the materials are known, dead load can be computed accurately from unit weights — which is precisely why IS 456 applies a **lower partial safety factor** to it than to the more variable loads.

Unit weights worth carrying:

| Material | Unit weight (kN/m³) |
|---|---|
| **Reinforced concrete** | **25** |
| Plain concrete | 24 |
| Brick masonry | 19 – 20 |
| Stone masonry | 24 – 26 |
| Cement mortar / plaster | 20 |
| Steel | 78.5 |
| Timber | 6 – 9 |

The load types compared:

| Load | Character | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Dead** | **Permanent, predictable** | Self-weight, finishes — IS 875 Part 1 |
| **Imposed (live)** | **Movable, variable** — occupants, furniture, stored goods | IS 875 Part 2 |
| Wind | Variable, direction-dependent, often **suction** | IS 875 Part 3 |
| Snow | Variable, seasonal | IS 875 Part 4 |
| **Seismic** | **Inertial**, proportional to mass | IS 1893 / NBC 105 |

Typical imposed loads: **2 kN/m²** for residential floors, 3 to 4 kN/m² for offices and classrooms, and **0.75 kN/m²** on an inaccessible flat roof.

**Two points where dead load behaves unlike the others.**

First, **seismic force is generated by dead load**. The base shear is proportional to the **seismic weight** — the dead load plus a fraction of the imposed load — so in an earthquake-prone country reducing dead load directly reduces the force the structure must resist. That is a real argument for lightweight partitions and roofing in Nepal, and it is why heavy stone or mud-mortar construction performs so badly.

Second, dead load can be **stabilising** rather than destabilising — it resists overturning, sliding and uplift. Where that is the case IS 456 requires the dead load to be taken at a **reduced** value, **0.9 DL**, so that the design does not rely on weight that might not be there. That is the reverse of the usual 1.5 factor, and forgetting it is a common error in checking a retaining wall or a wind-uplift case.

examTip.trick: **Dead load** is permanent and does not move: self-weight, floor finishes, permanent partitions, fixed services. **Live (imposed) load** is variable — occupants, furniture, stored goods.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dead load DOMINATES in concrete construction** — self weight plus slab often exceeds the imposed load, which is why a preliminary design must include the structure's own weight from the outset. And note the **0.9 DL** combination: where dead load is **stabilising** (overturning, uplift), it is factored **DOWN**, not up.

questions.stem: Which layout of a water distribution system gives the best reliability of supply during a pipe breakdown?
questions.solution:
**Grid iron system.**

In a grid iron (interconnected or reticular) layout the mains and sub-mains form a **network of closed loops**, so water can reach any point by **more than one route**. If a pipe has to be shut off for a burst or a repair, supply continues to the surrounding area from the other direction. That redundancy is exactly what reliability means, and it is what the other layouts lack.

The four layouts compared:

| Layout | Arrangement | Reliability | Dead ends | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Dead end (tree)** | Branching mains, no loops | **Poor** — one break cuts off everything downstream | **Many** | **Lowest** |
| **Grid iron** | **Interconnected loops** | **Best** | **None** | **Highest** |
| Circular (ring) | A ring main round each district, fed from it | Good | Few | Moderate |
| Radial | Zones fed outward from central distribution reservoirs | Good; **best for pressure** | Few | Moderate |

**Why dead ends are undesirable beyond the reliability question.** Water stagnates at the end of a branch, so the **chlorine residual decays** and quality deteriorates; there is no through-flow to scour sediment, so deposits accumulate; and firefighting draw-off at the tip causes a severe pressure drop. Dead-end mains therefore need **scour valves** at each end and periodic flushing.

**Why grid iron is preferred despite its cost.** Alongside reliability it gives **better pressure distribution** (flow arrives from several directions, so head loss is shared), **higher fire-fighting capacity** at any point, and no stagnation. The penalties are more pipe length, more valves and a **harder hydraulic analysis** — the loops make the flow distribution indeterminate, requiring iterative solution by the **Hardy Cross method** (balancing heads round each loop) or by network software.

It suits a town laid out on a **rectangular street grid**, which is also what makes it convenient to construct.

**Design requirements that apply to any layout:** a residual pressure of about **7 to 17 m** of water at the consumer's tap; velocity between roughly 0.6 and 3 m/s; sluice valves at intervals so sections can be isolated; **air valves at summits** and **scour valves at low points**; and the whole network sized for the **maximum hourly demand plus fire demand**, the latter from a formula such as Kuchling's, Q = 3182√P.

examTip.trick: The **grid iron (reticular)** layout provides **multiple paths** to every point, so a burst main can be isolated without cutting off supply, and dead ends are eliminated.
examTip.mnemonic: **Grid iron: best reliability and no stagnation, but the most pipe and the hardest to analyse (needs Hardy Cross). Dead end (tree): cheapest and simplest, but one break cuts off everything beyond it, and dead ends stagnate.** Ring and radial systems sit between.

questions.stem: A hydropower plant operating under a head of more than 250 m is classified as a:
questions.solution:
**High head plant.**

Head is the primary basis on which hydropower plants are classified, because it dictates the type of turbine, the layout of the waterway and the character of the civil works:

| Classification | Head | Turbine | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Low head** | **< 30 m** | **Kaplan / propeller** (axial flow) | Large discharge, small head; barrage on a wide river |
| **Medium head** | **30 – 250 m** | **Francis** (mixed flow) | Balanced discharge and head |
| **High head** | **> 250 m** | **Pelton** (impulse) | **Small discharge, very large head**; long tunnel and penstock |

The relationship is not arbitrary — it follows from **specific speed**, N_s = N√P/H^{5/4}. A high head gives a low specific speed, which suits a Pelton wheel; a low head gives a high specific speed, which suits a Kaplan. That is why the turbine choice follows from the head almost automatically, as tested in Set 1 Q65.

**Why high-head schemes dominate in Nepal.** The Himalayan terrain drops enormous heights over short horizontal distances, so a large head can be developed by a **headrace tunnel along the valley side** and a steep penstock, without impounding a large reservoir. The power available is P = ηγQH, so a high H means the same power is obtained from a **much smaller Q** — which in turn means smaller intakes, tunnels and penstocks for a given output. That is the fundamental economic advantage of Nepal's topography.

The accompanying difficulties are equally characteristic: **high pressure** in the penstock (needing thick steel and careful water-hammer control, hence the surge tank of Q35), and severe **abrasion of the runner** by hard Himalayan sediment, since abrasion damage rises steeply with head — which is why settling basins are designed to remove particles down to 0.1 mm for a high-head Pelton, as in Q50 and Q70 of this paper.

**Classification by capacity** is a separate scheme and should not be confused with the head classes:

| Class | Capacity |
|---|---|
| **Micro** | up to 100 kW |
| Mini | 100 kW – 1 MW |
| Small | 1 – 10 MW |
| Medium | 10 – 300 MW |
| Large | above 300 MW |

Option (d), micro hydro, belongs to this second scheme — and micro hydro schemes, which have brought electricity to many remote Nepali villages, may operate at any head at all.

examTip.trick: Head bands: **low below about 30 m, medium 30–250 m, high above 250 m** — and the band chooses the turbine.
examTip.mnemonic: **High head → PELTON (impulse). Medium → Francis. Low → Kaplan.** Nepal's Himalayan streams are the classic high-head, low-flow case, which is why Pelton machines dominate. At 300 m the jet velocity is **√(2 × 9.81 × 300) ≈ 76 m/s**, and the runner runs at half that.

questions.stem: The ratio of the average load to the installed capacity of a power plant is called the:
questions.solution:
**Capacity factor.**

> **Capacity factor = average load / installed capacity**

It measures how fully the **plant that was built** is actually used, and it is the figure that matters most to an investor, because the capital cost was incurred on the installed capacity whether or not it is used.

The factors are all ratios of loads, and the trick is to keep straight which two quantities each compares:

| Factor | Definition | Measures |
|---|---|---|
| **Load factor** | **Average load / peak demand** | How **evenly** the demand is spread |
| **Capacity factor** | **Average load / installed capacity** | How fully the **plant** is used |
| **Utilisation factor** | **Peak demand / installed capacity** | How much of the plant the peak calls on |
| **Demand factor** | Peak demand / total connected load | Simultaneity of consumer demand |
| Diversity factor | Σ individual peaks / system peak | Spread of consumers' peaks |
| Plant use factor | Energy generated / (capacity × hours **in operation**) | Efficiency while running |

Note the relationship: **capacity factor = load factor × utilisation factor**, since (average/capacity) = (average/peak) × (peak/capacity). And the load factor and capacity factor **coincide** only when the peak demand exactly equals the installed capacity.

**Why this matters for Nepal specifically.** A **run-of-river** plant generates only what the river carries at that moment, and Himalayan flows in the dry season are a small fraction of monsoon flows. Its capacity factor is therefore low — often **40 to 60%** — even though the machinery is available all year. A **storage** scheme with the same installed capacity can hold monsoon water for release in winter, so it achieves a much higher capacity factor and delivers far more annual energy from the same nameplate rating.

That is the quantitative reason installed capacity and annual energy are different commodities, and why they are contracted and priced separately. It is also why **pondage** (Q43 of this paper) is added wherever the topography allows: it raises the daily flexibility, even though it cannot fix the seasonal deficit.

The calculation is the one performed in Set 2 Q68: **E = P × capacity factor × 8760 hours**, giving 441 TWh from 84 GW at a 60% factor.

examTip.trap: **Load factor** and **capacity factor** are constantly swapped — both are ratios of the average load, but to **different denominators**.
examTip.trick: **Load factor = average load ÷ MAXIMUM DEMAND** (how evenly the plant is used). **Capacity factor = average load ÷ INSTALLED CAPACITY** (how fully it is used).
