examTip.mnemonic: **Load factor: how EVENLY. Capacity factor: how FULLY.** Both ≤ 1. And **diversity factor** is the odd one out — the sum of individual maximum demands ÷ the system maximum, always **greater than 1**, because consumers do not all peak together.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a mode of failure of a gravity dam?
questions.solution:
**Buckling.**

A gravity dam is a **massive** structure — its stability comes from its own weight, and its cross-section is enormously thick relative to its height. Buckling is a **slenderness** phenomenon, affecting long thin compression members; it simply cannot arise in a body of this proportion. The other three are all genuine and checked in every design.

The modes of failure of a gravity dam:

| Mode | Mechanism | Check |
|---|---|---|
| **Overturning** | Rotation about the downstream toe under water thrust | Resultant must fall **within the middle third** of the base |
| **Sliding** | Horizontal translation along the base or a weak seam | **Shear friction factor** ≥ 4 to 5 |
| **Tension / cracking** | Tension developing at the heel when the resultant falls outside the middle third | **No tension permitted** at the heel |
| **Crushing** | Compressive stress exceeding the strength of concrete or rock | σ_max ≤ permissible |
| **Piping** | Progressive erosion of foundation material by **seepage** | Uplift pressure, cut-offs, **drainage gallery** |

**The two elementary stability criteria** are worth stating precisely, because they carry most of the design:

> **Against overturning:** FoS = ΣM_resisting / ΣM_overturning ≥ **1.5**
> **Against sliding:** FoS = μ ΣV / ΣH ≥ **1.0**, with the shear friction factor ≥ 4–5

and the **middle-third rule**: if the resultant of all forces passes within the middle third of the base, the whole base remains in compression and no tension develops at the heel. Since concrete is weak in tension and a crack at the heel would admit water and raise the uplift, avoiding tension is the governing requirement for the profile.

**Uplift pressure** deserves emphasis because it is the mechanism candidates most often underestimate. Water seeping through the foundation acts **upward** on the base, reducing the effective weight and therefore reducing resistance to both overturning and sliding. It is countered by an upstream **cut-off wall or grout curtain** and by a **drainage gallery** with relief holes, which intercept the seepage and lower the uplift diagram — the same principle as the exit-gradient control examined in Set 2 Q56 under Bligh's and Khosla's theories.

Where a slender element *does* exist in a dam — a **buttress** dam's inclined deck and supporting buttresses, or an arch dam's thin shell — buckling and local stability genuinely must be checked. But not in a solid gravity section.

examTip.trap: Read the **NOT**. Buckling is a **slender member** failure — a gravity dam is a massive block and cannot buckle.
examTip.trick: A gravity dam's real failure modes are **overturning, sliding, crushing (excessive compressive stress) and tension at the heel**.
examTip.mnemonic: **No tension at the heel is the requirement that shapes the section** — the resultant must stay within the **middle third**. A crack at the heel would admit **full reservoir pressure into the crack**, which then propagates. And **UPLIFT** is the force most often underestimated, which is why a drainage gallery is provided.

questions.stem: In an earthen dam, the top flow line of the seepage through the body of the dam is called the:
questions.solution:
**Phreatic line**, also called the **seepage line** or top flow line.

Water seeping through the body of an earthen dam has a free upper surface at **atmospheric pressure**. That surface is the phreatic line: it is the uppermost flow line of the seepage, and it separates the saturated soil below from the unsaturated soil above.

**Its defining property** is what makes it useful: along the phreatic line the pressure is atmospheric, so **p = 0** and therefore the total head equals the **elevation** at every point on it. Each point where an equipotential line meets the phreatic line is thus at a known elevation, which is precisely what allows the flow net inside the dam to be drawn.

**How it is located.** Casagrande showed that the phreatic line is very nearly a **base parabola**, with its focus at the downstream toe of the drainage filter, corrected at the entry and exit points:
- At the **upstream face** the line must enter **perpendicular** to the face, since the upstream face is an equipotential.
- At the **downstream** end the exit condition depends on the drainage arrangement provided.

**Why it matters — the whole reason it is drawn:**

| Consequence | Why the phreatic line governs it |
|---|---|
| **Pore pressure and effective stress** | The saturated zone below the line has reduced effective stress, hence reduced shear strength |
| **Downstream slope stability** | This is the critical case; recall from Set 2 Q45 that steady seepage roughly **halves** the factor of safety of a slope |
| **Seepage discharge** | Computed from the flow net bounded above by the phreatic line |
| **Piping and sloughing** | If the line emerges on the downstream **face** rather than into a filter, the exiting water erodes the slope |

That last point is the design imperative: the phreatic line **must not** intersect the downstream face. It is kept inside the dam by providing a **horizontal drainage blanket, rock toe, or chimney (inclined) filter** so that seepage is intercepted and led safely away. Graded **inverted filters** ensure the water escapes while the soil particles do not.

Why the other options are wrong: the **hydraulic grade line** and **energy line** are terms from pipe and channel hydraulics (their difference is the velocity head, as in Q16 of this paper); an **equipotential line** is a line of constant total head, and the phreatic line is not one — its head varies along it, since its elevation varies.

examTip.trick: The phreatic line is the **top streamline**, and the **pore pressure on it is atmospheric** — so the pressure head is zero and the total head equals the elevation. That boundary condition is what makes the flow net solvable.
examTip.mnemonic: **Keep the phreatic line INSIDE the dam.** If it emerges on the downstream face, the face saturates and sloughs — which is exactly why a **downstream filter drain or rock toe** is provided, to draw the line safely back down inside the section.

questions.stem: Cavitation in a reaction turbine is most likely to occur at the:
options: Outlet of the runner and inlet of the draft tube
questions.solution:
**At the outlet of the runner and the inlet of the draft tube** — the point of **lowest pressure** in the machine.

**Why cavitation happens there.** In a reaction turbine the pressure falls continuously as water passes through the runner, converting pressure energy into work. The minimum pressure is therefore reached just as the water leaves the runner and enters the draft tube. If that pressure falls to the **vapour pressure** of water, vapour bubbles form; they are then carried into the higher-pressure region of the draft tube and **collapse violently**, and the repeated implosions against the blade and liner surfaces cause:

- **Pitting and erosion** of the runner blades and draft tube liner;
- **Noise and vibration**;
- A **fall in efficiency** and in power output, since the flow passage is disrupted.

**The governing parameter** is **Thoma's cavitation factor**:

> **σ = (H_a − H_v − H_s) / H**

where H_a is the atmospheric head, H_v the vapour pressure head, **H_s the suction head** (the height of the runner above the tailwater) and H the net head. Cavitation is avoided by keeping σ above the **critical value σ_c** for that turbine's specific speed — a value read from published curves and rising with specific speed, so Kaplan turbines are more cavitation-prone than Francis.

**The practical remedies** follow directly from the formula:
- **Lower the runner setting** — reduce H_s, even setting the runner *below* tailwater level, which makes H_s negative and raises σ. This is the principal control.
- Note that H_a **falls with altitude**, so a turbine at high elevation in Nepal has less margin and must be set lower than the same machine in the plains.
- Use **cavitation-resistant materials** — stainless steel runners, or stainless overlay on the vulnerable zones.
- Provide a properly proportioned **draft tube**, which recovers pressure gradually and raises the pressure at runner exit.
- Avoid prolonged operation far from the design point, where flow separation lowers local pressures.

Why the other options are wrong: the **spiral casing** and **guide vanes** (a, b) are the high-pressure end of the machine, where cavitation cannot occur. A **nozzle** (d) belongs to an impulse turbine — and a **Pelton wheel runs at atmospheric pressure throughout**, discharging freely into the tailrace, so it needs no draft tube and is essentially free of cavitation. That is one of the practical advantages of impulse machines at very high heads.

examTip.trick: Cavitation strikes where the **pressure is lowest**, and in a reaction turbine that is at the **runner exit / draft tube inlet**, downstream of all the energy extraction.
examTip.mnemonic: **Thoma's cavitation parameter σ = (H_atm − H_vapour − H_suction)/H compares the plant against a critical value.** The practical control is the **setting level** — placing the runner low enough (sometimes below tailwater) that the pressure never reaches vapour pressure. **At altitude H_atm is lower, so the permitted setting is lower** — a real constraint in Nepal.

questions.stem: The function of a governor in a hydro turbine is to:
options: Maintain constant speed irrespective of load variation
Increase the head available at the turbine
Prevent cavitation at the runner outlet
questions.solution:
**To maintain a constant speed irrespective of load variation.**

A generator's output **frequency** is fixed by the speed of the shaft:

> f = N·P/120,  so **N = 120 f / P**

with P the number of poles. To hold the frequency at 50 Hz the turbine must run at exactly its synchronous speed, whatever the electrical load happens to be.

**The problem the governor solves.** If load is suddenly thrown off, the turbine is still receiving the same water power but has less resistance, so it **accelerates**. If load is added, it **decelerates**. Either way the frequency drifts, which is unacceptable to the system and, in the extreme, dangerous to the machine.

**How it works.** The governor senses the shaft speed — traditionally by a centrifugal flyball mechanism, now electronically — and adjusts the **flow of water** to match the load:
- In a **Francis or Kaplan** turbine it rotates the **wicket (guide) vanes** to open or close the flow passage.
- In a **Pelton** wheel it moves the **spear (needle) valve** in the nozzle, and for rapid load rejection also operates a **deflector or jet deflector** to throw the jet clear of the buckets.

That last device matters because of the conflict at the heart of governing: closing the water passage quickly is exactly what generates **water hammer** in the penstock. The deflector allows the *jet* to be diverted instantly while the *valve* closes slowly — protecting both the speed and the pipe. On reaction turbines the same conflict is managed by the **surge tank** (Q35 of this paper) and by pressure relief valves.

**Runaway speed** is the related quantity examined alongside: the speed the turbine would reach if the load were lost entirely and the governor failed to act. It is roughly **1.8 times** the normal speed for a Pelton, **2.0 to 2.2** for a Francis, and **2.5 to 3.0** for a Kaplan. The generator rotor and the whole rotating assembly must be designed to survive it.

Why the other options belong to different components: head is fixed by the **site and the waterway**, not by any control device; sediment is removed by a **settling basin** (Q50 and Q70); and cavitation is controlled by the **runner setting and draft tube** (Q95).

examTip.trick: Generator frequency is tied to rotational speed, so the speed must be held constant as the electrical load varies. The governor senses speed and adjusts the **flow** — moving the guide vanes or the spear valve.
examTip.mnemonic: **Governor = speed control = frequency control.** It is also the origin of the **water hammer** problem: a sudden load rejection makes the governor close the gates fast, and the decelerating water column generates the surge. That is why the **surge tank and the governor timing are designed together**.

questions.stem: The CBR value of a soil is expressed as a percentage of the standard load required for:
questions.solution:
**Crushed stone** — the standard reference material.

The **California Bearing Ratio** compares the load a soil can carry against a plunger with the load that a **standard crushed stone** base carries at the same penetration:

> **CBR (%) = (test load / standard load) × 100**

The standard loads for the reference crushed stone are:

| Penetration | Standard load |
|---|---|
| **2.5 mm** | **1370 kg** (13.44 kN) |
| **5.0 mm** | **2055 kg** (20.15 kN) |

The CBR is computed at **both** penetrations and the **higher value is reported**. If the 5 mm value comes out higher, the test is repeated; if it is confirmed, that higher value is taken.

**Test conditions:** a plunger of **50 mm** diameter is driven at **1.25 mm/minute** into a specimen compacted in a 150 mm mould, with surcharge weights simulating the pavement above. For design the specimen is **soaked for four days** before testing, to represent the worst moisture condition the subgrade will experience in the monsoon — a critical requirement in Nepal, and one that is sometimes skipped in practice with serious consequences.

**Typical values:**

| Material | CBR |
|---|---|
| Soft clay | 2 – 5% |
| Silty / sandy subgrade | 5 – 10% |
| Good granular subgrade | 10 – 20% |
| Sub-base | 20 – 30% |
| **Granular base course** | **> 80%** |

**Why it is the central test in pavement design.** A **flexible pavement** transmits load to the subgrade by grain-to-grain contact, so its required thickness is governed by the strength of the subgrade beneath. IRC 37 and the DoR guidelines fix the pavement composition from two inputs: the **subgrade CBR** and the **cumulative standard axles (CSA)** — the latter computed with the vehicle damage factor and the lane distribution factor of Q68 of this paper. A weak subgrade demands a thicker pavement; raising the CBR by stabilisation or by importing a better capping layer can be cheaper than adding thickness.

Note the contrast with **rigid** pavements, which are designed on the **modulus of subgrade reaction k** through Westergaard's analysis rather than on CBR, because a concrete slab carries load by flexure rather than by spreading it through layers.

examTip.trick: **CBR = (test load ÷ standard load) × 100**, and the standard load is the value for a **standard crushed stone** at the same penetration (1370 kg at 2.5 mm, 2055 kg at 5 mm).
examTip.mnemonic: **CBR is a RATIO against crushed stone, expressed as a percentage — so crushed stone itself is 100%.** Take the value at **2.5 mm** normally; if the 5 mm value is higher, repeat the test, and if it repeats, use the 5 mm value. CBR is soaked for 4 days to model the worst monsoon condition.

questions.stem: Points through which the highway alignment must necessarily pass are called:
questions.solution:
**Obligatory points.**

An alignment is not free to take the shortest or cheapest route: certain locations either **must** be included or **must** be avoided, and these constraints are settled first, before the alignment between them is optimised. They fall into two classes:

| Type | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Points through which the alignment must pass** | An intermediate **town or village** to be served; a **bridge site** at a narrow, stable river crossing with good foundations; a **mountain pass** or saddle; an existing **industrial or tourist** centre |
| **Points the alignment must avoid** | Marshy or **unstable ground**; deep cuttings and landslide-prone slopes; religious and cultural sites; **forest and protected areas**; costly land and dense settlement |

**A bridge site is the classic obligatory point**, and worth understanding as the example. A river crossing demands a straight, square approach, a stable channel and sound foundations — conditions met at only a few places along a river. The bridge site is therefore fixed first, and the road is aligned **to** it, not the other way round. The same applies to a mountain pass, where the topography permits a crossing at one elevation and nowhere else.

**The requirements of a good alignment**, against which the route between obligatory points is judged:

| Requirement | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Short** | Directness reduces cost and travel time |
| **Easy** | To construct and maintain; gradients and curves within standards for the terrain |
| **Safe** | Adequate sight distance; stable slopes and embankments |
| **Economical** | Least total of construction, maintenance and vehicle operating cost |

Those four often conflict — the shortest route through hills may be neither easy nor safe — and reconciling them is the substance of alignment design.

**How the alignment is actually settled** follows the four survey stages of Set 1 Q47: **map study** (obligatory points identified on topographic sheets), **reconnaissance** (routes inspected in the field), **preliminary survey** (alternatives surveyed in detail, including the soil and materials survey), and **final location**.

In Nepal's hill terrain the dominant additional constraints are **slope stability and drainage** — an alignment that ignores geology may be short and cheap to build and then require rebuilding after every monsoon. That is why the geological and soil investigation carries so much weight at the preliminary stage.

examTip.trick: **Obligatory points** are of two kinds, and they pull in opposite directions: points the alignment **must pass through** (a bridge site, a mountain pass, an intermediate town) and points it **must avoid** (a lake, a religious site, unstable ground).
examTip.mnemonic: **Obligatory points fix the alignment before any curve is drawn.** In Nepal the two that dominate are the **bridge crossing site** (chosen for a straight, stable reach) and the **pass or saddle** — and the road is then designed backwards from those fixed points.

questions.stem: In first angle projection, the top view of an object is placed:
options: To the left of the front view
To the right of the front view
questions.solution:
**Below the front view.**

In **first angle** projection the object is imagined to lie **between the observer and the plane of projection**, so each view is pushed *through* the object onto the plane behind it. The consequence is that every view appears on the side **opposite** to the direction from which it was seen:

| View | Direction of viewing | Position on the drawing |
|---|---|---|
| Front elevation | From the front | Reference position |
| **Top view (plan)** | From **above** | **Below** the front view |
| Bottom view | From below | Above the front view |
| **Left side view** | From the **left** | **Right** of the front view |
| Right side view | From the right | Left of the front view |

The two conventions are **mirror opposites**, and this is the single most important comparison in the subject:

| | **First angle** | **Third angle** |
|---|---|---|
| Object lies | **Between observer and plane** | **Plane between observer and object** |
| Top view | **Below** front view | **Above** front view |
| Left side view | **Right** of front view | **Left** of front view |
| Used in | **India, Nepal, Europe** (ISO) | **USA, Canada, Australia** |

So in third angle projection each view sits on the **same** side as the direction of viewing, which is the more intuitive arrangement — and precisely why confusing the two is so dangerous. A component read in the wrong convention comes out **mirror-imaged**, and it will be manufactured wrong.

To prevent exactly that, the convention in use must be declared in the **title block** by a standard symbol — a truncated cone shown in the two views, whose arrangement differs between the systems. Never interpret an unfamiliar drawing without checking that symbol.

**Related conventions worth carrying:** the four **quadrants** are formed by the horizontal and vertical planes; only the **first and third** are used, because in the second and fourth the views would overlap when the planes are rotated into one plane. Dimensions are always in **millimetres** without repeating the unit, the **filing margin** is 20 mm on the left edge, and hidden edges are shown by **dashed** lines while centre lines are **thin chain** lines — as tested in Q4 of this paper.

examTip.trap: First and third angle projection place the views on **opposite sides**, and the two systems are the standard confusion.
examTip.trick: **First angle: the view is projected THROUGH the object onto a plane behind it**, so the top view lands **below** the front view. **Third angle: the plane is between the observer and the object**, so the top view lands **above**.
examTip.mnemonic: **First angle (Indian/European): top view BELOW. Third angle (American): top view ABOVE.** Every drawing must carry the projection **symbol** in its title block — because a drawing read in the wrong system is a mirror image of the intended part.

questions.stem: The bid security (earnest money) deposited by a bidder is primarily intended to:
options: Cover the cost of preparing the tender documents
Guarantee the quality of the completed work
Serve as an advance payment for the work
Discourage frivolous bids and secure the bidder's commitment
questions.solution:
**To discourage frivolous bids and secure the bidder's commitment.**

Bid security — **earnest money** — is a sum lodged with the tender, in cash or as a bank guarantee, that the employer may **forfeit** if the bidder misbehaves. Its whole purpose is to make a bid a serious undertaking rather than a costless option.

**It is forfeited if the bidder:**
- **withdraws** the bid during its period of validity;
- **refuses to sign** the contract after being awarded it;
- fails to furnish the required **performance security**.

The amount is typically **2 to 3% of the estimated cost**, and it is **returned** to unsuccessful bidders once the contract is awarded, and to the successful bidder once the performance security is furnished.

Why the other options are wrong — each names a different instrument, and the distinction is the substance of the question:

| Instrument | Purpose | Typical amount |
|---|---|---|
| **Bid security (earnest money)** | **Commitment to the bid** | **2 – 3%** of estimated cost |
| **Performance security** | **Guarantee of performance of the contract** | **5 – 10%** of contract price |
| **Retention money** | Withheld from each payment against defects | 5 – 10% of each bill |
| **Mobilisation advance** | An **advance payment** to start work, against a bank guarantee | 10 – 20%, recovered from bills |
| Defect liability / maintenance bond | Covers defects during the liability period | Part of retention |

So **option (c)** describes a **mobilisation advance** and **option (b)** the **performance security and retention money**. Bid security guarantees nothing about the *work* — it is spent and returned before construction begins.

**Why it matters to the procurement process.** Without bid security, a contractor could bid absurdly low to win, then withdraw on discovering the error, forcing the employer to re-tender and lose months. The deposit puts a price on that behaviour. It also filters out bidders without the financial standing to raise even a bank guarantee.

In Nepal these requirements are set by the **Public Procurement Act 2063 and Regulations 2064** and the PPMO standard bidding documents, which also fix the **bid validity period**, the evaluation criteria, and the grounds on which a bid may be rejected as **non-responsive**.

examTip.trick: Bid security is forfeited if a bidder **withdraws during the validity period** or **refuses to sign** the contract after award — so it makes a bid a serious commitment rather than a free option.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bid security (1–3% of the estimate) commits the BID; PERFORMANCE security (5–10% of the contract) commits the WORK; retention money (5–10% of each payment) covers DEFECTS.** Three securities, three stages, three different risks.
